cards.subject: arts
cards.title: The Mona Lisa became world-famous after it was stolen
lines: 1911: Vincenzo Peruggia, a former Louvre worker, walked out with it under his smock.
Newspapers worldwide ran the story; crowds came to stare at the empty space.
*It was recovered in Florence in 1913. Before the theft, it was respected but not iconic.*

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: Linear perspective
lines: Around 1415, Brunelleschi demonstrated a geometric way to show depth: parallel lines meet at a vanishing point.
Painters like Masaccio quickly adopted it.
*It's projective geometry, centuries before mathematicians formalised it.*

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: Van Gogh sold only one painting in his lifetime.
reveal: The Red Vineyard is the best-documented sale, but there's evidence of a few other sales and trades.
His fame really came after his death in 1890, helped by his sister-in-law Jo van Gogh-Bonger.

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: "Impressionism" started as mockery
cards.cliff: Duchamp's urinal changed what art means
lines: 1874: critic Louis Leroy titled a review after Monet's Impression, Sunrise, sneering at its sketchiness.
The painters adopted the label.
*Portable paint tubes, invented in the 1840s, helped them paint outdoors.*

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: Fountain, 1917
lines: Marcel Duchamp submitted a factory urinal signed "R. Mutt" to an exhibition that promised to accept everything.
It was rejected anyway.
*A 2004 poll of art experts named it the most influential modern artwork.*

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: An octave is a frequency doubling
lines: A440 Hz to A880 Hz is one octave up.
Pleasing intervals are simple ratios: a fifth is 3:2, a fourth 4:3.
*Pythagoras is said to have discovered this with strings of different lengths.*

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: Why a piano is slightly out of tune on purpose
lines: Stacking twelve perfect 3:2 fifths overshoots seven octaves by a small amount (the Pythagorean comma).
Equal temperament splits the octave into 12 equal steps of 2^(1/12) each.
*Every interval except the octave is a tiny bit off, but every key works equally.*

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: Beethoven conducted the Ninth unable to hear the applause
lines: By 1824 Beethoven was almost completely deaf.
At the Ninth Symphony's premiere, a singer turned him around to see the audience applauding.
*He composed by imagining sound, and by feeling vibrations.*

cards.subject: arts
cards.title: Four minutes and thirty-three seconds of "silence"
lines: John Cage's 1952 piece has a performer play nothing for its duration.
The music is the ambient sound in the room: coughs, rustles, rain.
*Cage had visited an anechoic chamber and still heard his own body, so concluded there's no true silence.*

cards.subject: lang
cards.title: There are about 7,000 languages
cards.cliff: Your language may shape how you think, a little
lines: Around half are endangered, with few or no children learning them.
Papua New Guinea alone has over 800.
*A language is lost roughly every few months, by some estimates.*

cards.subject: lang
cards.title: Linguistic relativity, the moderate version
cards.cliff: English spelling is chaotic for historical reasons
lines: The strong claim (language determines thought) is mostly rejected.
But some effects are real: Russian speakers, who have separate basic words for light and dark blue, distinguish those shades slightly faster.
*Kuuk Thaayorre speakers use compass directions instead of left and right, and stay oriented remarkably well.*

cards.subject: lang
cards.title: Why is "knight" spelled with a k and gh?
reveal: Old and Middle English pronounced the k and a throaty gh sound. Spelling was largely fixed by printing.
options: Both were once pronounced; spelling froze before pronunciation changed
French scribes added them for decoration

cards.subject: lang
cards.title: The Rosetta Stone
cards.cliff: Linear B was solved by an architect
lines: Found by French soldiers in 1799, it bears one decree in hieroglyphic, demotic Egyptian and ancient Greek.
Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs, announcing his breakthrough in 1822.
*He reportedly shouted "Je tiens l'affaire!" and fainted.*

cards.subject: lang
cards.title: An architect deciphered Linear B
lines: Michael Ventris, an architect and amateur, showed in 1952 that the Bronze Age script Linear B wrote an early form of Greek.
Many experts had assumed it wasn't Greek at all.
*Linear A, an older related script, is still undeciphered.*

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Wegener was mocked for continental drift
cards.cliff: Earth's core is as hot as the Sun's surface
lines: 1912: Alfred Wegener argued continents move, citing matching coastlines and fossils across oceans.
Geologists rejected it: he had no mechanism.
*Plate tectonics, confirmed in the 1960s from seafloor magnetic stripes, proved him broadly right. He'd died in Greenland in 1930.*

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Roughly how hot is Earth's inner core?
reveal: Comparable to the surface of the Sun. It's solid because of the immense pressure.

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: The deepest hole ever drilled is 12 km
lines: The Soviet Kola Superdeep Borehole reached about 12.3 km by 1989.
Rock temperatures reached about 180°C, much hotter than expected.
*That's about 0.2% of the way to Earth's centre.*

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Measured from base to peak, which mountain is tallest?
reveal: Mauna Kea rises about 10,200 m from the ocean floor, though only about 4,200 m above sea level.
Everest has the highest summit above sea level. Chimborazo's summit is farthest from Earth's centre.

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Weather vs climate
cards.cliff: The greenhouse effect was measured in the 1850s
lines: Weather: the atmosphere today. Climate: the long-term statistics, usually over 30 years.
"Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get."
*A cold week doesn't disprove a warming trend.*

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Eunice Foote and John Tyndall
cards.cliff: CO₂ levels are measured on a Hawaiian volcano
lines: 1856: Eunice Foote showed that CO₂ trapped heat in sunlit glass cylinders.
1859: John Tyndall precisely measured how CO₂ and water vapour absorb infrared.
*The physics of greenhouse warming is over 160 years old.*

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: The Keeling Curve
lines: Since 1958, CO₂ has been measured continuously at Mauna Loa, Hawaii.
It climbs every year, with a seasonal wiggle as Northern Hemisphere plants grow and decay.
*Levels rose from about 315 ppm in 1958 to over 420 ppm today.*

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Seasons aren't caused by distance from the Sun
cards.cliff: The Moon always shows us the same face
lines: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4°. Summer is when your hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.
Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
*That's why Australia has summer at Christmas.*

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Tidal locking
lines: The Moon rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.
Earth's tides gradually synchronised it.
*The Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 cm a year,* measured with lasers bounced off Apollo reflectors.

cards.subject: earth
cards.title: Light from the Andromeda galaxy, visible to the naked eye, left it about how long ago?
reveal: It's the most distant object most people can see without a telescope.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Your stomach lining replaces itself every few days
cards.cliff: Your blood vessels could circle the Earth
lines: Stomach acid has a pH around 1.5–3.5: strong enough to dissolve some metals.
A protective mucus layer and fast cell turnover stop it digesting you.
*Barry Marshall drank a culture of H. pylori in 1984 to prove bacteria cause ulcers. Nobel Prize, 2005.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Laid end to end, roughly how long are an adult's blood vessels?
cards.cliff: Bones are stronger than steel, by weight
reveal: Most of it is capillaries, each thinner than a hair. Estimates vary, but around 100,000 km is often cited.
That's about two and a half times around the Earth.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Bone: lightweight and self-repairing
lines: Bone's strength-to-weight ratio rivals some steels, and unlike steel it repairs itself.
Your skeleton is gradually remodelled throughout life; estimates suggest roughly 10% a year in adults.
*Astronauts lose bone mass in microgravity because bones respond to load.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: You shrink during the day
cards.cliff: Your nose can detect many smells
lines: The discs between your vertebrae compress while you're upright.
Most people are about 1 cm taller in the morning.
*Astronauts in orbit grow up to about 3% taller, then shrink back on Earth.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: How many smells can you detect?
lines: A 2014 study claimed humans can distinguish over a trillion odours.
Other researchers disputed the maths; the true number is uncertain.
*Either way, the old "10,000 smells" figure had no solid basis.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
cards.cliff: You don't need 8 glasses of water a day
reveal: Double-blind studies have repeatedly found no effect of sugar on children's behaviour.
Parents who were told their child had sugar rated them as more hyperactive, even when they'd had none.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Everyone needs to drink eight glasses of water a day on top of everything else.
reveal: Food and other drinks provide much of your water. Needs vary with size, activity and climate.
Thirst is a decent guide for most healthy people.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Is breakfast the most important meal?
lines: The phrase was popularised by cereal marketing in the early 1900s.
Randomised trials haven't shown that eating breakfast causes weight loss.
*Eat it if it suits you. It isn't magic.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: A calorie is a unit of energy
lines: A food calorie (kcal) is the energy to heat 1 kg of water by 1°C.
Bomb calorimeters burn food to measure it; digestion extracts less from some foods, like nuts.
*Weight change follows energy balance, but hunger and metabolism respond, which makes it hard.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Exercise grows new brain cells (in animals) and helps memory
lines: Aerobic exercise increases BDNF, a protein that supports neuron growth.
Studies in older adults found a year of walking enlarged the hippocampus slightly.
*It's one of the best-supported ways to protect memory.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: The muscle soreness you feel a day or two after exercise is caused by lactic acid build-up.
reveal: Lactate clears within about an hour after exercise.
Delayed-onset muscle soreness comes from microscopic damage and the inflammation that repairs it.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: VO₂ max: your aerobic engine size
lines: The maximum rate your body can use oxygen, in ml per kg per minute.
Untrained adults: around 35–45. Elite endurance athletes: 70–90.
*Higher VO₂ max is strongly associated with longer life.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Some people can taste a chemical others can't
cards.cliff: Coriander tastes of soap to some
lines: PTC tastes intensely bitter to some people and like nothing to others.
The difference is largely down to one gene, TAS2R38.
*It was discovered by accident in 1931 when a chemist's lab partner complained about the bitter dust.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Why coriander tastes like soap to some people
lines: A variant near olfactory receptor genes, including OR6A2, is linked to detecting soapy-smelling aldehydes in coriander.
Rates vary by population, from a few percent to over a fifth.
*It's partly genetic, partly familiarity.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Roughly how much Neanderthal DNA do people of non-African descent carry?
reveal: Interbreeding happened as modern humans spread out of Africa.
Some of those genes affect immunity and skin.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: The recurrent laryngeal nerve takes a detour
lines: It runs from the brain, down into the chest, loops under a major blood vessel, and back up to the larynx.
In giraffes, that's a detour of several metres.
*Evolution tinkers with what exists: in fish ancestors the route was direct.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: The vertebrate eye is wired inside out
cards.cliff: Hiccups may be a fishy leftover
lines: Light passes through nerve fibres and blood vessels before reaching photoreceptors.
That's what creates the blind spot.
*Octopus eyes evolved separately and have the wiring behind the receptors: no blind spot.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Hiccups might be an evolutionary leftover
lines: One hypothesis links hiccups to the reflex tadpoles use to push water over their gills while blocking the airway.
It's speculative, but the nerve pathways involved are ancient.
*The record for continuous hiccups: about 68 years (Charles Osborne).*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Eiffel Tower grows in summer
lines: Thermal expansion makes the iron tower around 15 cm taller on hot days.
It was meant to be temporary, built for the 1889 World's Fair, and survived partly as a radio antenna.
*Many Parisian artists signed a petition against it before it was built.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why suspension bridges can be so long
lines: Cables in pure tension carry the deck's weight to tall towers and anchorages.
Steel is far stronger in tension than stone is in compression over long spans.
*The longest spans exceed 2 km (Çanakkale, Turkey, 2022).*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: How tall is the Burj Khalifa?
cards.cliff: The Panama Canal lifts ships over a continent
reveal: Completed 2010. Its Y-shaped plan helps disrupt wind vortices.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Panama Canal is a water elevator
lines: Locks raise ships about 26 m to Gatun Lake, then lower them on the other side.
Each transit uses around 200 million litres of fresh water from the lake.
*Droughts in 2023 forced limits on how many ships could pass.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: How a microwave oven heats food
lines: Microwaves at about 2.45 GHz make water molecules rotate back and forth, generating heat.
Food heats unevenly because of standing-wave hot spots: that's why there's a turntable.
*Percy Spencer noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket near a radar magnetron in 1945.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A rainbow is a circle centred opposite the Sun
lines: Sunlight refracts into raindrops, reflects off the back, and exits at about 42° for red, 40° for violet.
Every observer sees their own rainbow from different drops.
*From a plane you can sometimes see the full circle.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why ice is slippery is still debated
lines: The old explanation, pressure melting, doesn't produce enough melting at normal temperatures.
Current explanations focus on a thin, liquid-like layer on the ice surface, and friction heating.
*A surprisingly unsettled question for something so familiar.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Magnus effect
cards.cliff: Why the sea is blue and salty
lines: A spinning ball drags air around with it, deflecting the airflow and pushing the ball sideways.
Roberto Carlos's 1997 free kick curved dramatically around a wall.
*Tennis topspin dives for the same reason.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why is the sea salty?
lines: Rain slowly weathers rocks, carrying dissolved minerals to the sea.
Water evaporates; the salt stays.
*About 3.5% salt by mass on average.*

reveal: Quotient rule: ((x² + 1) − 2x²)/(x² + 1)².

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f(x) = x³ − 12x. On [−3, 3], what's the absolute maximum?
reveal: Critical points x = ±2: f(−2) = 16, f(2) = −16. Endpoints: f(−3) = 9, f(3) = −9.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A particle has v(t) = 3t² − 6t. Displacement from t = 0 to t = 3?
reveal: Back where it started, though it travelled a distance of 8.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx ∫ₓ^(x²) sin t dt = ?
reveal: FTC with both limits variable: upper limit term minus lower limit term.

cards.subject: maths

cards.subject: maths

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫₀^∞ x e^(−x) dx = ?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ sec²x tan x dx = ?
reveal: u = tan x, du = sec²x dx.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Does ∫₁^∞ 1/x^1.01 dx converge?
reveal: p = 1.01 > 1. It converges (to 100), just barely.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Does Σ n/(n² + 1) converge?
reveal: Limit comparison with 1/n, which diverges.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Does Σ 1/2ⁿ · n converge? (Σ n/2ⁿ)
reveal: Ratio test gives 1/2 < 1. The exact sum is 2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Radius of convergence of Σ (x − 3)ⁿ/(n·4ⁿ)?
reveal: Ratio test: |x − 3|/4 < 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Maclaurin series of 1/(1 + x²) starts…
reveal: Geometric series with ratio −x².

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Σ from n=0 to ∞ of xⁿ/n! evaluated at x = ln 3?
reveal: That's e^x at x = ln 3.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Σ from n=1 to ∞ of 1/(n(n + 1)) = ?
reveal: Telescoping: 1/n − 1/(n + 1). Everything cancels except the first 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Taylor series of cos x about 0: the coefficient of x⁴?
reveal: cos x = 1 − x²/2 + x⁴/24 − …

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Which test settles Σ (−1)ⁿ/ln(n) for n ≥ 2?
reveal: 1/ln n decreases to 0. It converges, but not absolutely.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f(x, y) = e^(xy). f_x = ?
reveal: Treat y as a constant.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: curl of F = (y, −x, 0)?
reveal: z-component: ∂(−x)/∂x − ∂y/∂y = −1 − 1 = −2.
It rotates clockwise.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∮ (x dy − y dx) around the unit circle = ?
reveal: Green: ∬ (1 + 1) dA = 2 × π. In general ½∮(x dy − y dx) is the enclosed area.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Volume of the region under z = 4 − x² − y² and above z = 0?
reveal: Polar: ∫₀^2π ∫₀² (4 − r²) r dr dθ = 2π(8 − 4) = 8π.

cards.subject: maths

reveal: Divergence theorem: div F = 3 times volume 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A function is a machine with one rule: one input, exactly one output.
cards.cliff: Everything in calculus is about how these machines change
lines: Feed it 3, get 9. Feed it 3 again, still 9. That's f(x) = x².
A circle x² + y² = 1 is *not* a function of x: x = 0 gives y = 1 and y = −1.
Vertical line test: if any vertical line hits the graph twice, it fails.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Which of these is a function of x?
cards.cliff: Domain: the inputs a function will actually accept
reveal: Only y = x³ − 2x gives one y for every x.
The others give ± pairs: two outputs for one input.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Domain: the inputs a function accepts
cards.cliff: Combine two machines and you get composition
lines: f(x) = √x only takes x ≥ 0 (in the reals).
g(x) = 1/(x − 2) takes everything except x = 2.
h(x) = ln x needs x > 0.
*Roots of negatives, division by zero, logs of non-positives*: the three classic exclusions.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Composition: one machine feeding another
cards.cliff: Some machines can be run backwards
lines: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)): run g first, then f.
f(x) = x², g(x) = x + 1: f(g(x)) = (x + 1)², but g(f(x)) = x² + 1.
*Order matters.* Composition is not multiplication.
recall: If f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 3, what is f(g(1))?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Inverse functions run the machine backwards
cards.cliff: eˣ and ln x are the most important inverse pair in maths
lines: f(x) = 2x + 1. Solve y = 2x + 1 for x: f⁻¹(y) = (y − 1)/2.
The graph of f⁻¹ is f reflected in the line y = x.
Only one-to-one functions have inverses: x² on all reals doesn't (2 and −2 both give 4).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: What is f⁻¹(x) if f(x) = x³ + 2?
cards.cliff: Even and odd functions have symmetry you can exploit
reveal: Swap and solve: x = y³ + 2, so y = ∛(x − 2).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Even and odd functions
cards.cliff: Shifting and stretching graphs follows four simple rules
lines: Even: f(−x) = f(x). Mirror symmetry in the y-axis: x², cos x.
Odd: f(−x) = −f(x). Symmetry through the origin: x³, sin x.
*The integral of an odd function from −a to a is 0.* Free marks in exams.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Transformations: what happens to y = f(x)
cards.cliff: Why does f(x + 2) move left? Because x = −2 now does what x = 0 used to
lines: f(x) + c: shift up by c. f(x + c): shift *left* by c.
c·f(x): stretch vertically. f(cx): squeeze horizontally by c.
−f(x): flip over the x-axis. f(−x): flip over the y-axis.
Inside the brackets everything acts backwards.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: log₁₀ grows absurdly slowly. Roughly how big must x be for log₁₀(x) = 100?
cards.cliff: Exponentials are the opposite: they explode
reveal: log₁₀(x) = 100 means x = 10¹⁰⁰: a googol.
That's more than the number of atoms in the observable universe (about 10⁸⁰).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Exponential growth means "really fast growth".
cards.cliff: Next: what happens as x heads to infinity
reveal: Exponential means growth proportional to current size: y′ = ky.
Early on it can look slower than linear. 1.01ˣ only overtakes 100x after about 1,150 steps.
*It's not fast at first. It's relentless.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: What is 1/x when x is infinitely big?
cards.cliff: That idea tells you where every rational function ends up
lines: Not "zero divided by something". Infinity isn't a number you can plug in.
But as x grows, 1/x gets as close to 0 as you like.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Rational functions: compare the top and bottom degrees
lines: Degree top < degree bottom: limit at infinity is 0.
Equal degrees: ratio of the leading coefficients. (3x² + 1)/(5x² − x) → 3/5.
Top bigger: it blows up (no finite limit).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Horizontal asymptote of y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3)?
cards.cliff: Can a graph cross its own asymptote? Yes
reveal: Equal degrees: leading coefficients 2/1.
x = 3 is the *vertical* asymptote, where the bottom is zero.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A graph can never cross its horizontal asymptote.
reveal: y = sin(x)/x crosses y = 0 infinitely often while approaching it.
Horizontal asymptotes describe the far ends only.
Vertical asymptotes are the ones you can't cross (the function isn't defined there).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: As x → ∞, which wins: x¹⁰⁰ or 1.01ˣ?
reveal: Any exponential with base > 1 beats any polynomial in the end.
The crossover here is enormous, but it comes. Then x¹⁰⁰/1.01ˣ → 0.
options: x¹⁰⁰, it has a huge head start
They grow at the same rate

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The growth hierarchy
lines: ln x  ≪  xᵃ (any a > 0)  ≪  bˣ (b > 1)  ≪  x!  ≪  xˣ
Every function on the right eventually crushes everything on its left.
*Algorithm speeds use exactly this ladder*: log n, n, n², 2ⁿ, n!
recall: x!, since each new factor eventually exceeds 10

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: (1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e
cards.cliff: Jacob Bernoulli found this in 1683, asking about bank interest
lines: It's compound interest: 100% a year, compounded n times.
Compound every instant and £1 becomes *£e*, not infinity.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim x→∞ (√(x² + x) − x) = ?
cards.cliff: Infinity minus infinity can be anything. The conjugate trick decides
reveal: Multiply by the conjugate: x/(√(x² + x) + x).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∞ − ∞, 0·∞, ∞/∞: indeterminate forms
cards.cliff: Continuity: when a function behaves exactly as expected
lines: These don't have fixed values. They depend on how fast each part moves.
x² − x → ∞, but x − x → 0, and (x + 5) − x → 5.
*Rewrite, simplify or use L'Hôpital.* Never guess.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Continuous means: no surprises at the point
cards.cliff: A hole can be patched. A jump can't
lines: f is continuous at a if lim(x→a) f(x) exists *and* equals f(a).
Three ways to fail: a hole, a jump, or blowing up.
Polynomials, sin, cos, eˣ are continuous everywhere.
recall: Definition of continuity at x = a?
lim x→a f(x) exists and equals f(a)

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3). What kind of discontinuity at x = 3?
reveal: Factor: (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x − 3) = x + 3 for x ≠ 3.
The limit is 6. Define f(3) = 6 and the hole disappears.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A function that's continuous at exactly one point
cards.cliff: Dirichlet's version, 1 for rationals and 0 for irrationals, is continuous nowhere
lines: Let f(x) = x when x is rational, and 0 when x is irrational.
Near any point except 0, it jumps between two values infinitely often.
At x = 0 both rules give 0. *Continuous at one point, nowhere else.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: If you can draw a graph without lifting your pen, the function is differentiable.
cards.cliff: Corners, cusps and vertical tangents all break the derivative
reveal: |x| is continuous but has a corner at 0: no single tangent.
Weierstrass (1872) built a function continuous everywhere and differentiable *nowhere*.
Continuity is necessary for differentiability, not sufficient.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: You climbed a mountain from 8am to 6pm. Next day you walk down the same path, 8am to 6pm. Is there a time when you were at the same spot on both days?
cards.cliff: The IVT also guarantees roots exist, and bisection finds them
reveal: Overlay both days: one height curve goes up, the other down, so they must cross.
That's the Intermediate Value Theorem on the difference of the two.
options: Only if you walked at constant speed

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Bisection: the IVT as an algorithm
cards.cliff: One theorem says continuous functions always hit their max
lines: f(1) < 0 and f(2) > 0: a root is in [1, 2].
Check the midpoint, keep the half where the sign changes. Repeat.
Each step halves the interval: 10 steps give ~3 decimal places.
*Slow but unbreakable.* Newton's method is faster but can fail.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Extreme Value Theorem
cards.cliff: Next: the derivative rules you'll use a thousand times
lines: A continuous function on a *closed* interval [a, b] has a maximum and a minimum.
Open intervals break it: 1/x on (0, 1) has no maximum.
So in optimisation: check critical points *and* the endpoints.
recall: Why does the EVT need a closed interval?
On open intervals the function can approach a max/min without reaching it (e.g. 1/x on (0,1))

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx (3x⁴ − 5x² + 7) = ?
reveal: Power rule term by term. Constants vanish.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Product rule
cards.cliff: Quotients: the rule everyone forgets the sign in
lines: $ (fg)′ = f′g + fg′
Not f′g′. d/dx (x·x) = 2x, but (1)(1) = 1. Wrong.
Mnemonic: "left d-right plus right d-left".

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Quotient rule
lines: $ (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g²
"Low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared."
Or skip it: write f/g as f·g⁻¹ and use product + chain rule.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx (x²/(x + 1)) = ?
cards.cliff: Chain rule in disguise is everywhere

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx (2x + 1)⁵ = ?
reveal: Outer: 5(·)⁴. Inner derivative: 2. Multiply: 10(2x + 1)⁴.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx √x = ?
reveal: √x = x^(1/2). Bring down 1/2, drop the power to −1/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx (1/x³) = ?
cards.cliff: Second derivatives: the rate of change of the rate of change
reveal: x⁻³ → −3x⁻⁴.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The second derivative is acceleration
cards.cliff: There's even a name for the third derivative
lines: Position s(t). Velocity s′(t). Acceleration s″(t).
f″ > 0: concave up (holds water). f″ < 0: concave down.
Where f″ changes sign: an *inflection point*.
recall: The graph is concave up there (slope increasing)

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Jerk, snap, crackle, pop
cards.cliff: Next: trig functions and why radians matter
lines: The third derivative of position is *jerk*: how suddenly acceleration changes.
Lift and train designers limit jerk so passengers don't stumble.
The 4th, 5th and 6th derivatives are informally called snap, crackle and pop.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A car's position is s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t. When is it momentarily stopped?
cards.cliff: Next: derivatives of sin and cos

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The derivative of sin is cos. The derivative of cos is −sin.
lines: Differentiate sin four times and you're back where you started.
sin → cos → −sin → −cos → sin.
That cycle is why waves and oscillations obey calculus so neatly.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: In degrees, what is d/dx sin(x°)?
cards.cliff: tan has a derivative with a famous shape
reveal: x° = πx/180 radians, so the chain rule throws out π/180.
Radians are the units where the constant is exactly 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx tan x = ?
reveal: tan = sin/cos. Quotient rule: (cos² + sin²)/cos² = 1/cos² = sec² x.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx sin(3x²) = ?
cards.cliff: Inverse trig derivatives look nothing like trig
reveal: Outer: cos(3x²). Inner: 6x.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: arctan has an algebraic derivative
cards.cliff: Which leads to a formula for π
lines: $ d/dx arctan x = 1/(1 + x²)
$ d/dx arcsin x = 1/√(1 − x²)
A trig function's inverse differentiates to pure algebra. That's why arctan shows up when you integrate 1/(1 + x²).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: π from a derivative
cards.cliff: It converges painfully slowly: a million terms gets π to about 6 digits
lines: Integrate 1/(1 + x²) from 0 to 1: arctan 1 = π/4.
Expand 1/(1 + x²) as 1 − x² + x⁴ − …, integrate term by term.
*π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + …* (Leibniz, also Madhava centuries earlier).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Your phone's step counter is differentiating sine waves
lines: Walking makes your phone's accelerometer swing in a rough sine wave.
Peaks and zero crossings are where derivatives vanish or change sign.
*Count the cycles, count the steps.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: y = x·sin x. Find y″.
cards.cliff: Next: the derivative that equals itself
reveal: y′ = sin x + x cos x.
y″ = cos x + cos x − x sin x = 2cos x − x sin x.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx ln x = 1/x
cards.cliff: Other bases just pick up a log
lines: Because ln is the inverse of eˣ: if y = ln x, then x = eʸ, so dx/dy = eʸ = x.
Flip it: dy/dx = 1/x.
That's why ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C. The power rule fails at x⁻¹, and ln fills the gap.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx 2ˣ = ?
cards.cliff: The power rule versus the exponent rule is the #1 exam trap
reveal: 2ˣ = e^(x ln 2). Chain rule gives ln 2 · 2ˣ.
The power rule doesn't apply: the variable is in the exponent.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx xˣ = x·xˣ⁻¹
reveal: That treats it like a power. It's also an exponential. Neither rule works alone.
Write xˣ = e^(x ln x). Then d/dx = xˣ(ln x + 1).
Trick: *logarithmic differentiation*.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Logarithmic differentiation
cards.cliff: Logs also turn multiplication into addition, which built the slide rule
lines: For y = f(x)^g(x) or giant products, take ln of both sides first.
ln y = x ln x → y′/y = ln x + 1 → y′ = xˣ(ln x + 1).
Logs turn products into sums and powers into multipliers.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Logarithms were invented to save astronomers' time
cards.cliff: Here's the curve that makes ln special
lines: 1614: John Napier published logarithms so that multiplying huge numbers became adding.
Laplace later said they doubled an astronomer's working life.
Slide rules, which are just log scales, flew to the Moon with Apollo astronauts.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Find the slope of y = ln(x² + 1) at x = 1.
cards.cliff: Exponential decay is just a negative exponent

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Carbon dating is a derivative equation
cards.cliff: Next: when y won't come out on its own
lines: Living things keep a steady ratio of carbon-14. When they die, it decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years.
Measure what's left, solve N = N₀e^(−kt) for t.
*A bone with a quarter of its C-14 is about 11,460 years old.* Two half-lives.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Which is bigger: e^π or π^e?
reveal: Proof: x^(1/x) peaks at x = e, so e^(1/e) > π^(1/π). Raise both sides to eπ.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Implicit differentiation: differentiate first, solve later
cards.cliff: Every y term picks up a y′ from the chain rule
lines: x² + y² = 25 isn't y = f(x), but y still depends on x.
Differentiate both sides, treating y as a function: 2x + 2y·y′ = 0.
Solve: *y′ = −x/y*. At (3, 4) the slope is −3/4.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: xy = 6. Find dy/dx.
cards.cliff: It works on curves that aren't functions at all
reveal: Product rule: y + x·y′ = 0, so y′ = −y/x.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Find dy/dx for x³ + y³ = 6xy at (3, 3).
cards.cliff: That curve is the folium of Descartes
reveal: 3x² + 3y²y′ = 6y + 6xy′.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Descartes challenged Fermat with this curve
cards.cliff: Implicit differentiation also explains why the derivative of an inverse flips
lines: The folium x³ + y³ = 3axy was Descartes' challenge to Fermat over finding tangents.
Fermat found them easily with his early calculus-like method.
Descartes was annoyed. Calculus was decades away but already brewing.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Derivative of an inverse function
cards.cliff: Next: rates that depend on each other
lines: If y = f⁻¹(x), then f(y) = x. Differentiate: f′(y)·y′ = 1.
Slopes of inverse graphs are reciprocals at mirrored points.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Related rates: everything changes with time
cards.cliff: The classic: a balloon being inflated
lines: Write an equation linking the quantities. Differentiate with respect to t.
Plug in the numbers *after* differentiating, never before.
Units check everything: m/s, m²/s, m³/s.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A spherical balloon's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is volume growing when r = 10 cm?
cards.cliff: Ladders sliding down walls are an exam favourite
reveal: V = (4/3)πr³, so dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt = 4π(100)(2).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A 5 m ladder slides down a wall. The base moves out at 1 m/s. How fast does the top fall when the base is 3 m out?
cards.cliff: As the base slides out, the top moves faster and faster
reveal: y′ = −3/4: falling at 3/4 m/s.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: In the ideal model, what happens to the speed of the ladder's top just before it hits the ground?
reveal: y′ = −x·x′/y, and y → 0.
Real ladders lose contact with the wall first. The model breaks before the maths does.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A 2 m person walks away from a 6 m lamppost at 1.5 m/s. How fast does their shadow lengthen?
cards.cliff: Next: sketching any curve from its derivatives
reveal: Similar triangles: s/2 = (x + s)/6, so s = x/2.
ds/dt = (1/2)(1.5) = 0.75 m/s, whatever the distance.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Sketch any curve with four questions
cards.cliff: f′ tells you rising or falling. f″ tells you the bend
lines: Where is it zero? (intercepts)
Where is f′ = 0 or undefined? (critical points: peaks, valleys, flats)
Where does f″ change sign? (inflection points)
What happens as x → ±∞ and near any vertical asymptotes?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f(x) = x³ − 3x. Where are its local max and min?
cards.cliff: The second derivative test settles max vs min in one line
reveal: f″ = 6x: negative at −1 (max), positive at 1 (min).
options: Max at x = −1, min at x = 1
Max at x = 1, min at x = −1

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Second derivative test
cards.cliff: Inflection points are where the bend flips
lines: At a critical point c (f′(c) = 0):
f″(c) > 0: local minimum. f″(c) < 0: local maximum.
f″(c) = 0: the test says *nothing*. x⁴, −x⁴ and x³ all have f″(0) = 0.
recall: If f′(c)=0 and f″(c)=0, what does the second derivative test conclude?
Nothing. Use the first derivative test instead

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Where is the inflection point of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 5?
cards.cliff: The bell curve has two inflection points, exactly one standard deviation out
reveal: f″ = 6x − 12 = 0 at x = 2, and it changes sign there.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The normal distribution bends at ±1σ
cards.cliff: A cusp is where even the derivative gives up
lines: Zero at x = ±1: the bell switches from concave down to concave up there.
*That's literally where standard deviation sits on the curve.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: What does y = x^(2/3) look like at x = 0?
cards.cliff: Next: using all this to optimise real things
reveal: y′ = (2/3)x^(−1/3) → ±∞ from either side.
Both sides go vertical at the origin: a cusp.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The optimisation recipe
lines: 1. Write the thing to maximise as one formula.
2. Use the constraint to cut it to one variable.
3. Differentiate, set to zero, solve.
4. Check endpoints and that it really is a max (or min).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Cut equal squares of side x from the corners of a 12 × 12 sheet and fold up a box. Which x maximises volume?
cards.cliff: Drinks cans are an optimisation problem too
reveal: x = 6 gives zero volume. x = 2 gives V = 128.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: For a fixed volume, which cylinder uses the least metal?
cards.cliff: Light solves optimisation problems all the time
reveal: Minimise 2πr² + 2πrh with πr²h fixed: you get h = 2r.
Real cans are taller because the lids are thicker and cost more than the sides.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Light takes the fastest path, and that gives you Snell's law
cards.cliff: A lifeguard running then swimming solves the same problem
lines: Fermat (1662): light travels between two points along the path of least time.
Minimise travel time across two media with speeds v₁ and v₂.
$ sin θ₁ / v₁ = sin θ₂ / v₂
*Refraction falls out of a derivative set to zero.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A farmer fences a rectangle against a river (no fence on the river side) with 200 m of fence. Maximum area?
cards.cliff: Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Economists optimise with derivatives every day
lines: Profit P(q) = R(q) − C(q). Set P′(q) = 0.
So R′(q) = C′(q): *marginal revenue equals marginal cost*.
"Marginal" just means derivative.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Zoom in far enough and every smooth curve is a line
cards.cliff: Estimate square roots in your head
lines: Near x = a: f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a).
That's the tangent line used as a stand-in for the function.
It's the first term of a Taylor series.
recall: Linear approximation of f near a?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Use linear approximation to estimate √4.1.
cards.cliff: Physicists use this constantly: sin θ ≈ θ
reveal: True value: 2.02485…

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The small-angle approximation
cards.cliff: Error grows the further you go: the second derivative controls it
lines: Near 0 (in radians): sin θ ≈ θ, tan θ ≈ θ, cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2.
At 10° (0.1745 rad), sin θ = 0.1736. Less than 1% off.
*It turns the pendulum equation into simple harmonic motion.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Using (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx, what is 1.01¹⁰ roughly?
reveal: This "binomial approximation" appears everywhere in physics.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim x→0 (1 − cos x)/x² = ?
reveal: L'Hôpital twice: sin x/(2x) → cos x/2 → 1/2.
Or use cos x ≈ 1 − x²/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: You can use L'Hôpital's rule on any limit of a fraction.
cards.cliff: Exponent forms like 1^∞ need logs first
reveal: Only on 0/0 or ∞/∞ forms. Otherwise it gives wrong answers.
lim x→0 (x + 1)/(x + 2) = 1/2. L'Hôpital would wrongly give 1/1 = 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim x→0⁺ xˣ = ?
cards.cliff: 0⁰ is an argument mathematicians still have
reveal: Take logs: x ln x → 0 (since x beats ln x). So xˣ → e⁰ = 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Is 0⁰ equal to 1?
lines: In combinatorics and power series, 0⁰ = 1 makes every formula work.
As a limit form, 0⁰ is indeterminate: x⁰ → 1 but 0ˣ → 0.
Most programming languages return 1. *Context decides.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim x→∞ (ln x)/√x = ?
reveal: Logs lose to every positive power.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Antiderivatives: undo the derivative
cards.cliff: The +C isn't pedantry: it's a whole family of curves
lines: If F′ = f, then F is an antiderivative of f.
∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1.
*Always + C*: every constant differentiates to zero.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ (6x² − 4x + 3) dx = ?
reveal: Power rule backwards on each term.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f′(x) = 2x and f(1) = 5. What is f(x)?
cards.cliff: Physics runs on this: from acceleration back to position

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Drop a ball: integrate twice
cards.cliff: Some functions have no antiderivative you can write down
lines: a = −9.8 m/s². Integrate: v = −9.8t + v₀.
Integrate again: s = −4.9t² + v₀t + s₀.
*The two constants are the starting speed and height.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Every function you can write down has an antiderivative you can write down.
reveal: ∫ e^(−x²) dx, ∫ sin(x)/x dx and ∫ √(1 + x³) dx have no formula in elementary functions.
Liouville proved this in the 1830s. The antiderivatives exist; they just need new names, like erf(x).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The definite integral is signed area
cards.cliff: Some properties save a lot of work
lines: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx counts area above the axis as positive, below as negative.
∫₀^2π sin x dx = 0: the two humps cancel.
For total area, integrate |f|.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Integral properties worth knowing
cards.cliff: Average value is an integral too
lines: ∫ₐᵃ f = 0. ∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦₐ f.
∫ₐᵇ f + ∫ᵦᶜ f = ∫ₐᶜ f.
If f ≤ g on [a, b], then ∫ f ≤ ∫ g.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Average value of f(x) = x² on [0, 3]?
cards.cliff: There's a theorem guaranteeing f hits its average

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Mean Value Theorem for integrals
cards.cliff: Next: the Fundamental Theorem in practice
lines: A continuous f on [a, b] actually equals its average value somewhere in the interval.
$ f(c) = (1/(b − a)) ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx
Average temperature over a day? At some moment it really was that temperature.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫₀^π sin x dx = ?
cards.cliff: One hump of sine has area exactly 2

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx ∫₀ˣ cos(t²) dt = ?
cards.cliff: Variable limits bring in the chain rule
reveal: FTC part 1: differentiating the accumulated area gives back the integrand.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: d/dx ∫₀^(x²) eᵗ dt = ?
cards.cliff: A whole new function defined by an integral
reveal: FTC gives e^(x²), times the derivative of the upper limit, 2x.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ln x can be defined as an integral
cards.cliff: The error function is defined the same way
lines: $ ln x = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt
Every property of logs follows from this: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b is just splitting the area.
*Many textbooks build the logarithm exactly this way.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: erf(x): an integral with its own name
lines: erf(x) = (2/√π) ∫₀ˣ e^(−t²) dt. No elementary formula.
It gives the probability a normal measurement lands within a certain range.
Calculators and spreadsheets compute it numerically.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ x·e^(x²) dx = ?
cards.cliff: Look for an inner function whose derivative is lying around
reveal: u = x², du = 2x dx. ∫ ½eᵘ du = ½eᵘ.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ cos x / sin x dx = ?
cards.cliff: Change the limits when you substitute in a definite integral
reveal: u = sin x, du = cos x dx. ∫ du/u = ln|u|.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Definite integrals: change the limits too
lines: ∫₀¹ 2x(x² + 1)³ dx with u = x² + 1: when x = 0, u = 1; when x = 1, u = 2.
$ ∫₁² u³ du = [u⁴/4]₁² = 15/4
Change the limits and you never have to substitute back.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ tan x dx = ?
reveal: tan = sin/cos. u = cos x, du = −sin x dx.
−ln|cos x| = ln|sec x|.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Area between curves = top minus bottom
cards.cliff: Sometimes integrating in y is easier
lines: $ A = ∫ₐᵇ (top − bottom) dx
Find where the curves cross: those are often your limits.
If they swap places, split the integral.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Area between y = x and y = x² on [0, 1]?
cards.cliff: Area also gives you a famous inequality
reveal: x is on top. ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Area enclosed by y = 4 − x² and the x-axis?
reveal: Archimedes' rule: 4/3 of the inscribed triangle (area 8).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Disc method: slice it like salami
cards.cliff: Derive the volume of a sphere in one line
lines: Spin y = f(x) around the x-axis. Each slice is a disc of area πf(x)².
$ V = π ∫ₐᵇ f(x)² dx
Hollow middle? Subtract the inner disc: washers.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Spin y = √(r² − x²) around the x-axis. Volume?
cards.cliff: Archimedes wanted this result on his tomb
reveal: π∫₋ᵣʳ (r² − x²) dx = π(2r³ − 2r³/3) = (4/3)πr³.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Archimedes' tombstone had a sphere in a cylinder
lines: He proved a sphere has 2/3 the volume of the cylinder that wraps it, and 2/3 of its surface area too.
He asked for that diagram on his grave.
Cicero found the overgrown tomb in Syracuse around 75 BC, recognising it by the sphere and cylinder.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Shell method: slice into tubes
lines: Spin around the y-axis. Each thin vertical strip makes a cylindrical shell.
$ V = 2π ∫ₐᵇ x·f(x) dx
Use whichever method gives the easier integral.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: What it means for a sequence to converge
cards.cliff: The rationals have holes. The reals don't
lines: aₙ → L if for every ε > 0, eventually all terms are within ε of L.
"Eventually" = there's an N after which it holds.
1/n → 0: for any ε, pick N > 1/ε.
recall: For every ε > 0 there is N such that n > N implies |aₙ − L| < ε

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Completeness: why calculus needs the real numbers
cards.cliff: The least upper bound property is the engine
lines: The sequence 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, … is all rational, but its limit √2 isn't.
The reals fill every hole: any bounded increasing sequence converges.
*Without completeness, the Intermediate Value Theorem fails.* x² − 2 would skip zero on the rationals.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: What is the supremum (least upper bound) of {1 − 1/n : n ≥ 1}?
cards.cliff: Cauchy found a way to test convergence without knowing the limit
reveal: Every term is below 1 and gets arbitrarily close. 1 itself is never reached.
Supremum ≠ maximum: this set has no maximum.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Cauchy sequences converge without naming the limit
cards.cliff: Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence
lines: Terms get arbitrarily close to *each other*: |aₘ − aₙ| < ε for large m, n.
In the reals, Cauchy ⇔ convergent.
In the rationals, a Cauchy sequence can head towards a hole. That's another way to define completeness.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Bolzano–Weierstrass
lines: Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence.
Proof idea: keep halving the interval, always keeping a half with infinitely many terms.
It's the workhorse behind the Extreme Value Theorem.
recall: Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A sequence that keeps increasing must go to infinity.
reveal: 1 − 1/n increases forever but converges to 1.
Monotone convergence theorem: increasing and bounded ⇒ converges.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Uniform continuity: one δ for everywhere
cards.cliff: Heine–Cantor: on closed bounded intervals, the two coincide
lines: Continuous: for each point and each ε there's a δ (which may depend on the point).
Uniformly continuous: one δ works across the whole domain.
x² on all reals isn't uniform: it gets steeper, so δ must shrink as x grows.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Which is uniformly continuous on (0, 1)?
cards.cliff: Uniform convergence is the property that lets you swap limits
reveal: √x extends continuously to [0, 1], a compact interval, so it's uniformly continuous.
1/x and sin(1/x) oscillate or blow up near 0.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Pointwise vs uniform convergence
cards.cliff: This is exactly why Fourier series misbehave at jumps
lines: fₙ(x) = xⁿ on [0, 1] converges pointwise to 0 (for x < 1) and 1 (at x = 1): a discontinuous limit.
Each fₙ is continuous. The limit isn't.
*Uniform convergence preserves continuity.* Pointwise convergence doesn't.
recall: It preserves continuity and allows swapping limits with integrals

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Cauchy published a wrong theorem
cards.cliff: Calculus 1 is done. Calculus 2 builds integration into an art
lines: In 1821 Cauchy claimed a convergent sum of continuous functions is always continuous.
Fourier series of square waves are counterexamples: continuous sines summing to a jump.
The fix, uniform convergence, took decades to be stated clearly. *Even the founders of rigour slipped.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ x cos x dx = ?
cards.cliff: Sometimes you have to use parts twice
reveal: u = x, dv = cos x dx: x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.
options: x sin x + cos x + C
x sin x − cos x + C

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ x² eˣ dx = ?
cards.cliff: Tabular integration makes repeated parts painless
reveal: Parts once: x²eˣ − ∫2x eˣ dx. Parts again on that: 2xeˣ − 2eˣ.
Total: eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + C.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Tabular integration (the DI method)
cards.cliff: And some integrals loop back on themselves
lines: Column D: differentiate the polynomial until it hits 0. Column I: integrate the other part each row.
Multiply diagonally with alternating signs +, −, +, …
*∫ x³ eˣ dx in four lines instead of three rounds of parts.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The integral that solves itself
cards.cliff: Reduction formulas turn powers into ladders
lines: ∫ eˣ sin x dx: parts twice and the same integral reappears on the right-hand side.
Call it I: I = eˣ sin x − eˣ cos x − I.
Solve the equation: *I = ½eˣ(sin x − cos x) + C.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Reduction formulas
lines: Iₙ = ∫ sinⁿx dx satisfies Iₙ = −(1/n)sinⁿ⁻¹x cos x + ((n − 1)/n)Iₙ₋₂.
Each step drops the power by two until you hit I₀ or I₁.
Over [0, π/2] this gives Wallis's formula, a product that converges to π/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ arctan x dx = ?
reveal: u = arctan x, dv = dx: x arctan x − ∫ x/(1 + x²) dx.
The last integral is ½ln(1 + x²).
options: x arctan x − ½ln(1 + x²) + C

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Odd power of sine? Peel one off
cards.cliff: Even powers need the double-angle identity
lines: ∫ sin³x dx = ∫ (1 − cos²x) sin x dx.
Substitute u = cos x. It becomes a polynomial in u.
Odd power of cos? Same trick with u = sin x.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Even powers: use half-angle identities
cards.cliff: Here's an integral everyone gets wrong
lines: $ sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2,   cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2
∫ sin²x dx = x/2 − sin(2x)/4 + C.
*Over a full period, the average of sin² is exactly 1/2.* That's why AC power uses an RMS of V/√2.
recall: Average of sin²x over a full period?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫₀^π sin²x dx = ?
reveal: Average value 1/2 over an interval of length π.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ sec x dx was found by mapmakers before calculus
cards.cliff: ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C
lines: Mercator's 1569 map needed the vertical stretch at each latitude: a running sum of sec.
In 1645 Henry Bond noticed the tables matched ln|tan(x/2 + π/4)|.
*The integral of sec x was a conjecture from navigation tables.* Proved later by Barrow.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫ sin x cos x dx can be written as…
cards.cliff: Different-looking answers can all be right, because of +C
reveal: All three are correct. They differ only by constants.
½sin²x, −½cos²x and −¼cos 2x all have the same derivative.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Trig substitution undoes a square root
cards.cliff: Compute the area of a circle this way
lines: √(a² − x²): let x = a sin θ.
√(a² + x²): let x = a tan θ.
√(x² − a²): let x = a sec θ.
Each uses a Pythagorean identity to kill the square root.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Using x = r sin θ, what does ∫₋ᵣʳ √(r² − x²) dx equal?
cards.cliff: The inverse hyperbolic functions hide here too
reveal: It becomes r²∫ cos²θ dθ from −π/2 to π/2 = r²·π/2.
That's the area of a half disc. Double it: πr².

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Hyperbolic functions: trig for the hyperbola
cards.cliff: The Gateway Arch in St Louis is an upside-down catenary
lines: cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2.
cosh²x − sinh²x = 1, the hyperbola's version of sin² + cos² = 1.
A hanging chain makes a cosh curve: a *catenary*.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Gateway Arch is a weighted catenary
cards.cliff: Next: integrals that go to infinity
lines: An inverted hanging chain carries its weight in pure compression: no bending.
Gaudí designed by hanging weighted strings and photographing them upside down.
*Calculus of variations proves the catenary is the shape of minimum potential energy.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Improper integrals: infinite length, finite area
lines: ∫₁^∞ f(x) dx means lim b→∞ ∫₁ᵇ f(x) dx.
∫₁^∞ 1/x² dx = 1. Infinite region, area 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: For which p does ∫₁^∞ 1/xᵖ dx converge?
cards.cliff: Infinite spikes can have finite area too
reveal: p = 1 is the borderline: ln x → ∞.
Near 0 it flips: ∫₀¹ 1/xᵖ dx converges for p < 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫₀¹ 1/√x dx = ?
cards.cliff: Comparison tests save you computing anything
reveal: [2√x]₀¹ = 2. The function blows up at 0 but slowly enough.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Comparison test for integrals
cards.cliff: The gamma function extends factorials to fractions
lines: 0 ≤ f ≤ g and ∫g converges ⇒ ∫f converges.
∫₁^∞ e^(−x²) dx: compare with e^(−x), which converges.
*You often only need to know whether it converges, not the value.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: (½)! = √π / 2
cards.cliff: The √π comes from the Gaussian integral again
lines: Γ(s) = ∫₀^∞ x^(s−1) e^(−x) dx satisfies Γ(n + 1) = n!.
It works for non-integers too. Γ(1/2) = √π.
recall: Γ(n+1) equals what for whole n?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Trapezoid rule
lines: Replace the curve with straight segments between sample points.
$ ∫ₐᵇ f ≈ h[f₀/2 + f₁ + … + fₙ₋₁ + fₙ/2]
Error shrinks like h²: halve the step, quarter the error.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Simpson's rule fits parabolas
lines: Weights 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, …, 4, 1 times h/3.
Error shrinks like h⁴: halve the step, error drops 16×.
*It's exact for cubics*, which is a happy accident of symmetry.
recall: How does Simpson's rule error scale with step h?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Trapezoid rule on a concave-up function: over or under?
cards.cliff: Gauss found something better than equal spacing
reveal: The straight chord sits above a curve that bends upward.
Midpoint rule does the opposite: it underestimates.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Gaussian quadrature picks the best sample points
lines: Instead of equally spaced points, choose the points and weights cleverly.
n points integrate polynomials up to degree 2n − 1 exactly.
*Two well-chosen points match Simpson's three.* Used inside almost every physics simulation.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Arc length: add up tiny hypotenuses
cards.cliff: The ellipse's perimeter has no simple formula
lines: A short piece has length √(dx² + dy²).
$ L = ∫ₐᵇ √(1 + f′(x)²) dx
Square roots make these integrals nasty: few have closed forms.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Nobody has a simple formula for an ellipse's perimeter
cards.cliff: Surfaces of revolution use arc length too
lines: Arc length of an ellipse leads to an *elliptic integral*, which has no elementary form.
Ramanujan gave approximations accurate to staggering precision.
Elliptic integrals led to elliptic curves, now used in the cryptography securing your phone.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Arc length of y = (2/3)x^(3/2) from 0 to 3?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A sequence is a function on 1, 2, 3, …
cards.cliff: Recursion builds sequences from their own past

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Fibonacci ratios converge to the golden ratio
cards.cliff: Most "golden ratio in nature and art" claims are exaggerated, though
lines: Binet's formula gives Fₙ directly from powers of φ and its conjugate.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Parthenon and the Mona Lisa were designed using the golden ratio.
cards.cliff: Some sequences converge without you knowing the limit
reveal: There's no historical evidence for either. Measurements can be cherry-picked to fit almost anything.
Real golden-ratio patterns do appear in plant spirals (phyllotaxis).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim n→∞ n^(1/n) = ?
cards.cliff: The squeeze theorem handles oscillating sequences
reveal: ln(n^(1/n)) = (ln n)/n → 0, so the limit is e⁰ = 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim n→∞ sin(n)/n = ?
reveal: −1/n ≤ sin(n)/n ≤ 1/n. Both bounds → 0.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Divergence test: terms must shrink to zero
cards.cliff: Geometric series are the ones you can sum exactly
lines: If aₙ doesn't → 0, Σaₙ diverges. Immediately.
But aₙ → 0 is *not* enough: the harmonic series diverges anyway.

cards.subject: maths
cards.cliff: Ratio test: compare each term with the next
reveal: Geometric with r = 1/3: a/(1 − r) = 1/(2/3) = 3/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Ratio test
cards.cliff: Integral test: turn a sum into an area
lines: L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|.
L < 1: converges. L > 1: diverges. L = 1: no conclusion.
Perfect for factorials and exponentials.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Does Σ 1/(n ln n) (from n = 2) converge?
reveal: Integral test: ∫ dx/(x ln x) = ln(ln x) → ∞.
It diverges, but incredibly slowly: the partial sums grow like ln ln n.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Alternating series test
lines: If terms alternate in sign, shrink in size, and → 0, the series converges.
1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + … converges (to ln 2), even though the harmonic series doesn't.
Error after stopping ≤ the first term you left out.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Σ (−1)ⁿ/√n converges…
cards.cliff: Which test to use? A quick decision tree
reveal: Alternating test: converges. But Σ 1/√n diverges (p = 1/2).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Choosing a convergence test
lines: Terms don't → 0? Diverges.
Geometric or p-series? Known answers.
Factorials or nⁿ? Ratio test. Looks like a function? Integral test.
Looks like a known series? Comparison or limit comparison.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A power series is a polynomial that never ends
cards.cliff: The geometric series is the mother of them all
lines: $ Σ cₙ(x − a)ⁿ = c₀ + c₁(x − a) + c₂(x − a)² + …
It converges inside a *radius of convergence* R around a, and diverges outside.
At the two endpoints, anything can happen: check them separately.
recall: What's the radius of convergence of a power series?
The R such that it converges for |x − a| < R and diverges for |x − a| > R

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: 1/(1 − x) = 1 + x + x² + x³ + … for which x?
cards.cliff: Differentiate and integrate it to get new series for free
reveal: Geometric series with ratio x. Converges only for |x| < 1.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Integrate 1/(1 + x) = 1 − x + x² − … term by term. What series do you get?
cards.cliff: The radius of convergence can be set by trouble you can't see
reveal: ∫ 1/(1 + x) dx = ln(1 + x). Term by term gives the alternating series.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Why does 1/(1 + x²) stop converging at x = 1?
lines: Its series 1 − x² + x⁴ − … has radius 1, but the function is perfectly smooth on all real numbers.
The trouble is at x = ±i, where 1 + x² = 0.
*Power series feel the complex plane.* The radius is the distance to the nearest complex singularity.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Radius of convergence of Σ xⁿ/n! ?
cards.cliff: Next: building Taylor series by hand
reveal: Ratio test: |x|/(n + 1) → 0 for every x.
It's the series for eˣ, which converges everywhere.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Taylor's formula
cards.cliff: Five series worth knowing by heart
lines: $ f(x) = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x − a)ⁿ / n!
Each coefficient matches one more derivative at the point a.
At a = 0 it's called a Maclaurin series.
recall: General term of a Taylor series about a?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The five Maclaurin series to memorise
lines: sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …
cos x = 1 − x²/2! + x⁴/4! − …

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Maclaurin series for e^(−x²)?
cards.cliff: Series turn impossible limits into easy ones
reveal: Substitute −x² into eˣ.
Integrate it term by term and you can compute the error function by hand.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim x→0 (sin x − x)/x³ = ?
cards.cliff: Coefficients can be read straight off the series
reveal: sin x − x = −x³/6 + x⁵/120 − … Divide by x³ → −1/6.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f(x) = x·e^(x²). What is f⁽⁵⁾(0)?
reveal: x·e^(x²) = x + x³ + x⁵/2 + … so the x⁵ coefficient is 1/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Einstein's E = mc² hides in a Taylor series
cards.cliff: Next: how wrong is a truncated series?
lines: Relativistic energy is E = γmc², with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).
Expand for small v: γ ≈ 1 + v²/(2c²) + …
So E ≈ mc² + ½mv² + …: *rest energy plus the kinetic energy from school physics.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Lagrange remainder bounds your error
cards.cliff: How many terms for e to 6 decimals?
lines: Stop after the degree-n term. The error is f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! for some c between a and x.
Bound the (n + 1)th derivative and you bound the error.
recall: Lagrange remainder for a degree-n Taylor polynomial?
f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(c)(x − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! for some c between a and x

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: How many terms of 1 + 1 + 1/2! + 1/3! + … give e to within 10⁻⁶?
cards.cliff: Alternating series give an even simpler bound
reveal: The error after the 1/n! term is less than 3/(n + 1)!.
3/10! ≈ 8 × 10⁻⁷. Factorials crush errors fast.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Approximating sin(0.1) by 0.1, the error is at most…
cards.cliff: Calculators don't use raw Taylor series though
reveal: Alternating series: error ≤ first omitted term, x³/3!.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: How calculators actually compute sin x
cards.cliff: Next: curves defined by a moving point
lines: Many early calculators used CORDIC: rotate a vector by a sequence of fixed angles using only shifts and adds.
Modern chips use range reduction plus short, carefully optimised polynomials.
*The polynomials aren't Taylor series.* They minimise the worst-case error instead (minimax).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Parametric curves describe motion
cards.cliff: The cycloid answers two famous questions
lines: x = f(t), y = g(t): a point moving over time.
Slope: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
x = cos t, y = sin t traces a circle. x = t − sin t, y = 1 − cos t traces a cycloid.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The brachistochrone: the fastest slide is not a straight line
cards.cliff: The cycloid is also the tautochrone: every start point arrives at the bottom at the same time
lines: 1696: Johann Bernoulli asked for the curve along which a bead slides fastest between two points.
The answer is a cycloid. Newton solved it overnight and sent it in anonymously.
Bernoulli recognised the author anyway: *"the lion by his claw".*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: x = t², y = t³. What is dy/dx at t = 2?
reveal: dy/dt = 3t² = 12, dx/dt = 2t = 4. Ratio 3.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Arc length of x = cos t, y = sin t for t from 0 to 2π?
reveal: √(sin²t + cos²t) = 1. Integrate 1 over 2π.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Polar coordinates: distance and angle
cards.cliff: Area in polar uses wedges, not rectangles
lines: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. r² = x² + y².
r = 2 is a circle. θ = π/4 is a line. r = θ is a spiral.
Roses: r = cos(kθ) has k petals if k is odd, 2k if k is even.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Polar area
lines: A thin wedge has area ½r²dθ.
$ A = ½ ∫ r(θ)² dθ
The cardioid r = 1 + cos θ has area 3π/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Area enclosed by r = 2cos θ?
reveal: It's a circle of radius 1. Or: ½∫₋π/2^π/2 4cos²θ dθ = π.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Separable equations: split and integrate
cards.cliff: Newton's law of cooling is separable
lines: dy/dx = g(x)h(y). Rearrange: dy/h(y) = g(x)dx. Integrate both sides.
dy/dx = xy: ln|y| = x²/2 + C, so y = Ae^(x²/2).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Coffee at 90°C cools in a 20°C room: T′ = −k(T − 20). Solution?
cards.cliff: Detectives use this to estimate time of death
reveal: T − 20 decays exponentially from 70.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Time of death from cooling
cards.cliff: Linear first-order equations need an integrating factor
lines: A body cools roughly according to Newton's law of cooling.
Two temperature readings an hour apart give k. Then solve back to 37°C.
*Forensic estimates add corrections for clothing, air flow and the first hours of plateau.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The integrating factor
cards.cliff: Logistic growth: when exponentials hit a ceiling
lines: y′ + P(x)y = Q(x). Multiply by μ = e^(∫P dx).
The left side becomes (μy)′. Integrate both sides.
y′ + y = eˣ: μ = eˣ, (eˣy)′ = e²ˣ, y = eˣ/2 + Ce⁻ˣ.
recall: Integrating factor for y′ + P(x)y = Q(x)?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The logistic equation
lines: $ dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K)
Small P: exponential growth. Near the carrying capacity K: growth stops.
Solution is an S-curve. Epidemics, product adoption and yeast in a jar all follow it roughly.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Lorenz found chaos by rounding a number
lines: 1961: Edward Lorenz restarted a weather simulation, typing 0.506 instead of 0.506127.
The forecast diverged completely within simulated weeks.
*The butterfly effect.* His three simple ODEs became the most famous chaotic system.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Constant-coefficient ODEs: guess eʳˣ
cards.cliff: The spring is the most important ODE in physics
lines: ay″ + by′ + cy = 0. Try y = eʳˣ: ar² + br + c = 0.
Two real roots: two exponentials. Repeated root: eʳˣ and xeʳˣ.
Complex roots α ± iβ: e^(αx)(A cos βx + B sin βx). *Oscillation.*
recall: What does a complex root of the characteristic equation mean physically?
Oscillation (sines and cosines), damped or growing by e^(αx)

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: y″ + 9y = 0. General solution?
cards.cliff: Add friction and the oscillation dies away
reveal: Simple harmonic motion with angular frequency 3.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A damped spring: y″ + 2y′ + y = 0. Does it oscillate?
cards.cliff: Push it at the right frequency and you get resonance
reveal: r² + 2r + 1 = (r + 1)² = 0: a repeated root.
Critical damping returns fastest without overshooting. Car suspension aims near it.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Resonance
cards.cliff: Tacoma Narrows wasn't simple resonance, though
lines: y″ + ω₀²y = cos(ωt). If ω = ω₀, the solution contains t·sin(ω₀t): it grows without bound.
Real systems have damping, so the amplitude peaks instead of exploding.
*Opera singers shattering glass, swings going higher, MRI machines: all resonance.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed in 1940 because wind matched its resonant frequency.
reveal: The popular textbook story is a simplification.
The collapse is explained by aeroelastic flutter: the bridge's own motion fed energy from steady wind into a twisting mode.
Steady 64 km/h wind, no periodic pushing required.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Laplace transform turns calculus into algebra
cards.cliff: A table of transforms does most of the work
lines: $ F(s) = ∫₀^∞ f(t)e^(−st) dt
Derivatives become multiplication: L{f′} = sF(s) − f(0).
Solve the ODE as an algebra problem in s, then transform back.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: L{e^(at)} = ?
reveal: ∫₀^∞ e^((a − s)t) dt = 1/(s − a), for s > a.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Control engineers think in Laplace space
lines: Cruise control, drones and thermostats are designed as transfer functions G(s).
Stability means every pole of G(s) has negative real part.
*A pole in the right half-plane means the system blows up.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Finding Fourier coefficients
lines: f(x) = a₀/2 + Σ (aₙ cos nx + bₙ sin nx) on [−π, π].
$ aₙ = (1/π)∫ f(x)cos(nx) dx,  bₙ = (1/π)∫ f(x)sin(nx) dx
Works because sines and cosines of different frequencies are *orthogonal*: they integrate to zero against each other.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f(x) = x on [−π, π]. Which coefficients are zero?
cards.cliff: Fourier series prove the Basel result too
reveal: x is odd. Odd functions only need sines.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Parseval's theorem: energy is the same in both pictures
lines: The integral of f² equals the sum of the squares of the coefficients (suitably scaled).
Apply it to f(x) = x and out drops Σ1/n² = π²/6 again.
*Energy in time = energy in frequency.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Fourier transform: a spectrum for any signal
cards.cliff: A narrow pulse has a wide spectrum
lines: $ f̂(ω) = ∫ f(t)e^(−iωt) dt
It says how much of each frequency ω is in the signal.
Non-periodic signals get a continuous spectrum instead of discrete harmonics.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Squeeze a pulse to half the duration. What happens to its spectrum?
cards.cliff: The FFT made the transform practical
reveal: Time and frequency widths trade off: Δt·Δω ≥ a constant.
In quantum mechanics this same fact is the uncertainty principle.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The FFT: the algorithm that runs the modern world
cards.cliff: Convolution becomes multiplication under the transform
lines: 1965: Cooley and Tukey publish the Fast Fourier Transform: n log n operations instead of n².
Gauss had found essentially the same method around 1805 while tracking asteroids. Unpublished.
*Audio, Wi-Fi, 4G, image compression and MRI all depend on it.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The convolution theorem
lines: Convolution (f * g) smears one function by another: blurs, echoes, filters.
So filtering a song is just multiplying its spectrum. FFT, multiply, inverse FFT.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: i was invented to solve cubics, not x² = −1
cards.cliff: Multiply by i and you rotate by 90°
lines: 1500s: Cardano's formula for cubics sometimes needed √(negative numbers) along the way, even when all three answers were real.
Bombelli worked through the arithmetic and the imaginary parts cancelled to give real roots.
*Mathematicians were forced to accept them.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Complex multiplication is rotation and scaling
cards.cliff: De Moivre gives every trig identity for free
lines: Write z = re^(iθ). Multiply two: lengths multiply, angles add.
Multiplying by i rotates by 90°. i² = −1 is two quarter-turns: a half-turn.
*That's why complex numbers model waves and AC circuits so well.*
recall: What does multiplying by i do geometrically?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: (cos θ + i sin θ)³ = ?
cards.cliff: Roots of unity are evenly spaced around a circle
reveal: De Moivre: (e^(iθ))³ = e^(3iθ).
Expand the left side and match real parts: cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3cos θ.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: How many complex solutions does z⁶ = 1 have?
reveal: e^(2πik/6) for k = 0,…,5: the vertices of a regular hexagon.
Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: a degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex roots (with multiplicity).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A vector is an arrow: size and direction
cards.cliff: The dot product measures how aligned two vectors are
lines: v = (3, 4) means 3 across, 4 up. Its length is √(3² + 4²) = 5.
Add vectors tip to tail. Scale them by stretching.
Unit vector: divide by the length. (3, 4)/5 = (0.6, 0.8).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The dot product
cards.cliff: Find an angle without drawing anything
lines: $ a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ = |a||b|cos θ
Zero means perpendicular. Positive means pointing roughly the same way.
Work = force · displacement: only the aligned part of the force counts.
recall: When is a·b = 0 for non-zero vectors?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Angle between (1, 0, 1) and (0, 1, 1)?
cards.cliff: The cross product makes a perpendicular vector
reveal: Dot product 1. Lengths √2 each. cos θ = 1/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The cross product (3D only)
cards.cliff: Torque and magnetic force are both cross products
lines: a × b is perpendicular to both a and b. Direction by the right-hand rule.
Length |a||b|sin θ: the area of the parallelogram they span.
a × b = −(b × a). Order matters.
recall: |a||b|sin θ, the area of the parallelogram spanned

cards.subject: maths
reveal: i × j = k. Right-hand rule.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The scalar triple product is a volume
cards.cliff: Projections split a vector into useful pieces
lines: a·(b × c) = volume of the parallelepiped spanned by a, b, c (with sign).
It equals the 3×3 determinant of the three vectors.
*Zero volume means the three vectors lie in one plane.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Projection of (2, 3) onto (1, 0)?
reveal: Shadows, components of forces, least squares: all projections.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Lines in 3D: a point plus a direction
cards.cliff: A plane is defined by its normal
lines: r(t) = r₀ + t·v. Every value of t gives a point on the line.
In 3D two lines can be parallel, meet, or *skew*: never meet but not parallel.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A plane is everything perpendicular to a normal
cards.cliff: Distance to a plane is a projection
lines: Normal n = (a, b, c) through point P₀: n·(r − r₀) = 0.
That expands to ax + by + cz = d.
The coefficients of x, y, z *are* the normal vector.
recall: Normal vector of the plane 2x − y + 3z = 7?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Distance from the origin to the plane x + 2y + 2z = 6?
cards.cliff: Two planes meet in a line found by a cross product

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Direction of the line where x + y + z = 1 meets x − y = 0?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Vector-valued functions describe paths
cards.cliff: Curvature measures how sharply a path bends
lines: r(t) = (cos t, sin t, t) is a helix.
Velocity r′(t), speed |r′(t)|, acceleration r″(t).
Differentiate each component separately.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Curvature
cards.cliff: Road designers use curvature to stop cars flying off
lines: κ = |T′(s)|: how fast the unit tangent turns per unit length.
Formula: κ = |r′ × r″| / |r′|³.
A circle of radius R has κ = 1/R. A straight line has κ = 0.
recall: Curvature of a circle of radius R?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Motorway on-ramps are clothoids
cards.cliff: Acceleration splits into tangential and normal parts
lines: A straight road joined directly to a circular curve makes curvature jump: you'd have to yank the wheel.
Engineers use a clothoid, whose curvature grows linearly with distance.
*Roller coaster loops use similar shapes so the g-force builds smoothly.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Tangential and normal acceleration
lines: $ a = (d|v|/dt) T + κ|v|² N
The first term speeds you up. The second pulls you sideways.
At constant speed round a bend, all acceleration is sideways: κv².

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: z = f(x, y) is a landscape
cards.cliff: Limits in 2D are harder than in 1D
lines: Contour lines (level curves) are where f has a constant value.
Close contours: steep. Far apart: flat.
Weather maps, topographic maps and heat maps are all level-curve plots.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f(x, y) = xy/(x² + y²). Does it have a limit at (0, 0)?
cards.cliff: In 2D you can approach a point along infinitely many paths
reveal: Along y = 0 it's 0. Along y = x it's 1/2.
Different paths, different values: no limit.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A function that fools every straight line
lines: f(x, y) = x²y/(x⁴ + y²) → 0 along every straight line through the origin.
Along the parabola y = x² it equals 1/2.
*Checking straight lines isn't enough to prove a 2D limit.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: lim (x,y)→(0,0) of x³/(x² + y²) = ?
reveal: In polar: r³cos³θ/r² = r cos³θ → 0 regardless of θ.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f = x²y + sin y. ∂f/∂y = ?
reveal: Treat x as a constant and differentiate in y.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Clairaut: mixed partials commute
cards.cliff: Physics equations are written in partial derivatives
lines: If the second partials are continuous, f_xy = f_yx.
So it doesn't matter whether you differentiate in x first or y first.
There are pathological counterexamples when continuity fails.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: PDEs: the language of physics
cards.cliff: Check a solution of the wave equation
lines: Heat equation: u_t = α u_xx. Heat flows from hot spots to cold.
Wave equation: u_tt = c² u_xx. Disturbances travel at speed c.
Laplace's equation: u_xx + u_yy = 0. Steady states: potentials, soap films, temperature at equilibrium.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Which solves the wave equation u_tt = c²u_xx?
cards.cliff: d'Alembert's solution: f(x − ct) + g(x + ct)
reveal: u_tt = −c² sin(x − ct), u_xx = −sin(x − ct). ✓
Any f(x − ct) works: a shape moving right at speed c.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The chain rule with several paths
cards.cliff: A tree diagram keeps the bookkeeping straight
lines: z = f(x, y), with x and y depending on t.
$ dz/dt = (∂f/∂x)(dx/dt) + (∂f/∂y)(dy/dt)
Add up every route from t to z.
recall: Multivariable chain rule for z = f(x(t), y(t))?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: T = x²y, with x = cos t, y = sin t. dT/dt at t = 0?
cards.cliff: Implicit differentiation gets a clean formula

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Implicit function theorem shortcut
lines: If F(x, y) = 0 defines y(x), then dy/dx = −F_x / F_y.
x² + y² − 25 = 0: dy/dx = −2x/2y = −x/y.
It works whenever F_y ≠ 0: that's the theorem's condition.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Directional derivative: slope in any direction
lines: Rate of change of f moving in unit direction u: D_u f = ∇f · u.
Biggest when u points along ∇f. Zero when u runs along a contour.
recall: Directional derivative of f in unit direction u?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f = x² + y². Directional derivative at (1, 1) in direction (1, 0)?
cards.cliff: Maximum rate of change is the gradient's length

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Same f at (1, 1). Fastest rate of increase?
cards.cliff: Gradients are perpendicular to level curves, always

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Why ∇f is perpendicular to contours
cards.cliff: Gradient descent climbs down instead of up
lines: Along a contour f doesn't change, so D_u f = ∇f · u = 0.
Dot product zero means perpendicular.
*Water runs downhill at right angles to the contour lines.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Every neural network learns by gradient descent
lines: Loss function L(w) over millions of weights w.
Update: w ← w − η∇L. Step against the gradient, downhill.
*Backpropagation is just an efficient way to compute ∇L with the chain rule.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The tangent plane is the 2D linearisation
cards.cliff: For level surfaces, the gradient is the normal
lines: $ z ≈ f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x − a) + f_y(a, b)(y − b)
Zoom into a smooth surface far enough and it looks flat.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Normal vector to the sphere x² + y² + z² = 9 at (1, 2, 2)?
reveal: ∇F = (2x, 2y, 2z). Any multiple works: it points straight out from the centre.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Error propagation is a tangent plane
