lines: Volume of a cylinder V = πr²h. r and h each have measurement error.
dV ≈ V_r dr + V_h dh = 2πrh dr + πr² dh.
*A 1% error in r becomes about 2% in V.* Squares double relative errors.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Critical points in 2D
lines: Solve ∇f = 0: both partial derivatives zero at once.
Each solution is a max, a min or a saddle.
Use the Hessian test (D = f_xx f_yy − f_xy²) to decide.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: f = x² + y² − 4x + 6y. Critical point?
cards.cliff: Least squares is a calculus problem
reveal: Complete the square: f = (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² − 13. A bowl.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Least squares: fitting a line is minimising a sum
cards.cliff: On a closed region, check the boundary too
lines: Choose m, c to minimise Σ(yᵢ − mxᵢ − c)².
Set both partial derivatives to zero: two linear equations, the *normal equations*.
Gauss used this in 1801 to predict where the lost asteroid Ceres would reappear. It worked.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Max of f = xy on the disc x² + y² ≤ 2?
reveal: Inside, the only critical point is (0, 0), a saddle with f = 0.
On the boundary, x = y = 1 gives 1. That's the max.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Maximise f = x + y on the circle x² + y² = 1.
cards.cliff: Fixed perimeter, biggest rectangle: a square again

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Box with no lid, volume 32. Minimise surface area. Dimensions?
cards.cliff: Lagrange multipliers have meaning in economics
reveal: Minimise xy + 2xz + 2yz with xyz = 32. Symmetry and λ give x = y = 2z.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The multiplier is a shadow price
cards.cliff: Maximum entropy distributions come from Lagrange multipliers
lines: Maximise output subject to a budget. λ is how much output an extra £1 of budget buys.
In physics, λ often turns out to be a constraint force, like the tension in a pendulum rod.
*λ measures how much the constraint is costing you.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Boltzmann distribution is a Lagrange problem
lines: Maximise entropy −Σpᵢ ln pᵢ subject to Σpᵢ = 1 and fixed average energy.
Two multipliers. The solution: pᵢ ∝ e^(−βEᵢ).
*β, a Lagrange multiplier, turns out to be 1/k_BT.* Temperature is a multiplier.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Double integrals add up volume under a surface
lines: ∬_R f(x, y) dA: chop the region into tiny squares, multiply each by the height f, add.
On a rectangle: integrate in x, then in y (or the other way round).
f = 1 gives the area of R.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ y dy dx = ?
cards.cliff: Switching the order can rescue an impossible integral
reveal: Inner: ∫₀ˣ y dy = x²/2. Outer: ∫₀¹ x²/2 dx = 1/6.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫₀¹ ∫ᵧ¹ e^(x²) dx dy: what's the trick?
cards.cliff: Centres of mass are double integrals
reveal: Region: 0 ≤ y ≤ x ≤ 1. Swapped: ∫₀¹ ∫₀ˣ e^(x²) dy dx = ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx.
= (e − 1)/2. The impossible inner integral never has to be done.
options: Swap the order: it becomes ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Centre of mass
lines: x̄ = (1/M)∬ x ρ dA, ȳ = (1/M)∬ y ρ dA, with M = ∬ ρ dA.
Uniform semicircle of radius R: ȳ = 4R/(3π).
*Balance a shape on a pin at (x̄, ȳ).*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Pappus's theorem: volume = area × distance travelled by the centroid
cards.cliff: Next: double integrals in polar coordinates
lines: Spin a shape around an axis. Volume = (area) × (2π × distance of its centroid from the axis).
Torus: circle of radius r, centre R from the axis. V = πr² · 2πR = 2π²Rr².
Pappus of Alexandria knew this around 300 AD.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∬ over the unit disc of (x² + y²) dA = ?
reveal: In polar: ∫₀^2π ∫₀¹ r² · r dr dθ = 2π · 1/4 = π/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: In polar coordinates, dA = dr dθ.
cards.cliff: The Gaussian integral is the classic polar trick
reveal: dA = r dr dθ. The extra r is the Jacobian.
Far from the origin, the same dθ sweeps a wider arc.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Volume under z = e^(−(x² + y²)) over the whole plane?
reveal: ∫₀^2π ∫₀^∞ e^(−r²) r dr dθ = 2π · 1/2 = π.
Its square root is the Gaussian integral √π.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Triple integrals: mass of a solid
lines: ∭ ρ(x, y, z) dV: density times tiny volume, added up.
The hard part is the limits: describe the solid as z between two surfaces, over a region in the plane.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Volume of the tetrahedron x, y, z ≥ 0, x + y + z ≤ 1?
cards.cliff: Moments of inertia are triple integrals
reveal: In n dimensions the same corner simplex has volume 1/n!.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Moment of inertia
lines: I = ∭ r² ρ dV, where r is distance from the axis.
Solid sphere: (2/5)MR². Hollow sphere: (2/3)MR².
*Spin a raw egg and a hard-boiled egg: the cooked one spins smoothly; the raw one's liquid inside wobbles and drags.*
recall: Moment of inertia of a solid sphere about a diameter?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Cylindrical coordinates: polar plus height
lines: (r, θ, z), with dV = r dr dθ dz.
Perfect for cylinders, cones and anything with an axis.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Spherical coordinates
cards.cliff: Derive the sphere's volume in one line
lines: (ρ, θ, φ): distance from origin, polar angle from the z-axis, azimuth.
$ dV = ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ
Warning: maths and physics books swap the names θ and φ. Check before trusting a formula.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: ∫₀^2π ∫₀^π ∫₀^R ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ = ?
cards.cliff: Ice cream cones are a classic exam question

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Volume inside the sphere ρ = 2 and the cone θ = π/3 (ice cream cone)?
reveal: ∫₀^2π ∫₀^(π/3) ∫₀² ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ = 2π · (1 − cos(π/3)) · 8/3.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Jacobian generalises substitution
lines: Map (u, v) → (x, y). A small rectangle du dv becomes a parallelogram.
Its area is |det J| du dv, where J is the matrix of partial derivatives.
Polar r, spherical ρ² sin θ: special cases of |det J|.
recall: What does |det J| represent in a change of variables?
The local area (or volume) scaling factor of the map

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Area of the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² ≤ 1, using x = au, y = bv?
cards.cliff: Probability uses Jacobians when transforming random variables
reveal: The map turns the unit disc into the ellipse. Jacobian = ab.
Area = ab × π.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Changing variables in probability
lines: If Y = g(X), the density transforms by the Jacobian: f_Y(y) = f_X(x)|dx/dy|.
That's how you get the Box–Muller method: two uniform random numbers → two normal ones, via polar coordinates.
*Every simulation that needs normal random numbers relies on it.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A vector field puts an arrow at every point
cards.cliff: A line integral adds up how much the field pushes along a path
lines: Wind velocity, gravitational force, electric field.
F(x, y) = (−y, x) swirls anticlockwise around the origin.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Work is a line integral
lines: $ W = ∫_C F · dr
Only the component of F along the path does work.
Parametrise: ∫ F(r(t)) · r′(t) dt.
recall: Work done by force F along path C?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: F = (−y, x). Work around the unit circle anticlockwise?
cards.cliff: Some fields don't care about the path
reveal: r(t) = (cos t, sin t). F · r′ = sin²t + cos²t = 1. Integrate over 2π.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Conservative fields: path doesn't matter
cards.cliff: Test: curl F = 0 on a simply connected region
lines: If F = ∇φ, the work from A to B is just φ(B) − φ(A).
Around any closed loop the work is zero.
Gravity is conservative: climbing a hill costs the same energy by any route.
recall: Work by a conservative field F = ∇φ from A to B?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Is F = (2xy, x² + 3y²) conservative?
cards.cliff: A field can have zero curl and still not be conservative
reveal: ∂P/∂y = 2x = ∂Q/∂x. Integrate to find φ = x²y + y³.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The vortex field that breaks the rule
cards.cliff: That hole is detected by de Rham cohomology
lines: F = (−y, x)/(x² + y²) has zero curl everywhere it's defined.
But its work around the unit circle is 2π, not 0.
The catch: it's undefined at the origin, *a hole in the domain*. Topology beats calculus.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Flux: how much flows through a surface
cards.cliff: Parametrise surfaces like curves, with two parameters
lines: $ Φ = ∬_S F · n dS
Only the component of F through the surface (along n) counts.
Water through a net, electric field through a closed surface.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Surface area from a parametrisation
lines: r(u, v) traces a surface. r_u × r_v is normal, and its length gives the area scale.
$ dS = |r_u × r_v| du dv
For a sphere of radius R: dS = R² sin θ dθ dφ, total 4πR².

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Flux of F = (0, 0, 1) up through the unit disc in the plane z = 0?
reveal: n = (0, 0, 1), so F · n = 1. Area of the disc is π.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Stokes' theorem
cards.cliff: Practice turns a hard line integral into an easy flux
lines: $ ∮_C F · dr = ∬_S (∇ × F) · n dS
Circulation round the edge = total curl through any surface with that edge.
Any surface: a flat disc or a butterfly net on the same hoop gives the same answer.
recall: ∮_C F·dr = ∬_S (∇×F)·n dS for any surface S bounded by C

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: F = (−y, x, 0). ∮ F · dr round the unit circle using Stokes?
reveal: curl F = (0, 0, 2). Flux through the unit disc: 2 × π = 2π.
Same as the direct calculation.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Electric generators are Stokes' theorem
cards.cliff: Next: the divergence theorem in practice
lines: Faraday: ∇ × E = −∂B/∂t.
Integrate over a surface and apply Stokes: the EMF around a loop equals minus the rate of change of magnetic flux through it.
*Differential form ↔ integral form is always Stokes or Gauss.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Flux of F = (x, y, z) out of the sphere of radius 2?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Why gravity and electricity are inverse square
cards.cliff: In 4 spatial dimensions, gravity would be inverse cube
lines: F = r/|r|³ has zero divergence everywhere except the origin.
Its flux through any closed surface around the origin is 4π, whatever the shape.
*Inverse square is exactly what makes flux independent of distance.* In 3D, surfaces grow like r².

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Conservation laws come from the divergence theorem
cards.cliff: Next: the language that unifies everything
lines: Rate of change of stuff inside = −(flux out of the boundary) + sources.
Shrink the region to a point: ∂ρ/∂t + ∇ · J = 0.
*Charge, mass, probability: every conservation law is this equation.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Differential forms: what you integrate
cards.cliff: The exterior derivative replaces grad, curl and div
lines: 0-forms: functions. 1-forms: things like P dx + Q dy, integrated along curves.
2-forms: things like f dx∧dy, integrated over surfaces.
dx∧dy = −dy∧dx. That sign is orientation, and it's why the Jacobian has a determinant.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: One d to rule them all
lines: d on 0-forms is the gradient. On 1-forms in 3D, it's the curl. On 2-forms, the divergence.
d(dω) = 0 always.
Stokes for every dimension: ∫_∂M ω = ∫_M dω.
recall: What does d² = 0 encode in vector calculus?

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Maxwell's equations in forms: dF = 0, d⋆F = J
cards.cliff: Closed forms that aren't exact reveal holes
lines: F is the electromagnetic 2-form, combining E and B.
dF = 0 contains Faraday's law and no magnetic monopoles.
d⋆F = J contains Gauss's law and Ampère–Maxwell. *Four equations, two lines, any coordinates.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: de Rham cohomology counts holes with calculus
lines: Closed: dω = 0. Exact: ω = dη. Exact ⇒ closed always.
Closed but not exact signals a hole. The vortex field dθ on the punctured plane is the example.
*Calculus detects topology.* The plane minus a point has one independent such form.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A manifold looks flat up close
lines: A sphere is 2D: small patches look like the plane, but globally it's curved.
Charts map patches to ℝⁿ. An atlas covers everything.
*You can't flatten the whole sphere without distortion.* That's why every world map lies.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Theorema Egregium: an ant can measure curvature
cards.cliff: Tensors are how physics stays the same in every coordinate system
lines: Gauss (1827): a surface's curvature can be computed from distances measured within the surface alone.
So a flat sheet can roll into a cylinder (zero curvature) but never into a sphere.
*It's why you fold a pizza slice: bending it one way stiffens it the other way.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Tensors: objects that transform predictably
cards.cliff: The metric tensor measures lengths on curved spaces
lines: A vector's components change with coordinates, but the arrow doesn't.
Tensors generalise this: matrices, stress, the metric, the curvature.
*Write physics as tensor equations and it holds in every coordinate system.* That's how general relativity is built.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The metric tensor
cards.cliff: Calculus 3 done. On to the physics courses
lines: $ ds² = g_ij dxⁱ dxʲ
Flat plane: ds² = dx² + dy². Sphere of radius R: ds² = R²dθ² + R² sin²θ dφ².
In general relativity, gravity *is* the metric of spacetime.

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Mendeleev left gaps for elements nobody had found
cards.cliff: The table's shape comes from quantum mechanics
lines: 1869: Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic weight and chemical behaviour, leaving blanks.
He predicted the properties of the missing ones, including "eka-aluminium".
*Gallium was discovered in 1875 with almost exactly the properties he'd predicted.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Why the periodic table has its shape
lines: Rows fill electron shells; the blocks (s, p, d, f) correspond to the type of orbital being filled.
Elements in a column have the same outer electron arrangement, so they react alike.
*That's why sodium and potassium both explode in water.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Which group of elements rarely forms compounds because their outer shells are full?
cards.cliff: Most of an atom is empty space
reveal: Helium, neon, argon and co. Xenon does form a few compounds; the first was made in 1962.

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: If an atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a pea
lines: The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller across than the atom.
But it holds over 99.9% of the mass.
*Squeeze out the empty space from every human and all of humanity would fit in a sugar cube* (roughly, as neutron-star-like matter).

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Isotopes
lines: Same number of protons (so same element), different numbers of neutrons.
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 behave identically in chemistry; C-14 is radioactive.
*Heavy water (with deuterium) is about 11% denser than normal water: heavy-water ice sinks.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Three kinds of bond
lines: Ionic: electrons transferred (Na⁺Cl⁻, table salt).
Covalent: electrons shared (H₂O, CH₄).
Metallic: a sea of shared electrons, which is why metals conduct and bend.

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Why water is weird
lines: Its bent shape and polar O–H bonds make water a strong dipole that forms hydrogen bonds.
That gives it a high boiling point for its size, high surface tension, and ice that floats.
*If ice sank, lakes would freeze from the bottom up.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon. Why is graphite soft?
reveal: Within a sheet, bonds are strong. Between sheets, weak forces let them slide.
A single sheet is graphene.
options: Its carbon atoms form flat sheets held together only weakly

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Activation energy: why paper doesn't burst into flames
cards.cliff: The Haber process feeds half the world
lines: Burning paper releases energy overall, but needs a push to get started.
Catalysts lower that energy barrier without being used up.
*Enzymes are biological catalysts that can speed reactions by many orders of magnitude.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: The Haber–Bosch process feeds billions
lines: Making ammonia from nitrogen in the air (around 1910) enabled synthetic fertiliser on a massive scale.
Roughly half the nitrogen in your body passed through a Haber–Bosch plant.
*Fritz Haber also led Germany's WWI chemical weapons programme.* A complicated legacy.

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Le Chatelier's principle
lines: Push a system at equilibrium and it shifts to partly undo the push.
Add more reactant: more product forms. Heat an exothermic reaction: it shifts backward.
*Fizzy drinks go flat when opened: lower pressure pushes CO₂ out of solution.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Lemon juice has pH 2, coffee about pH 5. How much more acidic is lemon juice?
reveal: pH is −log₁₀[H⁺]. Three pH units = 10³.

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: The Maillard reaction makes browned food taste good
lines: Amino acids and sugars react above about 140°C, creating hundreds of flavour compounds.
Toast, seared steak, roasted coffee, beer's colour.
*Boiled food doesn't brown because water can't get much above 100°C.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Onion tears
cards.cliff: Soap works by having two ends
lines: Cutting an onion breaks cells, letting an enzyme make syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a volatile irritant.
It reaches your eyes and triggers tears.
*Chilling the onion slows the reaction; a sharp knife breaks fewer cells.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: How soap works
lines: Soap molecules have a water-loving head and an oil-loving tail.
Tails bury into grease; heads face the water, forming little balls (micelles) that rinse away.
*That's why soap tears apart viruses with fatty outer envelopes, like coronaviruses.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Why does salt melt ice on roads?
cards.cliff: Next: the chemistry of life and drugs
reveal: Dissolved salt disrupts ice formation. Below about −21°C, salty water freezes anyway.
options: It reacts with ice to release heat
It raises the temperature of the road

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Aspirin came from willow bark
lines: Willow bark was used for pain and fever for thousands of years; its active ingredient is related to salicylic acid.
Bayer chemists made acetylsalicylic acid, sold as Aspirin from 1899.
*Its mechanism (blocking COX enzymes) was only worked out in 1971.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Mirror-image molecules can act very differently
lines: Many molecules come in left- and right-handed versions, like gloves.
Carvone: one form smells of spearmint, its mirror image of caraway.
*Thalidomide's tragedy in the late 1950s led to much stricter testing of drugs.*

cards.subject: chem
cards.title: Benzene's ring came in a dream (allegedly)
lines: August Kekulé said the ring structure of benzene came to him in a daydream of a snake biting its own tail.
He told the story at a celebration in 1890, 25 years after proposing the structure.
*Some historians doubt the story, but it's chemistry's most famous dream.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The thin lens equation
lines: Magnification m = v/u (with sign conventions deciding upright or inverted).
Converging lens: real inverted image when the object is beyond f.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: An object 30 cm from a converging lens with f = 10 cm. Image distance?
reveal: Real, inverted, half the size.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Glasses are measured in dioptres
lines: Power P = 1/f in metres. A +2 D lens has f = 50 cm.
Short-sighted eyes focus too strongly: diverging (negative) lenses help.
*Long-sightedness from ageing (presbyopia) usually starts in your 40s, as the lens stiffens.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Big telescopes use mirrors, not lenses
lines: Large lenses sag under their own weight and bend different colours by different amounts (chromatic aberration).
Mirrors can be supported from behind and reflect all colours equally.
*The largest refractor ever built (Yerkes, 1897) has a 1 m lens. Mirrors now exceed 10 m.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Band theory: why some solids conduct
lines: In a crystal, atomic energy levels spread into bands.
Metals have a partly filled band: electrons move freely. Insulators have a big gap to the next empty band.
*Semiconductors have a small gap, around 1 eV for silicon.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Doping silicon
lines: Add phosphorus (5 outer electrons): extra electrons, n-type.
Add boron (3 outer electrons): missing electrons, "holes", p-type.
*Join them and you get a p–n junction: a diode, and the basis of solar cells and LEDs.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The transistor, 1947
cards.cliff: LED colour comes from the band gap
lines: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley at Bell Labs built the first transistor from germanium, a paperclip and gold foil.
It replaced fragile vacuum tubes.
*A modern phone chip has tens of billions of them.*
recall: What's the key property of a p–n junction?
Current flows easily one way but hardly the other (it rectifies)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: An LED's colour depends mainly on…
reveal: Photon energy ≈ band gap. Larger gap: bluer light.
Blue LEDs (Akasaki, Amano, Nakamura) won the 2014 Nobel Prize because they were so hard to make.
options: The band gap of its semiconductor
The colour of its plastic case

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Meissner effect
lines: A superconductor doesn't just have zero resistance: it actively expels magnetic fields.
That's why a magnet can levitate over one.
*BCS theory (1957): electrons pair up via lattice vibrations and move without scattering.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
cards.cliff: Neutron stars are city-sized atomic nuclei
lines: Plot stars by temperature and luminosity and they fall into groups, not random scatter.
Most stars sit on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen.
*Giants, supergiants and white dwarfs are stages of stellar life.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Neutron stars
cards.cliff: Jocelyn Bell Burnell found the first pulsar
lines: About 1.4 solar masses squeezed into a ball roughly 20 km across.
A teaspoon of its material would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.
*Pulsars are spinning neutron stars sweeping radio beams across us.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: "LGM-1": the signal nicknamed Little Green Men
lines: 1967: PhD student Jocelyn Bell Burnell noticed a tiny, perfectly regular radio signal pulsing every 1.33 seconds.
It turned out to be a rotating neutron star: a pulsar.
*The 1974 Nobel Prize went to her supervisor, not her. She later gave her $3 million Breakthrough Prize to fund physics students from under-represented groups.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: 2015: LIGO heard two black holes collide
lines: The waves from a merger 1.3 billion light-years away stretched LIGO's 4 km arms by less than a thousandth of a proton's width.
Einstein had predicted gravitational waves a century earlier but doubted they'd ever be detected.
*Nobel Prize 2017.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Hawking radiation
lines: Hawking (1974): quantum effects near the horizon make black holes emit thermal radiation.
Smaller black holes are hotter and evaporate faster.
*A solar-mass black hole would take around 10⁶⁷ years: far longer than the universe's age.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Euler's method: step along the slope
lines: For y′ = f(x, y): y_(n+1) = y_n + h·f(x_n, y_n).
Simple, but errors pile up: the error scales like h.
*Runge–Kutta (RK4) samples the slope four times per step; error scales like h⁴.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Catastrophic cancellation
lines: Subtracting nearly equal numbers loses most significant digits.
(1 + 10⁻¹⁶) − 1 = 0 in standard double precision.
*Rewriting formulas (like the quadratic formula for tiny roots) avoids it.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Estimate π by throwing darts
lines: Throw random points into a unit square. The fraction landing inside the quarter circle approaches π/4.
Error shrinks like 1/√N: slow, but it works in any number of dimensions.
*Monte Carlo was named by Ulam and von Neumann in the 1940s, after the casino.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Stiff equations
lines: When a system has processes on wildly different timescales, explicit methods need absurdly tiny steps.
Implicit methods (like backward Euler) stay stable with big steps.
*Chemical reaction networks are the classic stiff problem.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The heat equation smooths everything
lines: u_t = α u_xx: hot spots spread out, sharp corners round off instantly.
Fourier modes decay like e^(−αk²t): fine wiggles vanish fastest.
*Running it backwards in time is unstable: you can't un-blur.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Which PDE preserves sharp features as they travel (in 1D)?
reveal: Solutions f(x − ct) + g(x + ct) keep their shape.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Green's functions: the response to a single kick
cards.cliff: Fourier transforms turn PDEs into ODEs
lines: Solve the equation with a point source (a delta function). That's the Green's function G.
Any source is a sum of point sources, so the solution is ∫ G(x, x′) f(x′) dx′.
*In electrostatics, G for Laplace's equation is just the 1/(4π|r − r′|) potential of a point charge.*
recall: The response of a linear system to a point (delta) source; general solutions are integrals of it against the source

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Transform methods
lines: Fourier-transform a PDE in space: derivatives become multiplication by ik.
The PDE becomes an ODE in time for each mode.
*Solve it, transform back: that's how the heat kernel is found.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Expectation and variance
lines: E[X] = Σ x p(x). Var(X) = E[X²] − E[X]².
Variances of independent variables add.
*So the uncertainty of an average of N measurements shrinks like 1/√N.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Flip a fair coin 100 times. Standard deviation of the number of heads?
reveal: Getting 60+ heads is about a 2σ event: roughly 3% chance.

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Combining measurement errors
lines: Adding quantities: add absolute errors in quadrature: σ = √(σ₁² + σ₂²).
Multiplying: add relative errors in quadrature.
*That's why lab reports care whether errors are independent.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: The random walk
lines: Take N random unit steps. Average distance from the start grows like √N, not N.
It describes diffusion, Brownian motion and stock prices (roughly).
*A drunk walker in 2D always eventually returns home. In 3D, there's about a 66% chance they never do.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Supply and demand set the price
lines: Higher prices: buyers want less, sellers offer more.
Where the curves cross is the equilibrium price.
*Shortages and gluts push the price back toward it.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Price controls: good intentions, odd effects
lines: A cap below the market price means demand exceeds supply: queues and black markets.
A floor above it (like some minimum prices) can create surpluses.
*Economists argue a lot about how big these effects are in practice, especially for minimum wages.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Which typically has the most price-elastic demand?
cards.cliff: Opportunity cost is the real price
reveal: Close substitutes make demand elastic: raise one brand's price and people switch.
Necessities with no substitutes are inelastic.

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Opportunity cost
lines: The true cost of something is the next best thing you give up.
A free concert ticket still costs you the evening.
*University's biggest cost for many students is the wages they don't earn.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Nash equilibrium
lines: A set of strategies where no player gains by changing theirs alone.
John Nash proved in 1950 that every finite game has at least one (possibly with mixed strategies).
*An equilibrium can be bad for everyone, as in the prisoner's dilemma.*
recall: A strategy profile where no player can do better by changing only their own strategy

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: The ultimatum game
lines: One player splits £10 and offers some to the other. If refused, both get nothing.
Pure self-interest says accept any offer above zero.
*In experiments, offers below about 20–30% are often rejected: people pay to punish unfairness.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Chicken: whoever swerves loses
lines: Two drivers head at each other. Swerving is safe but humiliating; neither swerving is a disaster.
Committing visibly (throwing your steering wheel out of the window) can win.
*Cold War nuclear strategy was studied this way.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: The winner's curse
lines: In auctions for things of uncertain value, the winner is often whoever overestimated it most.
Oil companies bidding for drilling rights in the 1960s–70s found their winning tracts often underperformed.
*Smart bidders shade their bids down.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Nudges: changing choices without banning anything
lines: Switching pension schemes from opt-in to opt-out raised participation dramatically in many studies.
People stick with defaults.
*Thaler and Sunstein's 2008 book "Nudge" popularised the idea; Thaler won the 2017 Nobel.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Mental accounting
lines: People treat money differently depending on its label: a tax refund feels like "free money".
Losing a £20 theatre ticket feels different from losing a £20 note, though they're equivalent.
*Money is fungible; our minds don't treat it that way.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Present bias
lines: Many people prefer £100 today over £110 next week, but £110 in 53 weeks over £100 in 52.
Same one-week wait, opposite choices.
*That inconsistency is why gym memberships go unused.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: The mug experiment
lines: Students given a mug demanded about twice as much to sell it as other students would pay to buy one.
Owning something makes it feel more valuable.
*Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler, 1990.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Most money is created by banks making loans
lines: When a bank lends, it creates a new deposit: new money.
The Bank of England said so explicitly in a 2014 bulletin.
*Physical cash is a small fraction of the money supply in the UK.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Why central banks target about 2% inflation
lines: Zero risks tipping into deflation, which can freeze spending and make debts heavier.
A little inflation gives room to cut real interest rates in a slump.
*New Zealand pioneered explicit inflation targeting in 1990.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Hungary 1946: prices doubled roughly every 15 hours
cards.cliff: Interest rates are the main lever
lines: At its peak, Hungary's monthly inflation reached about 4 × 10¹⁶ percent.
The largest banknote issued was 100 quintillion pengő.
*The worst hyperinflation on record.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: A central bank raises interest rates. What is the usual intended effect?
reveal: Higher rates make borrowing costlier and saving more attractive.
They usually strengthen the currency too.
options: Slow borrowing and spending to bring inflation down

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Tulip mania was smaller than the legend
cards.cliff: Newton lost a fortune in the South Sea Bubble
lines: 1637: Dutch tulip bulb prices spiked and then collapsed.
Historians now think the economic damage was limited and many tales were exaggerated by moralising pamphlets.
*It's still the most famous bubble story.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Newton lost a fortune in the South Sea Bubble
lines: 1720: shares in the South Sea Company soared, then crashed.
Newton reportedly sold early at a profit, bought back near the top, and lost heavily.
*Attributed quote: "I can calculate the motions of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people."*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: 2008 in one card
lines: US banks issued mortgages to risky borrowers, bundled them into securities rated as safe, and sold them widely.
When house prices fell, losses spread through a highly leveraged, interconnected system.
*Lehman Brothers' collapse on 15 September 2008 triggered a global panic.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Index funds beat most professionals
lines: Most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index over 10–15 years, after fees.
Low-cost index funds just buy the whole market.
*Warren Buffett won a 10-year, $1 million bet (2008–2017) that an S&P 500 fund would beat a set of hedge funds.*

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Over 40 years at 6% growth, how much does a 1% annual fee cut your final pot, roughly?
reveal: Growth at 5% vs 6% for 40 years: 1.05⁴⁰/1.06⁴⁰ ≈ 7.04/10.29 ≈ 0.68.
Small percentages compound into big differences.

cards.subject: econ
cards.title: Starting at 25 vs 35
lines: Saving the same monthly amount from 25 instead of 35 can mean a much larger pot at 65, purely from 10 extra years of compounding.
At 7% growth, money roughly doubles every decade.
*Time in the market is the biggest lever you control.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Natural selection in three steps
cards.cliff: Darwin sat on his idea for 20 years
lines: Variation: individuals differ. Inheritance: some differences are passed on. Selection: some variants leave more offspring.
Over many generations, populations change.
*No goal or foresight required.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Darwin was nearly scooped
lines: Darwin developed natural selection by the early 1840s but didn't publish.
1858: Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay with the same idea.
*Their papers were presented together; Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: The peppered moth
lines: In industrial Britain, soot-darkened trees favoured dark moths over pale ones.
Dark forms became dominant near cities; after clean air laws, pale moths rebounded.
*A textbook case of natural selection, confirmed by later studies.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Whales' closest living relatives are hippos
lines: Fossils trace whales back about 50 million years to small, four-legged, land-dwelling ancestors.
Some modern whales still have tiny vestigial hip bones.
*DNA places hippos as their nearest living kin.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Mendel's peas were ignored for 35 years
lines: Gregor Mendel, a monk, published his pea-breeding laws of inheritance in 1866.
Hardly anyone noticed. Three scientists rediscovered them independently in 1900.
*He died thinking his work had been in vain.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Photo 51
cards.cliff: Humans share most of their DNA with each other
lines: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image of DNA, "Photo 51", was shown to James Watson without her knowledge.
Watson and Crick published the double helix in 1953.
*Franklin died in 1958; the 1962 Nobel went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Roughly how similar are any two humans' DNA sequences?
reveal: Most human variation is in that 0.1%: millions of letters.
Humans and chimpanzees are roughly 98–99% similar in comparable DNA.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: CRISPR: a bacterial immune system turned editing tool
lines: Bacteria store snippets of viral DNA and use Cas proteins to cut matching invaders.
Doudna and Charpentier showed in 2012 it can be programmed to cut any chosen DNA sequence.
*Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 2020. The first CRISPR-based therapy was approved in 2023, for sickle cell disease.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: We only use 10% of our brains.
reveal: Brain imaging shows activity across virtually all regions over a day.
The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of resting energy: evolution wouldn't keep a 90% idle organ.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his skull
lines: 1848: an explosion drove a 1 m tamping iron through the railway worker's left frontal lobe.
He survived, but friends said he was "no longer Gage": his personality changed.
*An early clue that specific brain regions shape character and judgement.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Roughly how many neurons are in the human brain?
reveal: Plus a similar number of glial cells, and an estimated 100 trillion or more synapses.

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: London taxi drivers grow their hippocampus
lines: Drivers learning "The Knowledge" of London's streets showed growth in the posterior hippocampus over training.
The hippocampus is key for spatial memory.
*Adult brains change with practice.* (Maguire et al., 2000s.)

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Fleming's messy lab discovered penicillin
cards.cliff: Antibiotic resistance is evolution in fast-forward
lines: 1928: Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find mould had killed bacteria on a culture plate.
Purifying it took until the 1940s, by Florey, Chain and colleagues.
*Antibiotics have since saved hundreds of millions of lives.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Antibiotic resistance
lines: Bacteria divide in as little as 20 minutes: billions of generations of variation.
Antibiotics kill the susceptible, leaving resistant strains to multiply.
*Antimicrobial resistance was linked to over a million deaths in 2019.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Edward Jenner and the milkmaids
lines: Milkmaids who caught mild cowpox seemed immune to deadly smallpox.
1796: Jenner inoculated a boy with cowpox, then exposed him to smallpox. He didn't get ill.
*"Vaccine" comes from vacca, Latin for cow. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Are viruses alive?
lines: Viruses can't reproduce or make energy on their own; they hijack cells.
Giant viruses like mimivirus have more genes than some bacteria.
*They sit on the blurry edge of what counts as life.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Crows solve multi-step puzzles
lines: New Caledonian crows make and use hook tools from twigs.
In experiments, they've solved puzzles needing several steps in the right order.
*Some crows recognise individual human faces and hold grudges.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: The mirror test
lines: Mark an animal's body where it can only see it in a mirror. Does it touch the mark on itself?
Great apes, dolphins, elephants and magpies have passed versions of it.
*Cleaner wrasse fish passed in a 2019 study, provoking debate about what the test measures.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: The waggle dance
lines: Honeybees communicate the direction and distance of flowers by dancing.
The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical encodes direction relative to the sun.
*Karl von Frisch decoded it and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize.*

cards.subject: bio
cards.title: Inky the octopus escaped to the sea
lines: 2016: an octopus at New Zealand's National Aquarium squeezed out of a gap in his tank.
He apparently slid across the floor and down a 50 m drainpipe into the ocean.
*Octopuses can squeeze through any gap larger than their beak.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The first emperor was buried with an army of clay soldiers
cards.cliff: China invented paper, printing, gunpowder and the compass
lines: Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC and standardised writing, weights, coins and even axle widths.
His tomb complex holds about 8,000 life-size terracotta warriors, each face different.
*Farmers digging a well found them in 1974. His main burial chamber is still unexcavated.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Which was NOT one of the "Four Great Inventions" of ancient China?
cards.cliff: The Great Wall isn't one wall
reveal: The four: papermaking, printing, gunpowder and the compass.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Great Wall of China is easily visible from space with the naked eye.
reveal: It's long but only a few metres wide, and similar in colour to its surroundings.
Astronauts, including Chinese astronaut Yang Liwei, have said they couldn't see it from orbit.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Ibn al-Haytham did experiments on light around 1020
cards.cliff: Our numbers came via Arabic scholars from India
lines: He showed vision works by light entering the eye, not rays leaving it.
His Book of Optics used controlled experiments, including the camera obscura.
*He's often called one of the first true experimental scientists.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Arabic numerals are Indian
lines: The digits 0–9 and place value developed in India.
Arabic mathematicians, like al-Khwarizmi, adopted and spread them.
*Europeans called them Arabic because that's who they learned them from.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Which English word comes from Arabic?
reveal: From "al-jabr" in al-Khwarizmi's book title: "restoring" or "reunion of broken parts".
Also: algorithm, alchemy, zero, sugar, coffee.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The largest contiguous land empire in history
lines: At its height in the late 1200s, it stretched from Korea to Hungary: about 24 million km².
Its postal relay system, the Yam, carried messages up to about 300 km a day.
*It linked East and West, carrying trade, ideas and, later, the Black Death.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: About 0.5% of men worldwide share one Y chromosome lineage
lines: A 2003 study found a Y-chromosome lineage in about 8% of men across a large region of Asia.
The researchers suggested it spread from Genghis Khan and his male relatives.
*That's an estimated 16 million men.* The link to Genghis himself is a hypothesis, not proven.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Magellan didn't sail around the world
lines: His expedition left Spain in 1519 with five ships and about 270 men.
Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521.
*Only one ship and 18 men made it back in 1522, led by Juan Sebastián Elcano.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: John Harrison and the longitude prize
lines: Ships could find latitude from the sun, but longitude needed accurate time at sea.
1714: Parliament offered £20,000 for a solution. Carpenter John Harrison spent decades building sea clocks.
*His H4 watch passed sea trials in the 1760s.* He had to fight the Board of Longitude for his money.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Columbian Exchange
lines: Tomatoes, potatoes, maize, chocolate and chillies went from the Americas to the rest of the world.
Wheat, horses, cattle and diseases like smallpox went the other way.
*Italian food had no tomatoes before the 1500s.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The French Revolution invented the metric system
cards.cliff: The guillotine was meant to be humane
lines: 1790s: revolutionaries wanted rational, universal units.
The metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator.
*They also tried a decimal clock with 10-hour days. It didn't catch on.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The guillotine was a reform
lines: Dr Joseph-Ignace Guillotin proposed a single, quick method of execution for all classes, replacing torture and botched beheadings.
He opposed the death penalty himself.
*The device was named after him, to his family's dismay.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Haiti: the only successful large-scale slave revolt to found a nation
lines: 1791–1804: enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose up, led by figures including Toussaint Louverture.
They defeated French, Spanish and British forces.
*Haiti declared independence in 1804.* France later forced it to pay a crippling indemnity for "lost property".

cards.subject: history
cards.title: John Snow stopped a cholera outbreak by removing a pump handle
lines: 1854: cholera killed hundreds around Broad Street, London.
Snow mapped the deaths and traced them to one water pump. The handle was removed.
*The founding story of epidemiology, decades before germ theory was accepted.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Great Stink of 1858
lines: A hot summer turned the sewage-filled Thames so foul that Parliament struggled to sit.
Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system followed, much of it still in use.
*He made pipes larger than needed, anticipating growth. That foresight saved London later.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Ada Lovelace published what's often called the first computer program
lines: 1843: translating a paper about Babbage's Analytical Engine, she added notes three times longer than the original.
Note G set out how the machine could compute Bernoulli numbers.
*She saw that it could manipulate symbols, even music, not just numbers.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Which country first gave women the vote in national elections (1893)?
reveal: New Zealand in 1893, after a petition signed by nearly a quarter of adult women.
UK women got equal voting rights in 1928; France in 1944.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Emily Davison and the 1913 Derby
lines: Suffragette Emily Wilding Davison stepped in front of the King's horse at the Epsom Derby. She died four days later.
Historians still debate whether she intended to die or to attach a banner.
*Her funeral drew huge crowds through London.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The 1918 flu killed more people than the First World War
lines: The pandemic infected roughly a third of the world's population.
Deaths are estimated at 17–50 million or more, with unusually many young adults.
*It's called "Spanish flu" because neutral Spain's press reported it freely while warring nations censored news.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Partition of India, 1947
lines: British India was divided into India and Pakistan along lines drawn in about five weeks.
Around 10–20 million people were displaced; estimates of deaths range up to around a million or more.
*The boundary was drawn by a lawyer who had never visited India before.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Mandela was imprisoned for 27 years
lines: Nelson Mandela was jailed in 1962 and released in 1990.
He was elected South Africa's first Black president in 1994, in its first fully democratic election.
*He shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The shipping container transformed the world economy
lines: Before 1956, ships were loaded piece by piece by armies of dockworkers.
Malcom McLean's standard steel boxes cut loading costs by more than 90%.
*Cheap shipping made global supply chains possible.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Fridges changed diets and cities
lines: Before refrigeration, food had to be salted, smoked, dried or eaten fast.
Refrigerated ships brought meat from Australia and Argentina to Britain from the 1880s.
*Stomach cancer rates fell as people ate fewer salted and smoked foods.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The bicycle as a liberation machine
lines: In the 1890s cycling craze, bicycles gave women unprecedented independent mobility.
Susan B. Anthony said the bicycle had "done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world".
*It also pushed changes in women's clothing.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years
lines: Built around 2560 BC to about 146 m tall.
It was overtaken only in the 1300s, by Lincoln Cathedral's central spire (which later collapsed).
*Its builders were paid workers, not slaves: archaeologists found their villages and bakeries.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Cleopatra was ethnically Egyptian.
cards.cliff: The Library of Alexandria didn't burn in one night
reveal: She was from the Ptolemaic dynasty, descended from one of Alexander the Great's Macedonian Greek generals.
She was, however, reportedly the first of her dynasty to learn the Egyptian language.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Library of Alexandria was destroyed in a single great fire.
reveal: Caesar's fire in 48 BC damaged part of the collection, but the library seems to have declined over centuries through lost funding and political purges.
There was no single catastrophic moment.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: A 3,800-year-old tablet lists Pythagorean triples
cards.cliff: The Antikythera mechanism is a 2,000-year-old computer
lines: Plimpton 322, a Babylonian clay tablet from around 1800 BC, lists sets of numbers like 119, 120, 169.
They satisfy a² + b² = c², over a thousand years before Pythagoras.
*The Babylonians also computed √2 to about six decimal places.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: A shipwreck held an ancient Greek analogue computer
lines: Divers found corroded bronze gears off the island of Antikythera in 1901.
X-ray scans revealed a geared device predicting eclipses and planetary positions, built around 100 BC.
*Nothing comparable is known for over a thousand years afterwards.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Roman concrete is still standing
lines: The Pantheon's unreinforced concrete dome, built around 125 AD, is still the largest of its kind.
Roman marine concrete actually strengthens over time as seawater reacts with volcanic ash.
*Modern engineers study it to make more durable concrete.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: When did the (Eastern) Roman Empire finally fall?
cards.cliff: Caesar's last words weren't "Et tu, Brute?"
reveal: The Western empire ended in 476. The Eastern (Byzantine) empire lasted until the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.
Its citizens called themselves Romans throughout.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Julius Caesar's last words were "Et tu, Brute?"
reveal: That line comes from Shakespeare.
Suetonius reports that some said Caesar spoke in Greek, "Kai su, teknon?" ("You too, child?"), but also that he may have said nothing.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Pompeii had dozens of street food counters
lines: Thermopolia were counters with built-in jars serving hot food and drink.
Many Romans in cramped flats had no kitchen and ate out.
*A beautifully painted one was excavated in 2020, with duck bones still in the pots.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Medieval people thought the Earth was flat.
cards.cliff: Columbus's real mistake was the Earth's size
reveal: Educated medieval Europeans knew Earth was a sphere. Bede, Aquinas and many others say so.
The myth was largely popularised in the 1800s, including by Washington Irving's romantic biography of Columbus.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Columbus got Earth's size badly wrong
cards.cliff: The Black Death killed a third of Europe
lines: Scholars of his time correctly estimated Earth's circumference. Columbus used figures making it much smaller.
He put Japan under 5,000 km west of the Canaries. It's nearly 20,000 km.
*Without the Americas in the way, his crew would have starved.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Roughly what fraction of Europe's population died in the Black Death (1347–1351)?
cards.cliff: The House of Wisdom kept Greek science alive
reveal: Estimates range from 30% to 50% or more in some regions.
Labour shortages afterwards raised wages for survivors.
options: Around a third to a half

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Baghdad's House of Wisdom
lines: In the 800s, scholars in Baghdad translated Greek works by Aristotle, Euclid and Ptolemy into Arabic.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote there; "algebra" comes from his book's title, and "algorithm" from his name.
*Many Greek works reached medieval Europe only via Arabic translations.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Gutenberg's press around 1450 changed everything
lines: Movable metal type, oil-based ink, and a press adapted from wine presses.
By 1500, millions of books had been printed in Europe.
*China had movable type centuries earlier* (Bi Sheng, 1040s), but thousands of characters made it less transformative there.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Luther went viral
lines: 1517: Luther's 95 Theses were printed and spread across Germany within weeks.
His pamphlets made him one of the best-selling authors of the early 1500s.
*Without the press, the Reformation might have been one more suppressed protest.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Printers shaped English spelling
lines: Early printers sometimes added letters to justify lines and charge by length.
Many came from Flanders and brought Dutch spellings: "ghost" gained its "h" that way.
*English spelling froze while pronunciation kept changing* (the Great Vowel Shift).

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Copernicus published as he died
lines: Copernicus's sun-centred model was printed in 1543, reportedly reaching him on his deathbed.
An unsigned preface by the editor, Osiander, called it a mere calculating device.
*Kepler later exposed who wrote that preface.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Galileo turned a toy into a revolution
lines: Telescopes were invented in the Netherlands in 1608. Galileo built better ones in 1609.
He saw mountains on the Moon, moons around Jupiter and the phases of Venus.
*Venus's phases were hard evidence that it orbits the Sun.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: In what year did the Catholic Church formally acknowledge it had erred in condemning Galileo?
cards.cliff: Newton spent more time on alchemy than physics
reveal: Pope John Paul II accepted the findings of a commission in 1992, 359 years after the trial.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Newton the alchemist
lines: Newton wrote over a million words on alchemy and theology, far more than on physics.
He also worked out a date for the end of the world from biblical prophecy: no earlier than 2060.
*Keynes called him "not the first of the age of reason, but the last of the magicians".*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Royal Society's motto "Nullius in verba" means…
reveal: Founded 1660. The motto rejects authority in favour of experiment.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Steam engines started as mine pumps
lines: Newcomen's 1712 engine pumped water out of coal mines. It was very inefficient.
James Watt's separate condenser (1769) improved efficiency several times over.
*The watt, the unit of power, is named after him.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Trains forced Britain onto one clock
lines: Before railways, towns kept local time: Bristol ran about 10 minutes behind London.
Railways adopted London time in 1840s timetables to avoid confusion and crashes.
*Legal standard time for Great Britain came in 1880.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Luddites hated technology itself.
cards.cliff: Life expectancy at birth was low partly due to infant deaths
reveal: They were skilled textile workers protesting machines used to cut wages and break labour agreements.
Their target was how the machines were used, not progress as such.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Low average life expectancy didn't mean everyone died at 40
lines: In many historical societies, very high infant and child mortality pulled the average down.
Adults who survived childhood often lived into their 60s or beyond.
*Averages can hide very different distributions.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: A wrong turn started the war
lines: 28 June 1914: Archduke Franz Ferdinand's driver took a wrong turn in Sarajevo and stalled the car.
Gavrilo Princip, a member of a group that had failed to kill the Archduke that morning, happened to be nearby.
*He fired two shots. A month later, Europe was at war.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Christmas truce of 1914
lines: On parts of the Western Front, British and German soldiers stopped fighting, sang carols and met in no man's land.
Some swapped cigarettes and souvenirs; there are accounts of football kickabouts.
*Commanders made sure it didn't happen again.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Why were tanks called "tanks"?
reveal: Early prototypes were described as water carriers for Mesopotamia. "Tank" stuck.
options: As a secrecy cover: workers were told they were water tanks

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Bletchley Park read Enigma
cards.cliff: Colossus was the first programmable electronic digital computer
lines: Polish mathematicians first broke Enigma in the 1930s and shared their work with Britain in 1939.
At Bletchley Park, Turing and others built electromechanical "bombes" to find daily settings.
*Historians estimate the intelligence shortened the war, possibly by around two years.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Colossus was kept secret for 30 years
cards.cliff: Operation Mincemeat fooled Hitler with a corpse
lines: Built by Tommy Flowers in 1943–44 to break German teleprinter codes (Lorenz, not Enigma).
Most units were dismantled after the war; its existence wasn't publicly revealed until the 1970s.
*ENIAC often gets called the first computer because Colossus was secret.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Operation Mincemeat
lines: 1943: British intelligence dressed a dead man as a fictional officer, "Major William Martin", with fake invasion plans.
His body washed up in Spain. The documents reached German intelligence.
*Germany reinforced Greece and Sardinia; the Allies invaded Sicily.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: D-Day depended on a weather forecast
lines: Eisenhower delayed the invasion by a day because of storms.
Group Captain James Stagg's team predicted a short break in the weather for 6 June 1944.
*German forecasters, lacking Atlantic weather data, expected the storms to continue.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Sputnik's beep shocked America
cards.cliff: The world came closest to nuclear war in 1962
lines: 4 October 1957: the USSR launched Sputnik 1, an 84 kg sphere that beeped on radio.
Anyone with a shortwave radio could hear it pass over.
*NASA was founded the next year.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Vasili Arkhipov may have prevented nuclear war
cards.cliff: Apollo 11's computer had less memory than a calculator
lines: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, a Soviet submarine was being forced to surface by US depth charges.
Its captain wanted to launch a nuclear torpedo. Launch needed agreement of three senior officers.
*Arkhipov refused.* The submarine surfaced.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Apollo's guidance computer
cards.cliff: The Berlin Wall fell by accident
lines: It had about 4 KB of erasable memory and 72 KB of read-only "core rope" memory, woven by hand.
During landing it threw "1202" alarms from overload; software designed by Margaret Hamilton's team kept it running.
*Armstrong landed with well under a minute of hover fuel to spare.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Berlin Wall opened because of a press conference mistake
lines: 9 November 1989: official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules, unprepared.
Asked when they took effect, he said "immediately, without delay".
*Crowds gathered at the checkpoints that night; overwhelmed guards opened the gates.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Zero arrived late in Europe
lines: Indian mathematicians treated zero as a number by the 600s (Brahmagupta gave rules for it in 628).
Fibonacci's 1202 book promoted Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe.
*Some Italian cities banned them in official records at first, fearing fraud.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Fermat's last theorem took 358 years
cards.cliff: Euler was the most productive mathematician ever
lines: Around 1637, Fermat scribbled in a margin that xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no whole-number solutions for n > 2, and that the margin was too small for his proof.
Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994, using mathematics Fermat couldn't have had.
*Wiles worked in near-secrecy for about seven years.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Euler kept working after going blind
lines: Leonhard Euler lost most of his sight but dictated research to assistants.
His collected works run to over 80 volumes. About half his output came in the last 17 years of his life.
*He worked out the orbital calculations in his head.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Ramanujan's letter to Hardy
lines: 1913: a clerk in Madras sent G. H. Hardy pages of extraordinary formulas without proofs.
Hardy said they "must be true, because, if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them".
*Ramanujan came to Cambridge, became a Fellow of the Royal Society, and died at 32.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in two sciences
lines: Physics (1903, shared) for radioactivity and Chemistry (1911) for discovering polonium and radium.
Her notebooks are still radioactive and kept in lead-lined boxes.
*She remains the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: 17 of 29 attendees were or became Nobel laureates
lines: The 1927 Solvay Conference on electrons and photons brought together Einstein, Bohr, Curie, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Dirac and more.
Einstein and Bohr argued over quantum mechanics at breakfast and dinner.
*Einstein: "God does not play dice." Bohr: stop telling God what to do.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Manhattan Project employed over 100,000 people
lines: Most workers had no idea what they were building.
Trinity, the first test, was on 16 July 1945 in New Mexico.
Oppenheimer later recalled a line from the Bhagavad Gita: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds."

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Great Emu War
cards.cliff: The shortest war lasted under an hour
lines: 1932: Australia sent soldiers with machine guns to cull emus destroying crops in Western Australia.
The emus scattered, dodged and survived in large numbers.
*The military withdrew. Newspapers declared the emus the winners.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted roughly how long?
reveal: Often called the shortest war in recorded history, it ended with Zanzibar's surrender after a short bombardment.

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Napoleon was ambushed by rabbits
lines: According to a popular account, after a 1807 treaty a rabbit hunt was arranged for Napoleon.
The rabbits, reportedly farm-raised and expecting food, swarmed toward the hunting party instead of fleeing.
*Napoleon is said to have retreated to his carriage.*

cards.subject: history
cards.title: Ketchup pills
lines: In the 1830s, tomato extracts were sold in America as cures for indigestion and other ailments.
Dr John Cook Bennett promoted tomatoes as medicine; tomato pills became a fad.
*The fad collapsed amid fraudulent imitations.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: We don't know how Shakespeare spelled his own name
lines: His six surviving signatures spell it several different ways, none of them "Shakespeare" exactly as we write it.
Spelling simply wasn't standardised in Elizabethan England.
*Only a handful of documents in his own hand survive at all.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Which is Shakespeare's longest play?
cards.cliff: Actors have a superstition about Macbeth
reveal: Hamlet runs to over 4,000 lines in its fullest version: about four hours uncut.
Macbeth is one of his shortest.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Why actors say "the Scottish play"
cards.cliff: His plays were performed in a theatre that burned down
lines: Theatre tradition holds that saying "Macbeth" inside a theatre brings disaster.
The cure, by legend: leave the theatre, spin around three times, spit, and knock to be let back in.
*The superstition seems to date from the late 1800s, not Shakespeare's time.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: The Globe burned down during Henry VIII
cards.cliff: Iambic pentameter is the heartbeat of his verse
lines: 1613: a stage cannon fired during a performance set the thatched roof alight.
The theatre burned to the ground in under two hours. One man's breeches caught fire; someone put it out with ale.
*The modern reconstruction opened in 1997, near the original site.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Iambic pentameter
cards.cliff: Some of his famous lines are misquoted
lines: Five pairs of syllables, each unstressed then stressed: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM.
"But SOFT, what LIGHT through YONder WINdow BREAKS?"
*Characters often drop into prose when they're low-born, mad, or joking.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Juliet's "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" means "Where are you, Romeo?"
reveal: "Wherefore" means "why". She's asking why he has to be a Montague, her family's enemy.
The next lines: "Deny thy father and refuse thy name."

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: The Iliad covers only a few weeks of a ten-year war
cards.cliff: The Odyssey took ten more years to get home
lines: It starts in the war's tenth year, with Achilles' rage at Agamemnon.
It ends with Hector's funeral, before the wooden horse.
*The Trojan Horse barely appears in Homer:* it's mentioned in the Odyssey and told fully in Virgil's Aeneid.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: What did Odysseus tell the Cyclops his name was?
reveal: When the blinded Polyphemus shouted for help, he said "Nobody is killing me." No one came.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Greek tragedy was a competition with prizes
cards.cliff: Oedipus is the original plot twist
lines: At Athens' Dionysia festival, playwrights each presented three tragedies and a satyr play.
Sophocles reportedly won about 20 times.
*Only a few dozen complete Greek tragedies survive, out of hundreds performed.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Dramatic irony in Oedipus Rex
cards.cliff: Aristotle wrote the first guide to plots
lines: Oedipus hunts the killer of the old king to lift a plague from Thebes.
The audience knows from the start that he is the killer, and that the king was his father.
*Every confident line he speaks lands differently for them.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Aristotle's Poetics: plot first
lines: A good tragedy has a beginning, middle and end, and a reversal of fortune.
Catharsis: the audience's pity and fear are purged.
*Screenwriting guides still quote it.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: War and Peace isn't just a novel
cards.cliff: Anna Karenina's first line is famous
lines: Tolstoy's book follows Russian families through Napoleon's invasion of 1812.
It breaks off into long essays on history and free will.
Tolstoy said it was "not a novel, even less is it a poem, and still less a historical chronicle."

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Complete Tolstoy's opening: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family…"
cards.cliff: Dostoevsky wrote to pay gambling debts
reveal: The opening of Anna Karenina (1877).
Researchers have since named an "Anna Karenina principle": success needs many things going right; failure needs only one going wrong.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: The Gambler was written in 26 days to beat a deadline
cards.cliff: Crime and Punishment is told from inside a murderer's head
lines: Dostoevsky had signed a contract that would hand his future rights to a publisher if he missed a deadline.
He hired a stenographer, Anna Snitkina, and dictated The Gambler in under a month.
*They married the next year.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Raskolnikov's theory
lines: A poor ex-student argues that extraordinary people may break moral laws for a greater good.
He murders a pawnbroker to test it, then unravels from guilt and fever.
*The novel is less a whodunit than a "why-and-what-then".*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Chekhov's quiet endings
lines: Chekhov's stories often end without resolution: characters simply carry on.
He was a practising doctor, and joked that medicine was his wife and literature his mistress.
*Modern short fiction owes him its ambiguity.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Dickens published in instalments, like a TV series
lines: His novels came out in monthly or weekly parts, with cliffhangers to sell the next issue.
A popular story says New York crowds at the docks shouted for news of whether Little Nell had died.
*Serial fiction invented binge-reading's cliffhanger 150 years early.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Jane Austen's novels said "By a Lady"
cards.cliff: The Brontës used male pen names
lines: Sense and Sensibility (1811) was credited only to "A Lady".
She earned modest sums in her lifetime; her name only appeared publicly after her death in 1817.
*She's now on the Bank of England £10 note.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: What pen names did Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë first publish under?
cards.cliff: Middlemarch is often called the greatest English novel
reveal: They kept their initials but used ambiguous names, partly to avoid prejudice against women writers.
George Eliot was Mary Ann Evans, a different novelist.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Middlemarch
lines: George Eliot's 1871–72 novel follows a provincial town through marriages, reform and failed ambitions.
Its last line praises "the number who lived faithfully a hidden life, and rest in unvisited tombs."
*Virginia Woolf called it "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people".*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Ulysses happens in one day
lines: Joyce's novel follows Leopold Bloom around Dublin on 16 June 1904.
Each chapter uses a different style, loosely mapped onto Homer's Odyssey.
*Fans celebrate 16 June every year as Bloomsday.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Stream of consciousness
cards.cliff: The Waste Land was edited heavily by a friend
lines: The narrative follows a character's thoughts as they flow: fragments, memories, associations.
Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway takes place over a single day in London, moving between minds.
*It tries to capture how thinking actually feels.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Ezra Pound cut The Waste Land nearly in half
cards.cliff: Kafka's opening line is one of literature's most famous
lines: T. S. Eliot's 1922 poem was much longer in draft.
Pound slashed whole sections; Eliot dedicated the poem to him as "il miglior fabbro" (the better craftsman).
*The draft manuscripts were rediscovered in 1968.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: What does Gregor Samsa wake up as in Kafka's The Metamorphosis?
reveal: Kafka's word "Ungeziefer" means vermin; the species is never named.
Kafka told his publisher the insect must not be drawn on the cover.
options: A beetle, as Kafka drew it on the cover

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Orwell's 1984 and Newspeak
cards.cliff: Huxley imagined control by pleasure instead
lines: The Party shrinks the language so that dissent becomes literally unthinkable.
"Doublethink": holding two contradictory beliefs and accepting both.
*Orwell wrote much of it on the remote Scottish island of Jura while seriously ill with tuberculosis.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Brave New World: control through comfort
lines: Huxley's 1932 society keeps people docile with engineered happiness, a drug called soma and endless entertainment.
No one needs banning books when no one wants to read them.
*Neil Postman argued in 1985 that Huxley's vision was the more accurate one.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: In Fahrenheit 451, what is 451?
reveal: Bradbury used 451°F as the ignition point of paper. Real figures vary.
options: The temperature at which paper burns, in °F (as Bradbury had it)

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: We: the dystopia that inspired Orwell
lines: Yevgeny Zamyatin's We (1920s) depicts citizens with numbers instead of names, living in glass houses.
It was banned in the Soviet Union.
*Orwell reviewed it in 1946, three years before 1984 was published.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: The sonnet: 14 lines and a turn
cards.cliff: Haiku in English often miss the point
lines: Petrarchan: 8 lines setting a problem, 6 answering it.
Shakespearean: three quatrains and a closing couplet with a twist.
*The "volta" (turn) is where the poem changes direction.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: A haiku is defined by having 5-7-5 syllables.
cards.cliff: Free verse dropped rhyme and metre
reveal: Japanese haiku count "on" (sound units), which don't match English syllables.
Traditionally they also include a seasonal reference (kigo) and a "cutting word" contrasting two images.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Who wrote "Do not go gentle into that good night"?
reveal: A villanelle, written for his dying father: only two rhymes and two refrains across 19 lines.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Emily Dickinson's 1,800 hidden poems
lines: Fewer than a dozen of her poems were published in her lifetime, mostly anonymously.
After her death in 1886, her sister found nearly 1,800 in her room, many sewn into little booklets.
*Her dashes were "corrected" by early editors. Modern editions restore them.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Jules Verne's moon cannon launched from Florida
cards.cliff: H. G. Wells imagined the atom bomb
lines: From the Earth to the Moon (1865) fires three men from a giant cannon in Florida.
Apollo 11 launched from Florida a century later, with three crew, and splashed down in the Pacific, as Verne's capsule did.
*A cannon launch would have flattened them, though.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: H. G. Wells coined "atomic bombs" in 1914
lines: In The World Set Free, Wells described bombs using radioactivity that kept exploding for days.
Physicist Leó Szilárd read it in 1932. The next year he conceived the nuclear chain reaction.
*Szilárd later drafted the letter Einstein signed warning Roosevelt.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics
cards.cliff: Ursula K. Le Guin rewrote gender
lines: 1. A robot may not injure a human or, through inaction, allow a human to come to harm.
2. It must obey humans, unless that conflicts with law 1. 3. It must protect itself, unless that conflicts with 1 or 2.
*Most of his robot stories are about the laws going wrong.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: The Left Hand of Darkness
lines: Le Guin's 1969 novel is set on a planet whose people have no fixed sex.
A human envoy struggles to see them as people rather than as "men" or "women".
*It won both the Hugo and Nebula awards.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Complete Arthur C. Clarke's third law: "Any sufficiently advanced technology is…"
reveal: From his 1973 revision of Profiles of the Future.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Show, don't tell
lines: Telling: "She was nervous." Showing: "She checked the door was locked. Then checked it again."
Showing lets readers infer, which makes them feel it.
*Chekhov: "Don't tell me the moon is shining; show me the glint of light on broken glass."* (A paraphrase of his letters.)

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Unreliable narrators
lines: A narrator who misleads you, or themselves.
Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day: a butler whose polished narration hides what he's lost.
*The story is in the gap between what's said and what's true.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Start in the middle
cards.cliff: The hero's journey is an influential template
lines: "In medias res": begin in the middle of the action, fill in the past later.
Homer did it: the Odyssey opens with Odysseus already stranded for years.
*Every good card in this feed tries to do the same.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: The hero's journey
lines: Joseph Campbell (1949): myths across cultures share a pattern of departure, trials, transformation and return.
George Lucas credited Campbell's work as an influence on Star Wars.
*Critics argue it's been applied too rigidly.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Magical realism
cards.cliff: Borges wrote stories like philosophy puzzles
lines: Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) mixes the miraculous with the everyday, without comment.
A woman ascends to heaven while folding sheets. A rain of yellow flowers falls.
*He said he learned the tone from his grandmother's deadpan storytelling.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Borges: Pierre Menard
cards.cliff: Borges was director of Argentina's National Library while going blind
lines: A French writer sets out to write Don Quixote, word for word, not by copying but by becoming someone who would write it.
Borges's narrator claims Menard's identical text is richer, because its context is different.
*A 1939 short story that anticipated decades of literary theory.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Borges ran a library he couldn't read
lines: In 1955 Borges became director of Argentina's National Library, just as his eyesight failed completely.
He wrote of God's irony in giving him "books and the night" at the same time.

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Lewis Carroll was a maths don
cards.cliff: Calvino's Invisible Cities is built like a mathematical structure
lines: Charles Dodgson lectured in mathematics at Christ Church, Oxford, and wrote on logic and determinants.
Alice in Wonderland is full of logic games and nonsense that's carefully exact.
*The Mad Hatter's "I see what I eat" vs "I eat what I see" is a lesson in converse statements.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: The Oulipo: writing with constraints
lines: A French group of writers and mathematicians founded in 1960.
Georges Perec wrote a 300-page novel, La Disparition, without the letter "e".
*Constraints, they argued, spark creativity rather than limit it.*

cards.subject: lit
cards.title: Gravity's Rainbow and the V-2
lines: Thomas Pynchon's 1973 novel revolves around the V-2 rocket, whose parabolic flight shapes the book.
A character's sexual encounters seem to predict where rockets will land in London.
*The Pulitzer board refused the fiction jury's recommendation to award it the prize.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A matrix is a function that moves space
lines: Multiply a vector by a matrix and you get a new vector: rotated, stretched, sheared or flipped.
The columns show where the basis vectors (1,0) and (0,1) land.
*Matrix multiplication is composing two such moves.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: For 2×2 matrices A and B, is AB always equal to BA?
reveal: Rotate then shear ≠ shear then rotate.
Matrices that do commute share eigenvectors (when diagonalisable).

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The determinant is the area (or volume) scale factor
lines: det = 2: areas double. det = −1: areas kept, orientation flipped.
det = 0: space is squashed flat, so the matrix has no inverse.
For [[a, b], [c, d]]: ad − bc.
recall: A squashes space into a lower dimension, so it isn't invertible

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Ax = b
cards.cliff: Rank tells you how many dimensions survive
lines: A system of linear equations is one matrix equation.
If det A ≠ 0, the unique solution is x = A⁻¹b.
*In practice, computers use Gaussian elimination rather than computing inverses.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Rank and nullity
lines: Rank: dimension of the output space (column space).
Nullity: dimension of the vectors sent to zero (null space).
Rank–nullity theorem: rank + nullity = number of columns.
recall: rank(A) + nullity(A) = number of columns of A

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Eigenvectors don't change direction
lines: Av = λv: the matrix only stretches v by the factor λ.
Find λ by solving det(A − λI) = 0.
*They're the natural axes of a transformation.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Eigenvalues of [[2, 0], [0, 5]]?
cards.cliff: Trace and determinant give them for free
reveal: Diagonal matrices have their eigenvalues on the diagonal.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Trace and determinant shortcut
lines: Sum of eigenvalues = trace (sum of the diagonal).
Product of eigenvalues = determinant.
*For 2×2 matrices that's enough to find them: solve λ² − (tr)λ + det = 0.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A 90° rotation matrix in 2D. Does it have real eigenvectors?
reveal: Every non-zero vector changes direction under a 90° rotation.
Complex eigenvalues e^(±iθ) encode the rotation angle.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Diagonalisation
lines: If A = PDP⁻¹ with D diagonal, then Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹.
Powers of a diagonal matrix are just powers of its entries.
