*Fibonacci numbers come out this way: the golden ratio is an eigenvalue.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The spectral theorem
lines: A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal set of eigenvectors.
So it's a pure stretch along perpendicular axes.
*Quantum observables are the complex version: Hermitian operators.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: PageRank is the top eigenvector of the web
lines: Build a matrix of links between pages. A page's importance is the weighted importance of pages linking to it.
That's an eigenvector equation: r = Mr, with eigenvalue 1.
*Brin and Page's 1998 paper launched Google on it.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A vector space is anything you can add and scale
lines: Arrows, but also polynomials, functions, matrices and quantum states.
Basis: a minimal set that spans everything. Dimension: how many basis vectors.
*The space of polynomials of degree ≤ 3 has dimension 4: 1, x, x², x³.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Inner products and orthogonality
lines: An inner product lets you measure lengths and angles.
For functions: ⟨f, g⟩ = ∫ f(x)g(x) dx.
*Fourier series are just expansions in an orthogonal basis of sines and cosines.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Gram–Schmidt
cards.cliff: The SVD is the most useful factorisation
lines: Take vectors one by one; subtract their projections onto the ones already done; normalise.
Out comes an orthonormal basis for the same space.
*Applied to 1, x, x², … on [−1, 1], it produces the Legendre polynomials.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Singular value decomposition
lines: Every matrix factors as A = UΣVᵀ: rotate, stretch along axes, rotate.
Keep only the largest singular values and you get the best low-rank approximation.
*Image compression, recommendation systems and PCA all use it.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Complex differentiability is a huge constraint
lines: f(z) is differentiable at z if the limit of [f(z + h) − f(z)]/h is the same from every direction in the plane.
Writing f = u + iv, that forces the Cauchy–Riemann equations: u_x = v_y, u_y = −v_x.
*Such functions are called holomorphic, and they're astonishingly rigid.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A complex function differentiable once is differentiable infinitely many times
lines: In real analysis, f′ can exist while f″ doesn't.
For holomorphic functions, one derivative guarantees all of them, and a convergent Taylor series.
*Know a holomorphic function on a tiny disc and you know it everywhere it extends.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Which function is holomorphic on the whole complex plane?
reveal: e^z satisfies Cauchy–Riemann everywhere.
|z|², z̄ and Re(z) fail them almost everywhere.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Liouville's theorem
lines: A function holomorphic on the whole plane and bounded must be constant.
So sin z, which is bounded on the real line, blows up along the imaginary axis.
*Liouville's theorem gives a two-line proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Cauchy's theorem
lines: The integral of a holomorphic function around any closed loop is zero, if there are no singularities inside.
Only the singularities matter.
*Integrals become a matter of counting what's inside the loop.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The residue theorem
cards.cliff: A real integral via complex analysis
lines: $ ∮ f(z) dz = 2πi × (sum of residues inside)
The residue at a simple pole a is lim (z − a)f(z).
*It evaluates real integrals that resist every other method.*
recall: ∮ f dz = 2πi × (sum of residues of f inside the contour)

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Using residues, ∫ from −∞ to ∞ of dx/(1 + x²) = ?
cards.cliff: Analytic continuation extends functions beyond their formula
reveal: Close the contour in the upper half-plane. The pole at z = i has residue 1/(2i).
2πi × 1/(2i) = π. Matches arctan from −π/2 to π/2.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: 1 + 2 + 3 + … = −1/12 (sort of)
lines: The zeta function ζ(s) = Σ 1/nˢ converges only for Re(s) > 1.
Analytic continuation extends it uniquely to almost the whole plane, giving ζ(−1) = −1/12.
*The sum doesn't equal −1/12. But −1/12 really appears in string theory and the Casimir effect via such regularisation.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Riemann hypothesis: a million dollars for the zeros of ζ
lines: Riemann (1859) conjectured all non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2.
Those zeros control the fine distribution of prime numbers.
*Over 10 trillion zeros have been checked numerically. No proof yet.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A group is the mathematics of symmetry
cards.cliff: How many ways can you place a square back on itself?
lines: A set with an operation that's associative, has an identity and inverses.
The rotations of a square, the integers under addition, invertible matrices.
*Symmetries of anything form a group.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: How many symmetries does a square have (rotations and reflections)?
reveal: 4 rotations and 4 reflections: the dihedral group D₄.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Rubik's cube group
lines: It has about 4.3 × 10¹⁹ reachable positions.
In 2010 it was proved every position can be solved in at most 20 moves ("God's number").
*The proof used about 35 CPU-years of computer time donated by Google.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Lie groups and the Standard Model
cards.cliff: The eightfold way predicted a particle
lines: Continuous symmetries like rotations form Lie groups.
The Standard Model's symmetry is SU(3) × SU(2) × U(1): strong, weak and electromagnetic.
*Particles sort into representations of these groups, which is how quarks were predicted.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Gell-Mann predicted the Ω⁻ from a pattern
lines: 1962: arranging known particles by SU(3) symmetry left a gap at the tip of a triangle.
Gell-Mann predicted its charge, strangeness and approximate mass.
*The Ω⁻ was found at Brookhaven in 1964.* Mendeleev's table, but for particles.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A qubit is a unit vector in 2D complex space
lines: Measure and you get 0 with probability |α|², 1 with |β|².
*n qubits need 2ⁿ complex numbers to describe in general.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: You can't copy an unknown quantum state
lines: No-cloning theorem (1982): no device can duplicate an arbitrary unknown quantum state.
Proof: cloning would have to be linear and non-linear at once.
*It's what makes quantum key distribution secure.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Quantum teleportation moves a state, not matter
lines: Share an entangled pair. Measure your qubit together with the one to send; phone the two-bit result.
The receiver applies a correction and holds the original state. The original is destroyed.
*No faster-than-light signalling: the classical phone call is essential.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Shor's algorithm factors numbers exponentially faster
lines: 1994: Peter Shor showed a quantum computer could factor large numbers in polynomial time.
It uses the quantum Fourier transform to find the period of a function.
*Breaking RSA-2048 would need many thousands of error-corrected logical qubits: far beyond today's machines.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Decoherence
lines: Interaction with the environment leaks quantum information, destroying superpositions.
Quantum computers fight it with isolation, low temperatures, and error correction.
*Error correction spreads one logical qubit across many physical ones.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Socrates never wrote a word
cards.cliff: "The unexamined life is not worth living" is from his trial speech
lines: Everything we know of him comes from students, mainly Plato, and critics like Aristophanes.
His method: ask questions until people discover they don't know what they thought they knew.
Athens executed him in 399 BC for "corrupting the youth" and impiety. He drank hemlock rather than flee.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Plato's cave
lines: Prisoners chained facing a wall see only shadows of objects carried behind them. They think the shadows are reality.
One escapes, sees the sun, returns, and is mocked by the others.
*Plato's point: the senses show shadows; reason reveals the real Forms.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Aristotle: look at the world
cards.cliff: His ethics is still taught today
lines: Where Plato put reality in abstract Forms, Aristotle studied actual things: animals, cities, arguments.
He founded formal logic, classified hundreds of species, and wrote on ethics, politics and physics.
*Some of his physics was wrong for 2,000 years* (heavy things don't fall faster).

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Aristotle's virtue: the golden mean
cards.cliff: The Stoics took a harder line
lines: Courage sits between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity between stinginess and extravagance.
Virtue is a habit, built by practice, like a skill.
The goal is eudaimonia: flourishing, not just pleasure.
recall: Virtue lies between two vices of excess and deficiency

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Which Greek philosopher said everything is made of atoms and void, centuries before chemistry?
cards.cliff: Heraclitus said you can't step in the same river twice
reveal: Democritus (with his teacher Leucippus), around 400 BC.
Atomos means "uncuttable".

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Diogenes lived in a large jar and mocked Alexander the Great
lines: Diogenes the Cynic rejected comfort and convention, living in a ceramic jar in Athens.
Legend: Alexander offered him any wish. Diogenes asked him to stop blocking his sunlight.
Alexander supposedly said: "If I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes."

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The Stoic dichotomy of control
lines: Some things are up to us: our judgements, intentions, responses. Most things aren't: other people, the weather, the past.
Epictetus: suffering comes from treating the second kind as if it were the first.
*Modern cognitive behavioural therapy borrows this directly.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Marcus Aurelius wrote a diary he never meant anyone to read
cards.cliff: Seneca wrote about the shortness of life
lines: The most powerful man in the Roman world wrote private notes to himself on staying calm, fair and humble.
We call them the *Meditations*. Many were written on military campaigns.
"You have power over your mind, not outside events" is a common paraphrase of his ideas.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Which Stoic was a former slave?
reveal: Epictetus was born into slavery in Hierapolis, later freed, and taught in Greece.
Marcus Aurelius was an emperor; Seneca was a wealthy statesman.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Negative visualisation
cards.cliff: Next: how to decide what's right
lines: Stoics regularly imagined losing the things they valued.
Not to be gloomy, but to appreciate them now and be prepared.
*Modern research on gratitude finds something similar.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Utilitarianism: maximise happiness
cards.cliff: Kant says consequences aren't the point
lines: Bentham and Mill: the right act produces the greatest good for the greatest number.
Consequences are all that matter.
Problem: it seems to allow terrible acts if the numbers work out.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Kant's categorical imperative
cards.cliff: Virtue ethics asks a different question
lines: Act only on rules you could will to be universal laws.
Treat people never merely as means, always also as ends.
*Lying is wrong even to a murderer at the door, Kant argued.* Many find that conclusion hard to accept.
recall: Act only on maxims you could will to become universal laws

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Which theory asks "what would a good person do?" rather than "what rule?" or "what outcome?"
reveal: Virtue ethics, from Aristotle, focuses on character.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Singer's drowning child
lines: You'd ruin your expensive shoes to save a child drowning in front of you.
A child dying of a preventable disease far away is no less real.
*So, Singer argued in 1972, failing to donate is morally similar.* It later inspired the effective altruism movement.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Moral luck
cards.cliff: Next: do we have free will?
lines: Two equally careless drivers. One hits a child who runs into the road; the other doesn't.
We blame the first far more, yet they did exactly the same thing.
*Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams named the problem in 1976.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The free will problem
lines: If every event is caused by earlier events, so are your choices.
If some events are random, randomness isn't freedom either.
*Either way, where does free will fit?*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Compatibilism
cards.cliff: The Libet experiments are often overstated
lines: Free will doesn't mean uncaused. It means acting from your own reasons without coercion.
Hume, and today Daniel Dennett, defend this view.
Most professional philosophers are compatibilists, according to the PhilPapers surveys.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Neuroscience experiments have shown that free will is an illusion.
cards.cliff: Frankfurt cases: could you have done otherwise?
reveal: Libet (1983) found brain activity rising before people reported deciding to move a finger.
But later work suggests that signal may be random background fluctuation crossing a threshold, not a hidden decision.
The experiments don't settle the philosophical question.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Frankfurt cases
lines: A neuroscientist secretly plans to force you to vote for X if you start to choose Y.
You choose X on your own. The device never activates.
*You couldn't have done otherwise, yet you seem responsible.* (Harry Frankfurt, 1969)

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The hard problem of consciousness
lines: Easy problems: explaining how the brain processes information, sorts inputs, controls behaviour.
Hard problem (David Chalmers, 1995): why is any of it accompanied by experience?
*Why does red look like anything at all?*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Dualism and the interaction problem
cards.cliff: What is it like to be a bat?
lines: Descartes: mind and body are different substances.
Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked him in 1643: how can a non-physical mind move a physical body?
*His answer, via the pineal gland, satisfied almost nobody.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Nagel's bat
lines: Bats navigate by echolocation. There's presumably something it is like to be one.
But no amount of physical knowledge seems to tell you what that is like *from the inside*.
Thomas Nagel (1974): subjective experience resists objective description.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Philosophical zombies
lines: Imagine a being physically identical to you, behaving identically, but with no inner experience.
If such a being is even conceivable, consciousness might not be purely physical.
*Critics say it only seems conceivable because we don't understand consciousness yet.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Rationalists vs empiricists
lines: Rationalists (Descartes, Leibniz): some knowledge comes from reason alone.
Empiricists (Locke, Hume): all knowledge comes from experience. The mind starts as a blank slate.
Kant tried to combine them: experience gives content, the mind supplies structure.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Hume's fork
lines: Every claim is either a relation of ideas (true by definition, like maths) or a matter of fact (learned by experience).
Anything that's neither, Hume said, should be "committed to the flames".
*That targeted much of metaphysics and theology.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Can you prove you're not a brain in a vat?
lines: Every experience you have could, in principle, be fed to a brain in a vat.
So how do you know you have hands?
G. E. Moore's reply: "Here is one hand." He was more certain of that than of any sceptical premise.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Which philosopher said "I think, therefore I am"?
reveal: "Cogito, ergo sum", from the Discourse on the Method (1637), in French as "je pense, donc je suis".

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The liar paradox
cards.cliff: Russell found the same knot in set theory
lines: "This sentence is false."
If it's true, it's false. If it's false, it's true.
*It's 2,000 years old and still has no universally accepted solution.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Russell's paradox broke the foundations of maths
cards.cliff: A barber who shaves everyone who doesn't shave themselves
lines: Consider the set of all sets that don't contain themselves. Does it contain itself?
Either answer leads to contradiction.
1902: Russell wrote to Frege, whose life's work depended on unrestricted sets. Frege replied that arithmetic itself was tottering.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The sorites paradox
lines: One grain of sand isn't a heap. Adding one grain never turns a non-heap into a heap.
So a million grains isn't a heap.
*Vague words like "tall", "bald" and "heap" resist sharp boundaries.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The surprise exam paradox
cards.cliff: Logic has a limit, proved by Gödel
lines: A teacher says there'll be a surprise exam next week.
It can't be Friday (you'd expect it by Thursday night). Then it can't be Thursday either… so none at all?
The exam comes on Wednesday. Everyone is surprised.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Gödel proved maths can never prove everything that's true
lines: 1931: any consistent formal system strong enough for arithmetic contains true statements it can't prove.
And it can't prove its own consistency.
*Hilbert's dream of a complete, provably consistent mathematics was dead.*
recall: Any consistent formal system capable of arithmetic has true statements it cannot prove

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: "Existence precedes essence"
cards.cliff: Camus asked whether life is worth living at all
lines: Sartre: a paper knife is designed for a purpose before it exists. Humans aren't.
We exist first, then define ourselves through our choices.
*So we're "condemned to be free": no excuses, no fixed nature to blame.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Camus and the absurd
lines: We demand meaning; the universe offers none. That clash is "the absurd".
Sisyphus is condemned to push a boulder uphill forever.
Camus's conclusion: "One must imagine Sisyphus happy."

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Kierkegaard wrote under a dozen pseudonyms
lines: The Danish philosopher published as Johannes de Silentio, Victor Eremita, Johannes Climacus and more.
Each pseudonym argued a different worldview.
*He wanted readers to choose for themselves, not just follow an author.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Nietzsche's eternal recurrence
lines: Imagine living your life again, exactly the same, infinitely many times.
Would you curse that thought, or welcome it?
*Nietzsche's test: live so you'd want it to repeat.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Hobbes: life without government is "nasty, brutish and short"
cards.cliff: Locke argued governments must earn their power
lines: Leviathan (1651): in a state of nature, everyone fears everyone.
Rational people would hand power to a sovereign in exchange for security.
He wrote it during and after the English Civil War.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Locke's natural rights
lines: People have rights to life, liberty and property before any government exists.
Governments exist to protect them; if they don't, people may replace them.
*Jefferson echoed him in the Declaration of Independence.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Rawls's veil of ignorance
lines: Design society's rules without knowing who you'll be: rich or poor, healthy or sick, which gender or ethnicity.
Rawls (1971) argued you'd choose equal basic liberties and allow inequality only if it benefits the worst off.
*A thought experiment for fairness you can apply to almost anything.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain argument
lines: Start with any distribution you think is fair.
A million fans each freely pay 25 cents to watch Wilt Chamberlain play. He ends up rich.
*Nozick (1974): if every step was voluntary, how is the result unjust?*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The Buddha's diagnosis
lines: Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering; suffering comes from craving; it can end; there's a path to ending it.
The self, he taught, isn't a fixed thing but a changing process (anattā).

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Confucius: ethics through roles and ritual
cards.cliff: Laozi taught the opposite of striving
lines: Social harmony comes from people fulfilling their roles well: parent, child, ruler, friend.
His version of the golden rule: don't do to others what you wouldn't want done to you.
*The Analects were compiled by his students after his death.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The Tao and wu wei
cards.cliff: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly
lines: The Tao Te Ching (traditionally attributed to Laozi): the Way that can be named is not the eternal Way.
Wu wei: effortless action, like water flowing around obstacles.
*Water is soft, yet it wears away stone.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Zhuangzi's butterfly dream
cards.cliff: Next: philosophy of time and physics
lines: Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, happily fluttering.
He woke up and wondered: was he Zhuangzi who dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was Zhuangzi?
*A Chinese brain-in-a-vat, more than 2,000 years earlier.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Does time flow?
lines: A-theory: there's a real "now" moving through time. Past is gone, future is open.
B-theory: all times exist equally, like points along a line. "Now" is just where you are.
*Relativity's lack of absolute simultaneity is often taken to favour the B-theory.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The block universe
cards.cliff: Can you travel back in time?
lines: In relativity, observers disagree about what's happening "now" elsewhere.
If there's no universal now, maybe past, present and future all exist together.
Einstein, after a friend's death: the distinction between past, present and future is "a stubbornly persistent illusion".

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The grandfather paradox
lines: Travel back and stop your grandparents meeting. Then you were never born, so you can't travel back.
Responses: you'll fail somehow (self-consistency), or you create a new branch of history.
*General relativity allows some solutions with closed time-like curves.* Whether physics really permits them is unknown.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Is maths discovered or invented?
lines: Platonists: numbers exist independently, and we discover their properties.
Formalists: maths is a game of symbols with rules we chose.
*Why maths fits physics so well is still debated.* Wigner called it "the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics" (1960).

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Constructive vs classical proof
cards.cliff: Some infinities are too big to compare
lines: Classical proof: "There exist irrational a, b with aᵇ rational." Proof: try √2^√2; if it's irrational, raise it to √2.
You get an answer without knowing which case holds.
*Constructivists reject such proofs: show me the example.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: The continuum hypothesis can't be settled
lines: Is there an infinity strictly between the whole numbers and the real numbers?
Gödel (1940) showed you can't disprove it; Cohen (1963) showed you can't prove it, from standard axioms.
*It's independent: maths can go either way.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s² for 4 s. Final speed?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Same car: distance covered in those 4 s?
reveal: s = ½at² = ½ × 3 × 16.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A ball is thrown up at 20 m/s (g = 10). Maximum height?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 10 kg box on a 30° frictionless slope. Acceleration down the slope? (g = 10)
reveal: a = g sin 30°.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Kinetic friction μ = 0.2 on a 5 kg block sliding on a level floor. Friction force? (g = 10)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 1,200 kg car rounds a 40 m radius bend at 10 m/s. Required centripetal force?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A projectile is launched horizontally at 15 m/s from a 20 m cliff (g = 10). How far out does it land?
reveal: Fall time √(2 × 20/10) = 2 s. Horizontal: 15 × 2.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Weight of a 70 kg astronaut on the Moon (g = 1.6 m/s²)?
reveal: W = mg. Mass stays 70 kg everywhere.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s. Kinetic energy?
reveal: ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 9.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 60 kg climber gains 500 m of height. Gain in potential energy? (g = 10)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 5 kg gun fires a 0.01 kg bullet at 500 m/s. Recoil speed?
reveal: Momentum: 0.01 × 500 = 5 × v.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 0.15 kg ball hits a wall at 20 m/s and rebounds at 20 m/s. Impulse magnitude?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A motor lifts 100 kg by 10 m in 20 s. Power output? (g = 10)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A disc (I = ½MR²) of mass 2 kg, radius 0.5 m spins at 10 rad/s. Rotational KE?
reveal: I = 0.25 kg m². KE = ½Iω² = ½ × 0.25 × 100.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A spring (k = 400 N/m) with a 1 kg mass. Period of oscillation?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Orbital speed of a satellite in low Earth orbit (r ≈ 6,700 km, g there ≈ 8.9 m/s²)?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Force between charges of 2 μC and 3 μC, 0.3 m apart? (k = 9 × 10⁹)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 3 μF capacitor at 100 V. Charge stored?
reveal: Q = CV.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Energy stored in that capacitor?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 2 kW kettle runs on 230 V. Current drawn?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Resistance of that kettle's element?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Field 5 cm from a long wire carrying 10 A? (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷)
reveal: Comparable to Earth's field (about 50 μT).

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A proton moves at 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a 0.1 T field. Radius of its circle? (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 500-turn coil of area 0.01 m² in a field that drops from 0.2 T to 0 in 0.05 s. Average EMF?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Energy of a photon with wavelength 600 nm? (hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Hydrogen electron drops from n = 2 to n = 1. Photon energy?
reveal: That's the ultraviolet Lyman-alpha line, 122 nm.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A muon's lifetime at rest is 2.2 μs. At γ = 10, how long does it last in the lab frame?
reveal: Time dilation: γτ.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A half-life of 6 hours. Fraction left after 1 day?
reveal: 24/6 = 4 half-lives: (1/2)⁴.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Rest energy of an electron?
reveal: mc² for the electron. 938 MeV is the proton's.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V? (h/√(2me·V) ≈ 1.23 nm/√V)
reveal: 1.23/√100 = 0.123 nm: similar to atomic spacings, so electrons diffract off crystals.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A Carnot fridge between −3°C and 27°C. Maximum coefficient of performance?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Particle in a box: ground state 0.5 eV. Energy of the photon emitted in the 2 → 1 transition?
reveal: E₂ = 4 × 0.5 = 2 eV. Difference 1.5 eV.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Dimensional analysis can predict physics without solving anything
cards.cliff: The same trick estimated the first atomic bomb's yield
lines: A pendulum's period can only depend on length L (m), g (m/s²) and mass m (kg).
The only combination with units of seconds is √(L/g). Mass can't appear.
*So T ∝ √(L/g).* The full answer is 2π√(L/g).

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: G. I. Taylor worked out a classified bomb yield from public photos
cards.cliff: Fermi had estimated it at the test itself, by dropping scraps of paper
lines: Photos of the 1945 Trinity fireball, with a scale bar and timestamps, were released after the war.
Taylor argued the blast radius could only depend on energy E, time t and air density ρ: R ∝ (Et²/ρ)^(1/5).
His 1950 estimate of about 17 kilotons was close to the still-secret official figure of about 20.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: What are the SI base units of force (the newton)?
cards.cliff: Fermi problems: estimate anything to within a factor of 10
reveal: F = ma: kilograms times metres per second squared.
kg·m²/s² is energy (joules).

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: How many piano tuners in Chicago? A Fermi estimate
cards.cliff: Scientific notation keeps the zeros under control
lines: ~3 million people, ~1 piano per 20 households of ~2 people: ~75,000 pianos.
Tuned once a year; a tuner does ~4 a day, ~250 days a year: ~1,000 a year each.
*Roughly 75 tuners.* Each step is rough, but errors partly cancel.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Roughly how many seconds in a year?
reveal: 365 × 24 × 3600 ≈ 3.15 × 10⁷. "π × 10⁷" is a famous physicist's shortcut.
8.6 × 10⁴ is seconds in a day.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The SUVAT equations (constant acceleration only)
cards.cliff: They all come from integrating a constant acceleration twice
lines: v = u + at
s = ut + ½at²
v² = u² + 2as
s = ½(u + v)t
recall: Which equation links v, u, a and s without t?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A car brakes from 30 m/s at 6 m/s². Stopping distance?
cards.cliff: Double the speed, quadruple the stopping distance

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why speeding is so much more dangerous than it feels
lines: Braking distance ∝ v². 40 mph needs four times the braking distance of 20 mph.
Kinetic energy ∝ v² too: crashing at 40 delivers four times the energy.
*Small speed increases have outsized consequences.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Reading motion graphs
cards.cliff: Free fall is the classic constant acceleration
lines: Position–time: slope is velocity.
Velocity–time: slope is acceleration, *area under it is displacement*.
Acceleration–time: area is change in velocity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Drop a stone off a 45 m cliff (g = 10 m/s²). Time to hit the ground?
cards.cliff: Throw it upward and the time up equals the time down (without air)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: You throw a ball straight up. At the very top, what is its acceleration?
reveal: Velocity is momentarily zero. Acceleration never is: gravity keeps pulling.
This is one of the most common exam mistakes.
options: It depends on how hard you threw it

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Projectiles: two independent motions
cards.cliff: Drop a bullet and fire one: which lands first?
lines: Horizontal: constant velocity (no air resistance).
Vertical: constant acceleration g.
They share only the time of flight.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A bullet is fired horizontally and another is dropped from the same height at the same moment. Which hits the ground first?
cards.cliff: Time of flight depends only on vertical motion
reveal: Vertical motion is identical for both. Horizontal speed doesn't change the fall.
(On a flat Earth with no air. The real bullet travels far enough for Earth's curvature to matter slightly.)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above flat ground. Time in the air (g = 10)?
cards.cliff: Range peaks at 45°, but only without air
reveal: Vertical speed 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s. Up for 1 s, down for 1 s.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why shot putters release below 45°
cards.cliff: Air resistance changes everything at high speed
lines: They release from shoulder height, above the landing point. That shifts the best angle below 45°.
Humans can also push harder at lower angles.
*Elite shot putters release around 35–40°.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Air resistance at speed goes as v²
lines: Drag force ≈ ½ρC_dAv².
Terminal velocity when drag equals weight: a skydiver tops out around 55 m/s belly-down.
With drag, trajectories aren't parabolas: they come down steeper than they went up.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Newton's three laws
lines: 1. No net force: velocity stays constant (including zero).
2. F_net = ma.
3. Forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different objects.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Aristotle thought motion needs a constant push
cards.cliff: Draw the free-body diagram first, always
lines: On Earth everything stops, so Aristotle concluded moving things need continuous force.
Galileo imagined ramps without friction: a ball would roll forever.
*Friction hid the true law for 2,000 years.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 2 kg box is pulled with 10 N on a frictionless floor. Acceleration?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Atwood machine: 3 kg and 5 kg over a frictionless pulley. Acceleration? (g = 10)
reveal: Net force (5 − 3) × 10 = 20 N. Total mass 8 kg. a = 2.5 m/s².

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: In that Atwood machine, is the string tension more or less than 30 N (the light mass's weight)?
cards.cliff: Normal force isn't always mg either
reveal: The 3 kg mass accelerates upward: T − 30 = 3 × 2.5, so T = 37.5 N.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The normal force on an object always equals its weight.
reveal: On a slope it's mg cos θ. In an accelerating lift it's m(g + a).
Push down on a book and the normal force grows. It's whatever stops you sinking into the surface.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Static vs kinetic friction
cards.cliff: On a slope, gravity splits into two parts
lines: Static friction adjusts up to a maximum μ_s N. Kinetic friction is μ_k N.
μ_s > μ_k: it's harder to start something sliding than to keep it going.
*That's why ABS brakes work: a rolling tyre uses static friction, a skidding one uses weaker kinetic friction.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Forces on an incline
lines: Along the slope: mg sin θ. Into the slope: mg cos θ.
Normal force N = mg cos θ.
A block starts sliding when tan θ > μ_s.
recall: Angle at which a block starts to slide on an incline?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A block just starts to slide when a ramp reaches 30°. μ_s = ?
cards.cliff: Friction is why you can walk at all
reveal: mg sin θ = μ_s mg cos θ gives μ_s = tan θ.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: When you walk forward, which way does friction on your foot point?
reveal: Your foot pushes the ground backward; friction pushes you forward.
On ice, there's too little of it and your foot slides back.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Moving in a circle means accelerating inward
cards.cliff: Centrifugal force is what it feels like from inside
lines: Even at constant speed, direction changes, so there's acceleration v²/r toward the centre.
Something must provide that force: tension, friction, gravity, normal force.
*Centripetal isn't a new force.* It's a job one of the real forces does.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: When you swing a ball on a string and let go, it flies straight outward from the centre.
cards.cliff: Banked tracks let cars turn without friction
reveal: It flies off along the tangent, in the direction it was moving at that instant.
Nothing was pushing it outward. The string was pulling it in.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A car takes a 50 m radius bend at 20 m/s. What friction coefficient is needed on a flat road? (g = 10)
cards.cliff: Loops need minimum speed at the top

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Minimum speed at the top of a vertical loop of radius r?
reveal: At the top, gravity alone can supply mv²/r when v² = gr.
Any slower and you fall off.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Work: force times distance along the force
cards.cliff: Energy is what's conserved when forces are conservative
lines: W = F·d = Fd cos θ.
Carrying a bag horizontally at constant speed: the gravity and lift forces do *zero* work.
Work-energy theorem: net work = change in kinetic energy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 2 kg ball drops 5 m. Speed at the bottom? (g = 10, no air)
reveal: mgh = ½mv²: v = √(2gh) = √100.
Mass cancels.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A spring (k = 200 N/m) is compressed 0.1 m. Stored energy?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: How much power do you produce climbing stairs?
cards.cliff: Energy is never destroyed, just harder to use
lines: 70 kg climbing 3 m of stairs in 3 s: mgh/t ≈ 70 × 10 × 3 / 3 = 700 W.
That's nearly one horsepower (746 W), for a few seconds.
*A fit cyclist sustains about 250–400 W for an hour.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Where the "lost" energy goes
lines: A sliding block stops. Its kinetic energy became heat in the surfaces.
Total energy is conserved. Mechanical energy isn't, when friction acts.
*"Losing" energy really means turning it into forms you can't easily use.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Momentum is conserved in every collision
lines: p = mv. With no external force, total momentum stays constant.
Energy may or may not be conserved; momentum always is.
Elastic: kinetic energy conserved too. Inelastic: some becomes heat and sound.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 1,000 kg car at 20 m/s hits a stationary 1,000 kg car and they lock together. Speed after?
cards.cliff: Impulse explains crumple zones and airbags
reveal: Half the kinetic energy turns into crumpled metal and heat.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Airbags work by making the stop take longer
cards.cliff: Elastic collisions between equal masses swap velocities
lines: Impulse: FΔt = Δp. The change in momentum is fixed by your speed.
Stretch the stopping time from 0.01 s to 0.1 s and the average force drops tenfold.
*Crumple zones, bent knees on landing, catching an egg gently: same physics.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A snooker ball hits an identical stationary ball head-on (elastic). What happens?
cards.cliff: Glancing collisions between equal masses leave at 90°
reveal: Equal masses in a head-on elastic collision swap velocities.
options: The first stops dead, the second moves off at the original speed
Both move forward at half speed

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Equal-mass elastic glancing collisions split at 90°
lines: Momentum: v = v₁ + v₂ (vectors). Energy: v² = v₁² + v₂².
Pythagoras means v₁ ⊥ v₂.
*Snooker players use the 90° rule to judge where the cue ball goes.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Torque: the rotational version of force
cards.cliff: Archimedes: give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth
lines: τ = r × F, size rF sin θ.
Push a door near the hinge and it barely moves. Push the handle: easy.
*Longer lever arm, same force, more torque.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 60 kg child sits 1.5 m from a seesaw's pivot. Where must a 90 kg adult sit to balance?
reveal: Torques balance: 60 × 1.5 = 90 × d.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: τ = Iα: rotational Newton's second law
lines: I (moment of inertia) plays the role of mass.
It depends on how far the mass sits from the axis: I = Σmr².
*A figure skater can't change their mass, but can change I.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A solid ball and a hollow ball of equal mass and radius race down a ramp. Which wins?
cards.cliff: Gyroscopes resist tipping because of angular momentum
reveal: Solid sphere I = (2/5)mr², hollow (2/3)mr². Less energy goes into spinning the solid one.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Angular momentum is conserved without external torque
cards.cliff: Cats use it to land on their feet
lines: L = Iω for a rigid body. L = r × p for a particle.
Pull mass inward and spin speeds up.
*Divers tuck to spin fast, then open out to slow down before entering the water.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: How a falling cat turns over without breaking physics
cards.cliff: Precession: why a spinning top doesn't fall
lines: A cat starting with zero angular momentum must keep zero overall.
It bends at the middle and twists its front and back halves in opposite directions, tucking legs to change their moments of inertia.
*Net rotation without net angular momentum.* Physicists published papers on this in 1969.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Precession
cards.cliff: Kepler's second law is angular momentum conservation
lines: Gravity's torque on a tilted spinning top points sideways, not down.
So the angular momentum vector swings around in a circle instead of toppling.
Earth precesses too: its axis traces a circle every ~26,000 years. Polaris won't always be the pole star.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why does a planet move fastest when it's closest to the Sun?
reveal: Gravity points toward the Sun: no torque. So rv sin θ stays constant.
Small r means large v. Equal areas in equal times.
options: Angular momentum r × mv is conserved
Energy is lost far from the Sun

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Newton's law of gravitation
cards.cliff: Weighing the Earth took a lead ball experiment
lines: $ F = GMm/r²
G = 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg²: tiny, which is why gravity between people is undetectable.
Same law for an apple and the Moon.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Cavendish weighed the Earth in a shed in 1798
cards.cliff: g changes with height, but slowly
lines: He hung lead balls from a torsion wire and measured the minute twist as bigger balls attracted them.
That fixed G, and from g at the surface, Earth's mass and density.
He found Earth is about 5.4 times denser than water: so its core must be heavy.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: At what height above the surface is g a quarter of its surface value?
cards.cliff: Escape velocity doesn't depend on the launch angle
reveal: g ∝ 1/r². Doubling r from the centre quarters g.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Escape velocity from Earth's surface?
cards.cliff: Make an object small enough and not even light escapes
reveal: ½v² = GM/R gives v = √(2GM/R).
7.9 km/s is the speed for a low circular orbit: escape is √2 times that.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Black holes were predicted in 1783
lines: John Michell: a star dense enough would have an escape velocity above the speed of light. It would be invisible.
Set √(2GM/R) = c: R = 2GM/c², exactly the Schwarzschild radius general relativity gives.
*Right answer, wrong theory.* Earth would need to be squeezed to about 9 mm.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: SHM: acceleration proportional to displacement, pointing back
cards.cliff: Galileo noticed the period trick in a cathedral
lines: a = −ω²x. Solution: x = A cos(ωt + φ).
Mass on a spring: ω = √(k/m). Pendulum: ω = √(g/L).
*Period doesn't depend on amplitude.* That's why pendulum clocks keep time.
recall: Angular frequency of a mass on a spring?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Galileo timed a swinging lamp with his pulse
lines: The story: in Pisa Cathedral, around 1583, Galileo saw a chandelier swing and timed it with his pulse.
Big swings and small swings seemed to take the same time.
*Isochronism became the basis of pendulum clocks.* (True only for small swings.)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 1 m pendulum on Earth: period roughly? (g ≈ 9.8)
cards.cliff: Energy sloshes between kinetic and potential
reveal: The metre was once nearly defined as the length of a pendulum with a 2 s period.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Energy in SHM
lines: At the ends: all potential, zero speed.
At the centre: all kinetic, maximum speed Aω.
Total energy ½kA² stays constant.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Damping: underdamped, critical, overdamped
cards.cliff: Driving at the natural frequency gives resonance
lines: Underdamped: oscillates while decaying. Car with worn shocks.
Critical: returns fastest without overshoot. Good suspension, door closers.
Overdamped: oozes back slowly.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Quality factor Q
cards.cliff: Why quartz watches are so accurate
lines: Q ≈ number of oscillations before the energy drops a lot (precisely: 2π × energy stored / energy lost per cycle).
A wine glass: Q around 1,000. A quartz watch crystal: around 10,000 or more.
*High Q: sharp resonance, long ringing.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Your watch counts 32,768 vibrations per second
lines: A tiny quartz tuning fork resonates at 32,768 Hz = 2¹⁵.
Fifteen halvings in a digital circuit give exactly one tick per second.
High Q means the frequency barely drifts: a few seconds a month.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth
lines: p = p₀ + ρgh.
Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere.
*Shape of the container doesn't matter*, only depth.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Archimedes and the crown
cards.cliff: Buoyancy is the weight of displaced fluid
lines: Story: King Hiero suspected his gold crown had silver mixed in.
Archimedes realised the crown's volume could be found by the water it displaced, then compared with pure gold of the same weight.
The "Eureka" bath story comes from Vitruvius, two centuries later.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: An iceberg floats in seawater. Roughly what fraction is underwater?
reveal: Fraction submerged = density of ice / density of seawater ≈ 917/1025 ≈ 0.89.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Bernoulli's principle
cards.cliff: But it isn't the whole story of how wings work
lines: Along a streamline: p + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant.
Faster flow, lower pressure.
Atomisers, carburettors and the shower curtain that sucks inward all use it.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Wings lift because air over the top must travel further to "catch up" with air underneath.
reveal: There's no rule that the two streams must meet at the trailing edge. In fact the top air arrives *earlier*.
Wings work by turning air downward (Newton's third law), with lower pressure above (consistent with Bernoulli).
Planes can fly upside down: the angle of attack matters.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Fictitious forces appear in accelerating frames
lines: In a braking bus, you lurch forward. No force pushed you: the bus decelerated under you.
In the bus's frame, physics works if you add a fictitious force −ma.
Centrifugal and Coriolis forces are fictitious forces of rotating frames.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Coriolis spins hurricanes, not bathtubs
cards.cliff: Foucault proved Earth rotates with a pendulum
lines: On a rotating Earth, moving air is deflected: right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern.
Hurricanes rotate anticlockwise in the north, clockwise in the south.
*Bathtubs and sinks are far too small:* their drain direction depends on how the water was poured.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Foucault's pendulum, Paris 1851
lines: A 67 m pendulum in the Panthéon swung in a plane that slowly rotated.
At latitude λ, the plane turns 360° in 24 h / sin λ: about 32 hours in Paris.
*The first direct proof of Earth's rotation without looking at the sky.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Lagrangian of a simple pendulum (length l, angle θ)?
reveal: T = ½ml²θ̇². With height measured from the pivot, V = −mgl cos θ, so L = T − V.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: What equation of motion does that Lagrangian give?
cards.cliff: Cyclic coordinates give conserved quantities for free
reveal: ∂L/∂θ̇ = ml²θ̇, its time derivative ml²θ̈. ∂L/∂θ = −mgl sin θ.
Small angles: sin θ ≈ θ gives SHM.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Cyclic coordinates
cards.cliff: Constraints disappear when you choose good coordinates
lines: If L doesn't depend on a coordinate q, then ∂L/∂q = 0.
Euler–Lagrange then says the momentum p = ∂L/∂q̇ is conserved.
*A free particle in polar coordinates: θ is cyclic, so angular momentum is conserved.*
recall: What's conserved if L doesn't depend on coordinate q?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why Lagrangians make constraints easy
lines: A bead on a wire, a pendulum, a rolling cylinder: Newton needs the constraint forces.
Lagrange uses coordinates that already obey the constraints: θ for the pendulum, not x and y.
*The constraint forces never appear.* (Use multipliers if you want them.)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The two-body problem reduces to one body
lines: Two masses orbiting each other = one particle of reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁ + m₂) moving in the same force.
Angular momentum conservation keeps the orbit in a plane.
An effective potential V(r) + L²/(2μr²) adds a centrifugal barrier.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Bertrand's theorem: only two forces give closed orbits
lines: For bound orbits to close for every starting condition, the force must be inverse square (planets) or linear (springs).
Any other central force makes orbits precess, tracing rosettes.
*Mercury's orbit precesses slightly too much for Newton.* General relativity accounts for the excess 43″ per century.
recall: Which central forces give closed orbits for all bound initial conditions?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A planet's orbit has total energy E < 0. What shape is it?
reveal: E < 0: bound ellipse. E = 0: parabola (just escapes). E > 0: hyperbola.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Normal modes: coupled oscillators untangled
cards.cliff: Coupled pendulums swap energy back and forth
lines: Two pendulums joined by a spring can swing in step or in opposition.
Each is a normal mode with its own frequency. Any motion is a mix of the two.
Finding them is an eigenvalue problem: det(K − ω²M) = 0.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Two identical pendulums are weakly coupled by a spring. You start one swinging. What happens?
cards.cliff: Molecules vibrate in normal modes too
reveal: Starting one pendulum excites both normal modes. Their slightly different frequencies beat.
The motion transfers back and forth at the beat frequency.
options: The energy slowly passes to the other and back again

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: CO₂ absorbs infrared because of a normal mode
lines: CO₂ has a symmetric stretch, an asymmetric stretch and bending modes.
The asymmetric stretch and bending modes change the dipole moment, so they absorb infrared radiation.
*That's the greenhouse effect at molecular scale.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The inertia tensor
cards.cliff: Spinning about the middle axis is unstable
lines: In 3D, L = Iω where I is a 3×3 matrix. L and ω need not be parallel.
Every body has three principal axes where they are parallel.
*A wobbling frisbee or a badly balanced tyre: L and ω misaligned.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The tennis racket theorem
lines: A body spins stably about its largest and smallest principal axes but not the intermediate one.
Throw a phone or tennis racket spinning around the middle axis and it flips over halfway.
*Astronaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov filmed a wingnut flipping repeatedly in orbit in 1985.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Euler's equations for rigid bodies
cards.cliff: Physics 1 done. Physics 2: electricity and magnetism
lines: $ I₁ω̇₁ = (I₂ − I₃)ω₂ω₃ (and cyclic)
Linearise around spin on each axis: the middle axis gives exponential growth of small wobbles.
That's the tennis racket instability, from three coupled ODEs.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Coulomb's law
lines: $ F = kq₁q₂/r²,  k = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N m²/C²
Like charges repel, opposite charges attract.
Same inverse-square shape as gravity, but about 10³⁶ times stronger between two protons.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Charge comes in lumps
cards.cliff: One coulomb is a ridiculous amount of charge
lines: Every free charge is a whole multiple of e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Millikan measured it in 1909 by balancing charged oil drops in an electric field.
Quarks carry ±1/3 and ±2/3 of e, but are never seen alone.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Two 1 C charges 1 m apart. Force between them?
cards.cliff: Why does a balloon stick to the wall?
reveal: F = k × 1 × 1 / 1² = 9 × 10⁹ N: roughly the weight of a million tonnes.
Static shocks involve microcoulombs.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Induced charge: why a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall
lines: The balloon's charge pushes electrons in the wall slightly away, leaving the near surface oppositely charged.
The nearby opposite charge attracts more strongly than the farther like charge repels.
*Net attraction to a neutral object.* Same reason dust clings to screens.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The electric field: force per unit charge
lines: E = F/q. A point charge makes E = kQ/r², pointing away from positive charge.
Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones.
*The field exists whether or not a test charge is there to feel it.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A dipole: +q and −q a distance d apart. Field far away falls off as…
cards.cliff: A uniform field is the parallel-plate capacitor's gift
reveal: The two 1/r² fields nearly cancel. The leftover depends on d/r, giving 1/r³.
Neutral molecules attract each other through such leftover fields.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: An electron in a uniform field E = 1000 N/C. Acceleration?
cards.cliff: Old TV tubes steered electrons with exactly this
reveal: Gravity is utterly negligible for electrons in fields.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Cathode ray tubes steered electrons with fields
lines: Old TVs fired electrons through deflecting fields (magnetic coils in most sets) to paint the screen line by line.
J. J. Thomson used electric and magnetic deflection to discover the electron in 1897.
*Every pixel on a CRT was an electron's landing spot.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Field inside a uniformly charged hollow spherical shell?
cards.cliff: Outside, the shell acts like a point charge
reveal: A Gaussian sphere inside encloses no charge, and by symmetry E is radial, so E = 0.
Newton proved the same for gravity inside a hollow planet.
options: It depends on where you are

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Field at distance r from an infinite line charge with density λ?
cards.cliff: Inside a uniform ball, E grows linearly
reveal: Gaussian cylinder: E × 2πrL = λL/ε₀.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Inside a uniformly charged solid ball (radius R), how does E depend on r?
cards.cliff: Drop through a tunnel through Earth and you'd arrive in about 42 minutes
reveal: Enclosed charge ∝ r³, surface area ∝ r²: E ∝ r.
Same for gravity inside a uniform planet: a tunnel through it gives SHM.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The gravity train: 42 minutes to anywhere
lines: In a frictionless straight tunnel between any two points on a uniform Earth, you'd oscillate in SHM.
The trip takes about 42 minutes, whatever the two cities are.
*Same period as a satellite skimming the surface, divided by two.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Potential: energy per unit charge
cards.cliff: An electron-volt is a unit of energy
lines: V = U/q, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).
Point charge: V = kQ/r. Fields point from high to low potential.
E = −∇V: the field is the downhill slope of the potential.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Energy gained by an electron accelerated through 1,000 V?
cards.cliff: Equipotentials are perpendicular to field lines
reveal: ΔU = qΔV = e × 1000 V.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why birds on power lines don't get shocked
lines: Current needs a potential *difference* across a path.
Both feet on the same wire sit at essentially the same potential: no current through the bird.
*Touch the wire and the ground (or a second wire) at once, and it's fatal.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Lightning rods and sharp points
lines: On a conductor, charge piles up where curvature is highest, making strong fields at sharp points.
Strong enough fields ionise air and leak charge away: corona discharge, St Elmo's fire.
Franklin's pointed rods give lightning a preferred path to ground.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Capacitance: charge stored per volt
lines: C = Q/V. Parallel plates: C = ε₀A/d.
Energy stored: ½CV².
*Defibrillators dump a capacitor's energy through the heart in milliseconds.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Dielectrics
lines: An insulator between the plates polarises, partly cancelling the field.
Capacitance rises by the dielectric constant κ (water: about 80).
That's how tiny capacitors in your phone store useful charge.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Two 4 μF capacitors in series. Total capacitance?
reveal: Series: 1/C = 1/4 + 1/4. Parallel would give 8 μF.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Your touchscreen measures capacitance
lines: A grid of electrodes under the glass forms tiny capacitors.
Your finger, a conductor, changes the capacitance where you touch.
*That's why gloves don't work and a sausage does.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Current, voltage, resistance
cards.cliff: Why transmit power at high voltage?
lines: Current I = charge per second (amps). V = IR (Ohm's law, for ohmic materials).
Resistance R = ρL/A: longer and thinner wires resist more.
Power dissipated: P = IV = I²R = V²/R.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Power lines carry P = IV. Raising the voltage 10× (same power) changes the wire losses by…
cards.cliff: The current war was about exactly this
reveal: Current drops 10×. Loss I²R drops 100×.
That's why grids step up to hundreds of kilovolts.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Edison vs Westinghouse: the war of the currents
cards.cliff: Resistance falls to zero in superconductors
lines: Edison backed DC. DC voltage was hard to step up, so it needed power stations every mile or so.
Westinghouse and Tesla backed AC, which transformers step up and down easily.
*AC won.* Today very long links use high-voltage DC again, thanks to modern electronics.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Superconductivity: zero resistance, discovered 1911
lines: Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury to 4.2 K and its resistance vanished.
Currents in superconducting loops have persisted for years without measurable decay.
*MRI magnets are superconducting coils cooled with liquid helium.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: 6 Ω and 3 Ω resistors in parallel. Total?
reveal: Parallel total is always less than the smallest branch.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Internal resistance
lines: Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir drops as you draw more current.
Short-circuit current is ε/r: why a car battery can melt a spanner.
*Maximum power transfer when the load resistance equals r.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 12 V battery drives 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series. Voltage across the 4 Ω?
reveal: Current 12/6 = 2 A. V = 2 × 4.
Voltage divider: V_out = V × R₂/(R₁ + R₂).

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Wheatstone bridge
cards.cliff: Next: circuits that change over time
lines: Four resistors in a diamond with a meter across the middle.
When the meter reads zero, R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄.
Strain gauges in bathroom scales use it to detect tiny resistance changes.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Charging a capacitor
lines: q(t) = CV(1 − e^(−t/RC)). Current decays as e^(−t/RC).
After one time constant RC: 63% charged. After 5RC: >99%.
*Camera flashes charge a capacitor slowly, then dump it in a millisecond.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Inductors: electrical inertia
cards.cliff: Combine L and C and you get oscillation
lines: V = L dI/dt. An inductor fights any change in current.
Switch off current through an inductor suddenly and the voltage spikes: that's how car ignition coils make sparks.
RL time constant: L/R.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: An LC circuit oscillates at what angular frequency?
cards.cliff: Every radio tuner is an LC circuit
reveal: L q̈ + q/C = 0: SHM with ω² = 1/(LC).
Energy swaps between the capacitor's field and the inductor's field.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Tuning a radio is resonance
lines: Turn the dial and you change C in an LC circuit.
Only the station at the resonant frequency gets a big response.
*Same maths as a mass on a spring.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Lorentz force
cards.cliff: So charges in a uniform B field go in circles
lines: $ F = q(E + v × B)
The magnetic part is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work.
*Magnetic fields bend paths but never change speed.*
recall: Why does a magnetic field do no work on a moving charge?
The force qv×B is always perpendicular to the velocity

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Radius of a charged particle's circle in a magnetic field?
cards.cliff: The cyclotron frequency doesn't depend on speed
reveal: qvB = mv²/r.
Heavier ions curve less: that's how a mass spectrometer sorts them.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The cyclotron trick
lines: Period of the circle: 2πm/(qB). Independent of speed.
So a fixed-frequency alternating voltage can kick particles every half turn as they spiral outward.
*Ernest Lawrence's first cyclotron (1931) fitted in his hand.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Auroras are particles spiralling along Earth's field lines
lines: Charged particles from the Sun spiral around magnetic field lines toward the poles.
They hit oxygen and nitrogen high in the atmosphere, which glow green and red.
*The Van Allen belts are the trapped particles that bounce between the poles.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Force on a 2 m wire carrying 3 A at right angles to a 0.5 T field?
cards.cliff: Next: where magnetic fields come from
reveal: Every electric motor is this force turning a coil.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Ørsted saw a compass twitch during a lecture, 1820
lines: Hans Christian Ørsted noticed a compass needle move when he switched on a current nearby.
Within weeks, Ampère and Biot and Savart had worked out the laws.
*Electricity and magnetism were connected.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Magnetic field at distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I?
reveal: Ampère's law: B × 2πr = μ₀I.
Circles around the wire, by the right-hand grip rule.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Parallel currents attract
lines: Each wire's field pushes on the other's current.
Same direction: attract. Opposite directions: repel.
The ampere was defined from this force until 2019.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Field inside a long solenoid with n turns per metre carrying I?
cards.cliff: No magnetic monopoles: field lines always close
reveal: Ampère's law on a rectangle half inside: B L = μ₀ n L I.
Field outside is nearly zero.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Cutting a bar magnet in half gives a separate north pole and south pole.
reveal: You get two smaller magnets, each with both poles.
∇·B = 0: no isolated magnetic charges have ever been found.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A 100-turn coil's flux changes by 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s. Induced EMF?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Lenz's law is energy conservation
lines: If induced currents *helped* the change, a nudge would create a runaway current from nothing.
So they always oppose it.
*Push a magnet into a coil and you feel resistance: that's the work becoming electrical energy.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Induction hobs heat the pan, not the hob
lines: A coil under the glass makes a rapidly changing magnetic field.
It induces eddy currents in the pan's metal base, which heat it directly.
*Aluminium and glass pans don't work well: the base needs to be magnetic and resistive enough.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A transformer has 100 primary turns and 2,000 secondary turns. 230 V in gives…
reveal: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = 20.
Current steps down by the same factor: power is (ideally) conserved.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: RMS: the honest average of AC
cards.cliff: Capacitors and inductors have frequency-dependent resistance
lines: Mains voltage is a sine wave. Its average is zero, but heating depends on V².
RMS = peak/√2. UK mains is 230 V RMS, about 325 V peak.
*A 230 V AC heater runs exactly like a 230 V DC one.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Reactance
cards.cliff: Phasors turn AC into complex algebra
lines: Capacitor: X_C = 1/(ωC). Blocks low frequencies, passes high ones.
Inductor: X_L = ωL. Blocks high frequencies, passes low ones.
*Speaker crossovers send bass to the woofer and treble to the tweeter this way.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Impedance is complex resistance
lines: Z_R = R, Z_L = iωL, Z_C = 1/(iωC).
Then V = IZ works for AC, with Z combining like resistances.
*The imaginary part is the 90° phase shift.* Electrical engineers write j instead of i.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A series RLC circuit draws maximum current at what frequency?
reveal: At resonance X_L = X_C, they cancel, and Z = R is minimal.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Light is a transverse EM wave
cards.cliff: Hertz proved the waves exist in 1887
lines: E and B oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel.
E/B = c in vacuum.
Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma: same thing, different wavelengths.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Hertz said his discovery had no use
cards.cliff: Visible light is a tiny sliver of the spectrum
lines: 1887: Heinrich Hertz generated and detected radio waves with spark gaps.
Asked about applications, he reportedly said it was of no use whatsoever.
*By 1899, Marconi was sending wireless signals across the Channel.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Roughly what wavelength range can human eyes see?
cards.cliff: Light carries momentum, so it can push
reveal: Violet ~380 nm to red ~750 nm.
Less than one octave, out of a spectrum spanning over 20 orders of magnitude.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Solar sails really work
cards.cliff: Next: reflection and refraction from Maxwell
lines: Light has momentum p = E/c. Reflecting it pushes the sail.
Japan's IKAROS probe (2010) sailed using sunlight alone.
*The push is tiny, but it never stops.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Refraction: light slows down in materials
lines: Speed in a medium: v = c/n. Glass n ≈ 1.5, water n ≈ 1.33.
Snell's law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
*Light bends toward the normal entering a denser medium.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Critical angle for light leaving glass (n = 1.5) into air?
cards.cliff: The internet runs on total internal reflection
reveal: Beyond 42° the light can't escape: it reflects completely.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Fibre optics are trapped light
cards.cliff: Polarisation is the direction E oscillates
lines: A glass core with a slightly lower-index cladding keeps light bouncing inside.
Modern fibre loses only about 0.2 dB per km: a signal travels around 15 km before halving.
*Undersea cables carry the vast majority of intercontinental internet traffic.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Polarised sunglasses
lines: Glare from water and roads is mostly horizontally polarised (Brewster's angle effect).
Polarising lenses block horizontal E-field oscillations.
Tilt your head with polarised glasses and phone screens can go dark: they're polarised too.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: In charge-free regions, ∇²V = 0
cards.cliff: That's why ion traps need oscillating fields
lines: Laplace's equation: the potential is the average of its surroundings.
So V has no local maxima or minima in empty space.
*Earnshaw's theorem: you can't trap a charge with static electric fields alone.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Earnshaw's theorem and the Paul trap
cards.cliff: Image charges solve conductor problems by trickery
lines: Static fields can't hold a charge stably: there's always an escape direction.
Wolfgang Paul used a rapidly oscillating field that averages to a trap. Nobel Prize 1989.
*Ion traps now hold single atoms for quantum computers.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Method of images
cards.cliff: Separation of variables handles boxes and spheres
lines: A charge q near a grounded conducting plane.
Replace the plane with a fake charge −q at the mirror position. The potential on the plane is zero, as required.
*Uniqueness theorem: if it satisfies the boundary conditions, it's the answer.*
recall: Why is the method of images valid?
The uniqueness theorem: a solution matching the boundary conditions is the only solution

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Separation of variables
lines: Guess V(x, y) = X(x)Y(y). Laplace's equation splits into two ODEs.
Boundary conditions pick out sines, sinhs, or Legendre polynomials on spheres.
*Sum the pieces with Fourier coefficients to match any boundary.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Multipole expansion: far away, any charge looks simple
cards.cliff: Water's dipole explains half of chemistry
lines: V = monopole (1/r) + dipole (1/r²) + quadrupole (1/r³) + …
Net charge sets the monopole. Separation of charge sets the dipole.
*Far enough away, only the first non-zero term matters.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Water is a strong electric dipole
lines: The O–H bonds pull electrons toward oxygen, and the bent shape doesn't cancel the dipoles.
That makes water dissolve salts, form hydrogen bonds, and absorb microwaves.
*Microwave ovens jiggle water molecules' dipoles back and forth.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: D and H: fields that track free charges and currents
lines: Materials polarise (P) and magnetise (M).
D = ε₀E + P and H = B/μ₀ − M separate free sources from bound ones.
∇·D = ρ_free, ∇×H = J_free + ∂D/∂t.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Ferromagnetism and hysteresis
lines: Iron's atomic magnetic moments align in domains.
Apply a field and domains grow; remove it and some alignment stays.
*That memory stored data on hard drives for decades.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The levitating frog, 2000 Ig Nobel Prize
lines: Water (and so frogs) is weakly diamagnetic: repelled by magnetic fields.
In a 16 T magnet, Andre Geim levitated a live frog.
*Ten years later he won a real Nobel Prize, for graphene.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Only accelerating charges radiate
lines: A charge at constant velocity just carries its field along.
Accelerate it and a kink in the field races outward at c: radiation.
Larmor: power P = q²a²/(6πε₀c³).

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The classical atom should collapse in about 10⁻¹¹ s
cards.cliff: Synchrotron light is radiation used on purpose
lines: An electron orbiting a nucleus is accelerating, so it should radiate and spiral in.
Classical physics predicts collapse in tens of picoseconds.
*Atoms exist. Quantum mechanics was needed to explain why.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Synchrotrons: X-ray factories
lines: Electrons forced round a ring at nearly c radiate intense, narrow beams of X-rays.
Biologists use them to work out protein structures.
Diamond Light Source in Oxfordshire is one: a ring about half a kilometre round.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Maxwell's equations were already relativistic
cards.cliff: E and B mix under boosts
lines: Lorentz found the transformations that leave them unchanged before Einstein explained why.
Einstein's 1905 paper was titled *On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies*.
*Special relativity came out of electromagnetism.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Which quantity is the same for every inertial observer?
cards.cliff: The four-potential unifies φ and A
reveal: E and B change with the frame, but E² − c²B² and E·B are Lorentz invariants.
A pure E field in one frame can't become a pure B field in another.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Four-vectors package it neatly
cards.cliff: Physics 2 done. Physics 3: waves, heat and the quantum
lines: A^μ = (φ/c, A) and J^μ = (cρ, J).
Lorenz gauge: ∂_μA^μ = 0. Then each component of A^μ obeys a wave equation sourced by J^μ.
*Charge conservation is ∂_μJ^μ = 0.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Every wave obeys v = fλ
cards.cliff: Sound needs a medium, light doesn't
lines: Speed = frequency × wavelength.
Sound in air: about 343 m/s. Middle C (262 Hz) has a wavelength of about 1.3 m.
Light: 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Green light (550 nm) oscillates about 5.5 × 10¹⁴ times a second.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Count seconds between lightning and thunder: 6 s. Roughly how far away?
reveal: Sound covers ~343 m per second: 6 × 343 ≈ 2 km.
Light arrives essentially instantly.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Decibels are logarithmic
cards.cliff: Beats: two close notes make a wobble
lines: +10 dB means 10× the intensity. +20 dB means 100×.
A rock concert (110 dB) is a billion times the intensity of a whisper (20 dB).
*Your ears perceive roughly every +10 dB as "twice as loud".*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Tuning forks of 440 Hz and 444 Hz sound together. What do you hear?
cards.cliff: Breaking the sound barrier makes a cone of sound
reveal: Superposition gives an average frequency with an amplitude envelope at the difference frequency.
Musicians tune by listening for beats to slow and vanish.
options: A 442 Hz tone pulsing 4 times a second

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Sonic booms
lines: A plane faster than sound outruns its own pressure waves.
They pile up into a cone-shaped shock front: the Mach cone, with sin θ = v_sound/v.
*The boom follows the plane along the ground the whole time it's supersonic,* not just once.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Double slit: slit spacing d, wavelength λ, screen distance L. Fringe spacing?
cards.cliff: Young's experiment was evidence for light as a wave in 1801
reveal: Bright fringes where path difference d sin θ = mλ. Small angles give spacing λL/d.
Closer slits spread the pattern out.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Thomas Young fought Newton's ghost
lines: Newton had argued light was particles. His reputation made the idea hard to challenge.
Around 1801–1803 Young showed interference fringes with light, which only waves can make.
*A century later, quantum theory said both of them were partly right.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why soap bubbles and oil slicks shimmer
cards.cliff: Diffraction limits how sharply anything can see
lines: Light reflects off the top and bottom of a thin film and the two reflections interfere.
Which wavelengths reinforce depends on film thickness, so colours shift as the film thins.
*Just before a bubble pops, it goes black: too thin for any visible light to reinforce.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The diffraction limit
cards.cliff: CDs and DVDs are diffraction gratings
lines: A lens of diameter D can't resolve angles smaller than about 1.22λ/D (Rayleigh criterion).
Bigger telescopes see finer detail. So do shorter wavelengths.
*Electron microscopes beat light microscopes because electrons have far shorter wavelengths.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why does a Blu-ray hold more than a DVD?
reveal: 405 nm versus 650 nm. A smaller diffraction-limited spot means denser data.
options: It uses a shorter-wavelength (blue-violet) laser, so pits can be smaller

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The four laws of thermodynamics
cards.cliff: A famous summary: you can't win, you can't break even, you can't quit
lines: Zeroth: things in equilibrium with a third thing are in equilibrium with each other (temperature makes sense).
First: energy is conserved. ΔU = Q − W.
Second: entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
Third: you can't reach absolute zero in finitely many steps.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: 1 kg of water warmed by 10°C. Heat needed? (c = 4,200 J/kg·K)
cards.cliff: Phase changes eat energy without changing temperature
reveal: Q = mcΔT.
Water's high heat capacity is why oceans moderate coastal climates.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Latent heat
lines: Melting ice at 0°C absorbs about 334 kJ/kg without warming at all.
Boiling water absorbs about 2,260 kJ/kg.
*That's why steam burns are worse than boiling-water burns.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Kelvin realised there's a bottom to temperature
lines: Gases shrink by a fixed fraction per degree. Extrapolate and their pressure hits zero at −273.15°C.
William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) built a temperature scale from that absolute zero in 1848.
*The coldest labs now reach billionths of a kelvin, but never zero.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Temperature is average kinetic energy
cards.cliff: pV = nRT falls out of collisions
lines: For a monatomic ideal gas: ⟨½mv²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT.
Air molecules at room temperature move at around 500 m/s.
*Pressure is the drumming of trillions of collisions on the walls.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Double the absolute temperature of a gas at fixed volume. Pressure…
reveal: pV = nRT, so p ∝ T.
Molecular speed rises by √2, and both collision rate and impulse per collision scale with speed.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Einstein used pollen jitter to prove atoms exist (1905)
lines: Robert Brown saw pollen particles jiggling in water in 1827, without explanation.
Einstein showed random molecular kicks predict a specific diffusion rate.
Jean Perrin measured it in 1908, giving Avogadro's number. *The last atom sceptics gave up.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Speeds follow the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution
lines: Few molecules are slow, few are very fast; most are in between.
The high-speed tail grows steeply with temperature.
*Reaction rates depend on that tail, which is why cooking is so sensitive to temperature.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: No engine can turn all heat into work
lines: A heat engine takes heat from a hot source, does work, and dumps the rest to a cold sink.
Carnot: max efficiency 1 − T_c/T_h.
*Car engines manage roughly 25–40%. Big combined-cycle power stations reach around 60%.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A heat pump moves heat from 0°C outside to a 20°C house. Ideal heat delivered per joule of work?
reveal: Ideal COP = T_h/(T_h − T_c) = 293/20 ≈ 15.
Real ones manage 3–4: still 3–4 J of heat per joule of electricity.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Melting 1 kg of ice at 0°C (L = 334 kJ/kg). Entropy change of the ice?
cards.cliff: Entropy and the arrow of time

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why the past is different from the future
lines: Microscopic laws (almost) don't care about the direction of time.
But the universe began in a low-entropy state, and entropy has been rising ever since.
*Eggs break and don't unbreak because there are vastly more broken arrangements.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Two postulates rebuild space and time
lines: 1. Physics is the same in every inertial frame.
2. Light's speed in vacuum is the same for every observer.
From these alone: time dilation, length contraction, and simultaneity that depends on who's watching.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: At v = 0.6c, the Lorentz factor γ is…

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The train and the platform
cards.cliff: Spacetime interval: what everyone agrees on
lines: Lightning strikes both ends of a moving train. The platform observer sees both flashes at once.
The train observer is moving toward one flash: they see that one first, and conclude the strikes weren't simultaneous.
*Both are right.* "At the same time" depends on the frame.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The spacetime interval is invariant
lines: $ s² = c²t² − x² − y² − z²
Observers disagree on times and distances but agree on s².
*Spacetime geometry with a minus sign.* It's why the travelling twin's path is shorter in proper time.
recall: What quantity do all inertial observers agree on between two events?
The spacetime interval c²Δt² − Δx² (− Δy² − Δz²)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A spaceship at 0.5c fires a probe forward at 0.5c relative to the ship. Speed relative to Earth?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The energy-momentum relation
cards.cliff: Nuclear binding energy is missing mass
lines: $ E² = (pc)² + (mc²)²
