At rest: E = mc². Massless particles: E = pc.
*Photons have momentum but no mass.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Fusing four hydrogen nuclei into helium-4 converts about what fraction of the mass to energy?
reveal: Helium-4 is about 0.7% lighter than four protons. The difference powers the Sun.
The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: PET scans detect annihilation
cards.cliff: Next: the birth of quantum theory
lines: A tracer releases positrons. Each annihilates with an electron, making two 511 keV gamma rays in opposite directions.
511 keV is exactly the electron's rest energy, mc².
*The scanner traces back the lines to find where the tracer collected.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Planck introduced quanta "as an act of desperation"
lines: Classical physics predicted a hot object should radiate infinite energy at short wavelengths: the ultraviolet catastrophe.
In 1900 Planck assumed energy comes in chunks E = hf, and the formula matched experiments perfectly.
*He later described it as an act of desperation.* He didn't believe the chunks were physically real.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Light of 4 eV photons hits a metal with work function 2.5 eV. Max kinetic energy of ejected electrons?
cards.cliff: Compton scattering: photons bounce like billiard balls
reveal: Einstein: KE_max = hf − φ.
Brighter light gives more electrons, not faster ones.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Compton scattering
lines: X-rays scattered off electrons come out with longer wavelengths.
Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cos θ): exactly what particle collisions with momentum p = h/λ predict.
*1923: the clinching evidence that photons carry momentum.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Bohr's model of hydrogen
cards.cliff: de Broglie: matter has a wavelength
lines: Electrons only allowed in orbits with angular momentum nħ.
Energies E_n = −13.6 eV/n². Jumps between them emit or absorb specific frequencies.
*Wrong picture, right energies.* It explained hydrogen's spectral lines exactly.
recall: Energy levels of hydrogen in the Bohr model?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: de Broglie wavelength of an electron with momentum p?
reveal: Confirmed in 1927 by Davisson and Germer, who saw electrons diffract off a nickel crystal.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Schrödinger equation
lines: $ iħ ∂ψ/∂t = −(ħ²/2m) ∂²ψ/∂x² + Vψ
ψ is a complex wavefunction. |ψ|² is a probability density (Born, 1926).
It's deterministic: ψ evolves smoothly. Randomness only enters at measurement.
recall: The probability density of finding the particle at x

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Stationary states
lines: If ψ = φ(x)e^(−iEt/ħ), the time-independent equation is Hφ = Eφ.
|ψ|² doesn't change in time: nothing observable moves.
*Atoms in stationary states don't radiate.* That fixes Bohr's problem.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: ψ(x) = A for 0 < x < 2 and zero elsewhere. What must A be?
cards.cliff: Expectation values are averages over many measurements
reveal: ∫|ψ|² dx = 2A² = 1.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Expectation values
lines: ⟨x⟩ = ∫ψ* x ψ dx. ⟨p⟩ = ∫ψ*(−iħ ∂/∂x)ψ dx.
They're the average results of measuring many identically prepared systems.
*Ehrenfest's theorem: expectation values obey Newton's laws* (approximately).

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Electron in a 1 nm infinite well. If the ground state energy is E₁, what is E₃?
cards.cliff: The quantum harmonic oscillator has equally spaced levels
reveal: Eₙ ∝ n².

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The quantum harmonic oscillator
lines: $ Eₙ = ħω(n + ½)
Equally spaced, and the lowest energy is ½ħω, not zero: *zero-point energy*.
Molecular vibrations, phonons and the electromagnetic field are all harmonic oscillators.
recall: Energy levels of the quantum harmonic oscillator?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Ladder operators
cards.cliff: Tunnelling depends exponentially on barrier width
lines: Define a and a† from x and p. Then H = ħω(a†a + ½).
a† raises the energy by ħω; a lowers it. a|0⟩ = 0.
*In quantum field theory, a† creates a particle.* The same algebra, promoted.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Doubling a barrier's width changes the tunnelling probability roughly how?
cards.cliff: STMs image individual atoms this way
reveal: Transmission ≈ e^(−2κL). Double L: square the factor.
That exponential sensitivity is what scanning tunnelling microscopes exploit.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The scanning tunnelling microscope
lines: A sharp tip hovers a few atoms above a surface. Electrons tunnel across the gap.
The current changes about 10× for every 0.1 nm, so it maps atomic bumps.
*1990: IBM spelled out "IBM" with 35 xenon atoms using one.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Four quantum numbers label every electron state
cards.cliff: Count the states in a shell
lines: n (energy shell), l = 0…n−1 (orbital angular momentum), m_l = −l…l, m_s = ±½.
l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are called s, p, d, f.
*The periodic table's shape is these rules plus Pauli exclusion.*
recall: Allowed values of l for a given n?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: How many electron states (including spin) in the n = 3 shell?
reveal: 2n² = 18: one 3s, three 3p, five 3d orbitals, two spins each.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Helium was discovered in the Sun before Earth
cards.cliff: Fine structure: relativity tweaks the levels
lines: 1868: a yellow spectral line in sunlight matched no known element.
It was named after Helios. Helium wasn't isolated on Earth until 1895.
*Spectroscopy tells us what stars are made of without visiting.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Fine structure and the 21 cm line
lines: Relativistic and spin-orbit corrections split levels by about α² ≈ 1/18,800 of the gross energies.
α ≈ 1/137 is the fine-structure constant.
Hyperfine splitting of hydrogen's ground state emits the 21 cm radio line that maps our galaxy's gas.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Stern–Gerlach: silver atoms split in two
lines: 1922: a beam of silver atoms through a non-uniform magnetic field split into two spots, not a smear.
Angular momentum along any axis comes in discrete values.
*Stern and Gerlach didn't know it, but they'd seen electron spin.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: A spin-½ particle is measured "up" along z, then measured along x. Probability of "up" along x?
reveal: Measuring along z again afterwards gives 50/50 too: the x measurement erased the z information.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: You can't know Lx and Lz together
lines: [Lx, Ly] = iħLz and cyclic.
So you can only know L² and one component simultaneously.
*That's why we label states by l and m_l but not by three components.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Fermions and bosons
cards.cliff: Fermions avoid each other, bosons pile up
lines: Swap two identical particles: the wavefunction picks up +1 (bosons) or −1 (fermions).
Half-integer spin: fermions (electrons, quarks). Integer spin: bosons (photons, gluons).
*Spin-statistics theorem: this link follows from relativity plus quantum mechanics.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Lasers are bosons piling into one state
cards.cliff: Neutron stars are held up by fermions refusing to share
lines: Photons are bosons: stimulated emission makes more photons copying an existing one.
Billions end up in the same mode: same frequency, phase and direction.
*Laser = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.* Einstein predicted the process in 1917.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Degeneracy pressure holds up dead stars
lines: White dwarfs are supported by electrons that can't be squeezed into the same states.
Above about 1.4 solar masses (Chandrasekhar's limit), electrons lose and the star collapses further.
*Neutron stars are held up mainly by neutron degeneracy pressure* plus nuclear forces.
recall: About 1.4 solar masses, the maximum mass of a white dwarf

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Radioactive decay
cards.cliff: Iron is the bottom of the energy valley
lines: Alpha: emits a helium nucleus. Beta: a neutron turns into a proton, emitting an electron and antineutrino. Gamma: a high-energy photon.
Each nucleus decays at random. Large numbers follow N = N₀e^(−λt).
Half-life t½ = ln 2/λ.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The binding energy curve
cards.cliff: Gold was forged in colliding neutron stars
lines: Binding energy per nucleon peaks around iron and nickel.
Fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both release energy.
*Stars build elements up to iron. Heavier ones come mostly from supernovae and neutron star mergers.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Much of the universe's gold came from neutron star collisions
lines: 2017: gravitational waves from merging neutron stars (GW170817) were seen along with light from the explosion.
The light showed signs of freshly made heavy elements.
*A substantial share of the gold in your jewellery was likely forged this way.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Lise Meitner explained fission on a winter walk
lines: 1938: Hahn and Strassmann found barium after bombarding uranium with neutrons.
Meitner and Frisch, walking in the snow in Sweden, worked out that the nucleus had split, using E = mc².
*Hahn got the 1944 Nobel Prize alone.* Meitner's role is now widely recognised.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Standard Model in one card
lines: Matter: 6 quarks and 6 leptons (electron, muon, tau and three neutrinos).
Forces: photon (EM), W and Z (weak), 8 gluons (strong).
The Higgs boson gives mass to the W, Z and fermions.
*Gravity isn't in it.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Confinement: why you can't pull quarks apart
lines: The strong force between quarks doesn't weaken with distance like gravity or EM does.
Pull two apart and the energy in the gluon field makes new quark–antiquark pairs.
*You get more hadrons, never a free quark.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: 48 years from prediction to discovery
cards.cliff: Neutrinos pass through you by the trillion
lines: 1964: Higgs and others predicted a field that gives particles mass, and a boson to go with it.
2012: CERN's ATLAS and CMS experiments found it at about 125 GeV.
*Higgs and Englert shared the 2013 Nobel Prize.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: About how many solar neutrinos pass through your thumbnail each second?
cards.cliff: Neutrinos change flavour as they travel
reveal: Roughly 6 × 10¹⁰ per cm² per second. Almost all pass straight through Earth too.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The solar neutrino problem
lines: From the 1960s, Ray Davis's detector found only about a third of the expected solar neutrinos.
The answer, confirmed around 2001: neutrinos oscillate between types, so detectors that see one type miss the others.
*Oscillation means neutrinos have mass,* which the original Standard Model didn't allow.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Boltzmann factor
cards.cliff: Equipartition: ½k_BT per quadratic degree of freedom
lines: At temperature T, a state with energy E is occupied with probability ∝ e^(−E/k_BT).
k_BT at room temperature ≈ 1/40 eV.
*That's why chemistry happens at room temperature but nuclear reactions don't.*
recall: k_BT at room temperature, in eV?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Equipartition: average energy of a diatomic gas molecule at room temperature?
reveal: 3 translational + 2 rotational degrees of freedom. Vibrations are "frozen out" at room temperature.
Classical physics couldn't explain the freezing. Quantum energy gaps do.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Universality at critical points
cards.cliff: Next: the formal machinery of quantum mechanics
lines: Near a critical point, a magnet and a liquid–gas system obey identical scaling laws.
Microscopic details wash out: only dimension and symmetry matter.
*Kenneth Wilson's renormalisation group explained this. Nobel Prize, 1982.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Bras, kets and inner products
lines: A state is a ket |ψ⟩: a vector in a Hilbert space.
⟨φ|ψ⟩ is the overlap. |⟨φ|ψ⟩|² is the probability of finding φ when in state ψ.
*Change basis and the vector stays the same; only its components change.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Observables and eigenvalues
cards.cliff: Time evolution is a unitary operator
lines: Each measurable quantity is a Hermitian operator A.
Possible outcomes are its eigenvalues (always real). After measuring, the state is the eigenvector.
Probability of outcome aᵢ: |⟨aᵢ|ψ⟩|².
recall: What are the possible results of measuring observable A?
The eigenvalues of the Hermitian operator A

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Two observables can be measured simultaneously with certainty when their operators…
cards.cliff: Density matrices handle uncertainty about the state itself
reveal: Commuting operators share a set of eigenvectors.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Density matrices
cards.cliff: Next: approximations when exact solutions fail
lines: ρ = Σpᵢ|ψᵢ⟩⟨ψᵢ| describes a statistical mix of states.
Pure state: Tr(ρ²) = 1. Mixed: less than 1.
*Entangle a qubit with its environment and it looks mixed: decoherence.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: First-order energy shift
lines: H = H₀ + λV, with V small.
$ Eₙ⁽¹⁾ = ⟨n|V|n⟩
The first-order shift is just the average of the perturbation in the unperturbed state.
recall: First-order energy correction in perturbation theory?

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Level repulsion
cards.cliff: Fermi's golden rule gives transition rates
lines: Second order: Eₙ⁽²⁾ = Σ |⟨m|V|n⟩|²/(Eₙ − Eₘ) over m ≠ n.
The ground state always goes down at second order.
*Coupled levels repel each other:* the avoided crossings seen all over molecular physics.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Fermi's golden rule
lines: $ Γ = (2π/ħ)|⟨f|V|i⟩|² ρ(E_f)
Transition rate = (coupling squared) × (density of final states).
*Radioactive decay rates, light absorption and scattering cross-sections all use it.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Rutherford found the nucleus by surprise
cards.cliff: The cross-section measures effective target size
lines: 1909: Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. A few bounced almost straight back.
Rutherford: "as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you".
*Atoms are almost entirely empty, with a tiny dense nucleus.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Cross-sections
cards.cliff: The Born approximation is a Fourier transform
lines: dσ/dΩ: how many particles scatter into a given direction, per unit incoming flux.
Rutherford: dσ/dΩ ∝ 1/sin⁴(θ/2).
Units of area: particle physicists use the barn, 10⁻²⁸ m² ("as big as a barn" for a nucleus).

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Born approximation
lines: For weak potentials, the scattering amplitude ∝ Fourier transform of V at momentum transfer q.
Scattering experiments literally measure the Fourier transform of the target.
*X-ray crystallography works the same way.* That's how DNA's double helix was read.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Particles are excitations of fields
lines: Every particle type is a ripple in its own field filling all of space.
Every electron is identical because they're all excitations of one electron field.
Creation and annihilation operators add and remove quanta.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Feynman diagrams
lines: Lines are particles; vertices are interactions with a coupling strength.
Each diagram is one term in a perturbation series.
*QED predicts the electron's magnetic moment to over 10 significant figures.* One of the most precise matches in science.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Virtual particles pop in and out of existence everywhere, as real particles briefly borrowing energy.
reveal: Virtual particles are internal lines in a perturbation calculation, not observable things.
The "borrowing energy" story is a popular metaphor, not what the maths says.
Vacuum effects like the Casimir force and the Lamb shift are real, though.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Renormalisation: infinities that cancel
lines: Early QED calculations gave infinite answers.
Feynman, Schwinger and Tomonaga showed the infinities can be absorbed into the measured mass and charge.
*Nobel Prize 1965.* Feynman still called it "a dippy process".

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Einstein's field equations
lines: $ G_μν = (8πG/c⁴) T_μν
Left: curvature of spacetime. Right: energy and momentum.
*"Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve."* (John Wheeler)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: 1919: the eclipse that made Einstein famous
lines: GR predicted starlight grazing the Sun bends by 1.75 arcseconds, twice the Newtonian value.
Eddington's expedition to Príncipe measured it during a total eclipse.
*Headlines worldwide: "Revolution in Science".*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Hubble's law: v = H₀d with H₀ ≈ 70 km/s per megaparsec. Recession speed of a galaxy 100 Mpc away?
cards.cliff: The cosmic microwave background is the Big Bang's afterglow
reveal: 1/H₀ gives roughly the age of the universe: about 14 billion years.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Two engineers mistook the Big Bang for pigeon droppings
cards.cliff: Most of the universe is stuff we can't see
lines: 1964: Penzias and Wilson found a persistent microwave hiss from every direction.
They cleaned pigeon droppings out of their antenna. The hiss stayed.
*It was the 2.7 K afterglow of the early universe. Nobel Prize, 1978.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Dark matter and dark energy
cards.cliff: Physics 3 done. That's the whole physics track
lines: Ordinary matter: about 5% of the universe's energy. Dark matter: about 27%. Dark energy: about 68%.
Dark matter shows up in galaxy rotation and gravitational lensing.
Dark energy drives the accelerating expansion, discovered in 1998 using supernovae.

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Milgram: ordinary people, lethal shocks
cards.cliff: Asch showed people deny their own eyes
lines: 1961: volunteers were told to give increasing electric shocks to a "learner" who got answers wrong. The shocks were fake; the screams were acted.
In the best-known version, about 65% went all the way to the maximum 450 volts when calmly told to continue.
*Later analyses note many participants doubted the shocks were real.* The core finding still shook psychology.

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Asch's line experiment
cards.cliff: The Stanford prison experiment is shakier than its fame
lines: 1951: participants judged which of three lines matched a reference line. The answer was obvious.
Planted actors all gave the same wrong answer first.
*About three-quarters of participants conformed at least once.* But most answers were still correct.

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The Stanford Prison Experiment proved that ordinary people turn cruel when given power.
cards.cliff: The marshmallow test has been reinterpreted
reveal: Recordings and interviews later showed guards were coached toward toughness, and some prisoners said they were acting.
It was never published as a peer-reviewed study in the usual way and can't support strong conclusions.

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The marshmallow test, revisited
lines: 1970s: children who waited longer for a second marshmallow later did better on various life measures.
A larger 2018 replication found the link shrank a lot once family background and early ability were accounted for.
*Waiting may partly reflect whether a child has reason to trust that the reward will come.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The bystander effect
lines: People are less likely to help when others are present: responsibility diffuses.
The famous 1964 Kitty Genovese story ("38 witnesses did nothing") was heavily exaggerated by the press.
*A 2019 study of real CCTV found someone intervened in about 90% of public conflicts.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The habit loop
cards.cliff: How long does a habit take?
lines: Cue → routine → reward. Repeat enough and the routine becomes automatic.
Habits shift control from deliberate goal-directed brain systems toward automatic ones.
*That's why you can drive home and not remember the journey.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: It takes 21 days to form a habit.
reveal: The 21-day figure traces back loosely to a 1960 self-help book about plastic surgery patients.
A 2009 study found new habits took anywhere from 18 to 254 days, with a median around 66.

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Variable rewards: the slot-machine schedule
cards.cliff: Dopamine is about wanting, not liking
lines: Skinner found behaviour rewarded on an unpredictable schedule is the hardest to extinguish.
Pigeons pecked hundreds of times for an occasional, random reward.
*It's the engine behind slot machines, social feeds, and the mystery drops in this app.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Dopamine signals surprise, not pleasure
lines: Dopamine neurons fire most for unexpected rewards, less for expected ones, and dip when an expected reward doesn't come.
This "reward prediction error" is how the brain learns what to expect.
*It's the same maths as reinforcement learning in AI.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Rewards can kill interest
lines: 1973: children who loved drawing were promised a reward for it. Later they drew less in free time than children who weren't.
Expected external rewards can crowd out intrinsic motivation (the overjustification effect).
*Unexpected rewards don't seem to do the same damage.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The goal gradient effect
lines: People speed up as they get closer to a goal: rats run faster near the food, coffee-card holders buy faster near the free drink.
A card with 12 stamps and 2 pre-filled gets completed faster than a card with 10 and none filled.
*Same work remaining; the head start changes behaviour.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Self-determination theory says intrinsic motivation needs three things. Which is NOT one of them?
cards.cliff: Flow is the sweet spot of challenge
reveal: Deci and Ryan: autonomy (choice), competence (mastery), relatedness (connection).

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Flow
lines: Csikszentmihalyi: deep absorption when challenge matches skill.
Too easy: boredom. Too hard: anxiety. Just right: time disappears.
*Good games and good teachers keep you right on that edge.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Sleep cycles last about 90 minutes
lines: Light sleep, deep sleep, then REM (when most vivid dreaming happens).
Deep sleep dominates early in the night, REM later.
*Waking from deep sleep is what makes you groggy.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The glymphatic system
lines: 2013 mouse studies found the spaces between brain cells widen during sleep, letting fluid flush out waste.
Waste products include amyloid-beta, linked to Alzheimer's disease.
*Research in humans is ongoing, but it's one more reason sleep matters.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Randy Gardner stayed awake for 11 days
cards.cliff: Teenagers' clocks really do shift later
lines: 1964: a 17-year-old stayed awake for about 264 hours for a science fair.
He developed mood changes, memory problems and hallucinations, but recovered after sleeping.
*Guinness stopped accepting the record because it's dangerous.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Why teenagers can't get up
lines: Puberty shifts the body clock later: melatonin is released later in the evening.
Some schools that moved start times later saw better attendance and sleep.
*It's biology, not just laziness.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The dress: blue and black, or white and gold?
cards.cliff: You have a blind spot in each eye
lines: 2015: a photo of a dress split the internet.
People's brains made different assumptions about the lighting: shadow (so it's white/gold) or warm light (so it's blue/black).
*The real dress was blue and black.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Your blind spot
lines: Where the optic nerve leaves the retina there are no light receptors.
Your brain fills in the gap using the surroundings, so you never notice.
*Close one eye and you can make a dot on a page vanish.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Swapping a person mid-conversation
lines: 1998: an experimenter asked strangers for directions. Mid-conversation, workers carrying a door passed between them, and a different person took the asker's place.
About half of the strangers didn't notice.
*We see far less than we think we do.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: In the famous "invisible gorilla" study, what fraction of viewers missed the gorilla?
reveal: Viewers counting basketball passes often failed to see a person in a gorilla suit walk through (Simons & Chabris, 1999).

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The fundamental attribution error
lines: Someone cuts you up in traffic: they're a jerk. You cut someone up: you were late for something important.
We explain others' behaviour by character, our own by circumstance.
*Cultures vary in how strongly they do this.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The spotlight effect
lines: Students wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half of the room noticed. Only about a quarter did.
People think others notice them far more than they do.
*Everyone else is busy worrying about themselves.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Dunbar's number
lines: Robin Dunbar proposed humans can maintain about 150 stable relationships, based on primate brain sizes.
Layers: about 5 intimate, 15 close, 50 good friends, 150 meaningful contacts.
*Critics question how precise the number is, but the layered pattern shows up in many datasets.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: In 2015, most famous psychology results failed to replicate
lines: The Open Science Collaboration re-ran 100 published psychology studies.
About 36% of the replications found statistically significant results, compared with 97% of the originals.
*Effect sizes were on average about half as large.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Standing in a "power pose" for two minutes raises testosterone and lowers stress hormones.
reveal: The original 2010 hormone results didn't replicate in larger studies.
One co-author later publicly said she no longer believed the effect was real.

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: How false findings get published
cards.cliff: Ego depletion took a hit too
lines: Small samples, many measured outcomes, and flexible analysis let random noise look significant.
Journals favoured surprising positive results.
*Fixes: pre-registration, larger samples, sharing data.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Willpower as a battery: the ego depletion debate
lines: Studies suggested self-control uses up a limited resource, even that sugar drinks restored it.
A large 2016 multi-lab replication found an effect close to zero.
*The debate continues, but the simple "battery" story is in doubt.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Stress isn't always bad
lines: Short bursts of stress sharpen focus and memory (the Yerkes–Dodson inverted U).
Chronic stress, lasting weeks or months, harms sleep, immunity and memory.
*Some studies suggest that viewing stress as useful can change how the body responds.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Affect labelling
lines: Putting feelings into words ("I feel anxious") reduces amygdala activity in brain scans.
It's one reason journaling and talking help.
*"Name it to tame it."*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: What did a large 2021 study find about income and happiness?
reveal: Killingsworth (2021) found experienced well-being kept rising with income.
A 2023 follow-up with Kahneman found the plateau held only for the unhappiest group.
options: Well-being kept rising with income, with no plateau at $75,000
Money has no link to happiness

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The best study techniques, ranked
lines: A 2013 review (Dunlosky et al.) rated practice testing and spaced practice as the most effective.
Highlighting, re-reading and summarising rated low.
*Feeling productive and being productive are different things.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Interleave your practice
lines: Mixing different problem types feels harder than doing one type in a block.
But it trains you to choose the method, which is what exams test.
*In one study, interleaved maths practice led to much higher test scores a week later.*
recall: Why does interleaving help exam performance?
It trains you to identify which method a problem needs, not just to execute one method

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: The Feynman technique
lines: Explain the idea in simple words as if teaching a child.
Where you get stuck or use jargon, you've found a gap. Go back and learn it.
*Teaching is one of the best ways to learn.*

cards.subject: psych
cards.title: Which study habit is LEAST supported by evidence?
reveal: Studies matching teaching to learning styles haven't found benefits.
The other three are among the best-supported techniques.
options: Studying in your preferred "learning style" (visual, auditory…)

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Sun holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass
lines: Jupiter holds most of the rest: more than twice all the other planets combined.
The centre of mass of the Sun and Jupiter lies just outside the Sun's surface.
*So the Sun wobbles, which is one way we detect planets around other stars.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Which planet has the hottest surface?
cards.cliff: A day on Venus is longer than its year
reveal: About 465°C, hot enough to melt lead, from a runaway greenhouse effect under thick CO₂.
Mercury is closer to the Sun but has no atmosphere to trap heat.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Venus spins backwards, very slowly
lines: It rotates once every 243 Earth days, in the opposite direction to most planets.
It orbits the Sun in 225 days.
*From the surface, the Sun would rise in the west.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Saturn's average density is less than water's.
reveal: About 0.69 g/cm³. In a big enough bathtub, it would (theoretically) float.
Its rings are mostly water ice, and less than 1 km thick in most places.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Why Pluto was demoted
cards.cliff: Mars has the tallest volcano known
lines: 2005: Eris was found, about as big as Pluto, with more surely to come.
The IAU defined a planet in 2006: it must have cleared its orbital neighbourhood. Pluto hasn't.
*New Horizons flew past in 2015 and found mountains of water ice and glaciers of nitrogen.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Olympus Mons on Mars is about how tall?
cards.cliff: Europa may have more water than Earth
reveal: Roughly two and a half times Everest's height above sea level.
Mars's low gravity and lack of moving plates let lava pile up in one place.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Ocean moons
lines: Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's Enceladus have liquid water oceans under ice.
Enceladus shoots geysers of water into space; Cassini flew through them.
*They're among the best places to look for life beyond Earth.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Stars are fusion reactors held together by gravity
lines: Gravity squeezes inward; pressure from fusion heat pushes outward.
The Sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen per second.
*It has enough fuel for about another 5 billion years.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Which lives longest?
cards.cliff: Light from the Sun's core takes ages to escape
reveal: Red dwarfs burn so slowly they can last trillions of years: longer than the universe has existed.
Massive stars burn out in a few million years.
options: A red dwarf with 0.2 solar masses
A blue giant with 20 solar masses
They all live about 10 billion years

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Sunlight is old
lines: A photon made in the Sun's core is absorbed and re-emitted countless times.
It takes on the order of 100,000 years (estimates vary widely) to random-walk out.
*Then just 8 minutes to reach you.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Where the elements came from
lines: Hydrogen and most helium: the Big Bang.
Carbon, oxygen and up to iron: fusion in stars.
*Heavier elements: supernovae and neutron star mergers.* The calcium in your bones was made in stars.

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Great Dimming of Betelgeuse
lines: Late 2019, the red supergiant Betelgeuse dimmed dramatically. People wondered if it was about to explode.
Observations showed a dust cloud from material it had ejected.
*It will go supernova someday, but probably not for about 100,000 years.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Milky Way has 100–400 billion stars
lines: We're about 26,000 light-years from its centre, in a spiral arm.
At its centre is a black hole of about 4 million solar masses: Sagittarius A*.
*Its image was released in 2022 by the Event Horizon Telescope.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Andromeda is heading our way
lines: The Andromeda galaxy approaches at about 110 km/s.
In roughly 4–5 billion years, the two galaxies will merge.
*Stars are so far apart that almost none will actually collide.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Before 1924, the Milky Way was thought to be the whole universe
lines: Spiral "nebulae" were debated: gas clouds within our galaxy, or galaxies of their own?
Edwin Hubble measured Cepheid variable stars in Andromeda and showed it was far outside the Milky Way.
*The universe got unimaginably bigger overnight.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Henrietta Leavitt's ruler for the universe
lines: Working at Harvard as a "computer" in the 1900s–1910s, she found Cepheid stars' brightness pulses relate to their true luminosity.
That made them standard candles for measuring distance.
*Hubble's discoveries were built on her law.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Over 5,000 exoplanets are confirmed
lines: The first around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, was found in 1995: a gas giant orbiting in 4 days.
Most are found by the transit method: a tiny dip as a planet crosses its star.
*Mayor and Queloz won the 2019 Nobel Prize for 51 Peg b.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The habitable zone
lines: The range of distances where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface.
TRAPPIST-1, a red dwarf 40 light-years away, has seven Earth-sized planets, several in this zone.
*Habitable zone doesn't mean inhabited.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The James Webb telescope reads exoplanet atmospheres
lines: As a planet transits, starlight filters through its atmosphere. Molecules absorb specific wavelengths.
JWST detected carbon dioxide in an exoplanet atmosphere in 2022.
*We're starting to check alien skies for the chemistry of life.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Fermi paradox: where is everybody?
lines: Billions of stars, many with planets, and billions of years for civilisations to spread.
Yet no evidence of anyone.
*Possible answers: life is rare, civilisations self-destruct, they're quiet, or we're not looking right.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Voyager carries a golden record
lines: Voyager 1 and 2, launched in 1977, each carry a gold-plated record of sounds and images from Earth.
Greetings in 55 languages, music from Bach to Chuck Berry, and a diagram showing how to play it.
*Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: The Pale Blue Dot
cards.cliff: Hubble launched with a blurry mirror
lines: 1990: Carl Sagan persuaded NASA to turn Voyager 1's camera back toward Earth from about 6 billion km away.
Earth appears as a speck less than a pixel wide in a sunbeam.
*"That's here. That's home. That's us."*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Hubble was launched short-sighted
lines: 1990: Hubble's main mirror had been ground to the wrong shape by about 2 micrometres.
Astronauts installed corrective optics in 1993, like glasses for a telescope.
*It went on to become one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built.*

cards.subject: physics
cards.title: Opportunity was designed to last 90 Martian days. How long did it actually operate?
reveal: It landed in 2004 and last communicated in 2018, before a dust storm covered its solar panels.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes
lines: Suppose there were finitely many. Multiply them all and add 1.
The new number isn't divisible by any prime on the list, so the list was incomplete.
*About 2,300 years old and still one of the most elegant proofs.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The prime number theorem
lines: Near a large number N, about 1 in every ln N numbers is prime.
Near a million, about 1 in 14. Near a billion, about 1 in 21.
*Gauss guessed this as a teenager from tables.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Most of the largest known primes are of what form?
reveal: There's a fast test for them (Lucas–Lehmer). The record has over 41 million digits.
Found by the volunteer GIMPS project.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Twin primes and the gap problem
lines: Twin primes differ by 2: (11, 13), (17, 19), (41, 43).
Are there infinitely many? Unknown.
*2013: Yitang Zhang proved there are infinitely many prime pairs within 70 million of each other. That bound has since been cut to 246.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Goldbach's conjecture
lines: Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes: 4 = 2 + 2, 28 = 11 + 17.
Checked by computer up to 4 × 10¹⁸.
*Still unproved since 1742.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Your bank relies on prime numbers
lines: Encryption like RSA uses the product of two huge primes.
Multiplying them is fast; finding them from the product is believed to be infeasible for large enough numbers.
*Ulam spiral: plot integers in a square spiral and the primes form strange diagonal lines.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The Collatz conjecture
lines: Take any positive integer. If even, halve it. If odd, triple it and add 1. Repeat.
It always seems to reach 1. 27 takes 111 steps and climbs to 9,232 first.
*Erdős: "Mathematics may not be ready for such problems."*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Seven million-dollar problems
lines: In 2000 the Clay Institute offered $1 million each for seven problems, including P vs NP and the Riemann hypothesis.
One has been solved: the Poincaré conjecture.
*Grigori Perelman solved it, then turned down both the prize and the Fields Medal.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The moving sofa problem
lines: What's the largest area of sofa you can move around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1?
Gerver's shape (1992) gives about 2.2195.
*A proof that it's optimal was announced in 2024 and is being checked.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The happy ending problem
lines: Esther Klein showed that any 5 points in general position include 4 forming a convex quadrilateral.
Erdős and Szekeres generalised it; Klein and Szekeres then married.
*Erdős named it the "happy ending problem".*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: π is irrational and transcendental
lines: Lambert proved it irrational in 1761. Lindemann proved it transcendental in 1882.
That settled an ancient question: you can't square the circle with ruler and compass.
*Over 100 trillion digits have now been computed.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The secretary problem and 1/e
lines: Interviewing candidates one at a time, you must accept or reject each on the spot.
Best strategy: reject the first 37% (1/e), then take the first who beats them all.
*You pick the best candidate about 37% of the time.* Some apply it to dating, half-jokingly.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Kaprekar's constant, 6174
lines: Take any four-digit number with at least two different digits. Arrange digits high to low, then low to high, subtract.
Repeat. You always reach 6174 within seven steps.

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Graham's number
lines: An upper bound from a 1970s problem about colouring hypercubes. It's so large the observable universe can't hold its digits.
It needs special notation (Knuth's up-arrows) even to describe.
*Yet we know its last digits: it ends in …7262464195387.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: 1729: "a very interesting number"
lines: Hardy visited Ramanujan in hospital in a taxi numbered 1729 and called it dull.
Ramanujan replied it's the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two ways: 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.
*Numbers like it are now called taxicab numbers.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: A Möbius strip has one side and one edge
cards.cliff: A coffee mug is a doughnut
lines: Take a strip of paper, give it a half-twist, tape the ends.
Draw a line along the middle: it covers both "sides" before returning.
*Cut it along the middle and it stays in one piece, twice as long.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: To a topologist, a mug is a doughnut
cards.cliff: The four colour theorem needed a computer
lines: Topology ignores stretching and bending, but not tearing or gluing.
A mug and a doughnut each have exactly one hole, so they're equivalent.
*A topologist can't tell their coffee mug from their breakfast.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: The four colour theorem
lines: Any map can be coloured with four colours so no neighbouring regions match.
Proved in 1976 by Appel and Haken with over 1,000 hours of computer checking.
*The first major theorem proved with essential computer help; many mathematicians were uneasy.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: Banach–Tarski: one ball becomes two
lines: Using the axiom of choice, a solid ball can be cut into finitely many pieces and reassembled into two balls the same size as the original.
The pieces are so bizarre they have no well-defined volume.
*It's a theorem, not a trick. Physical matter can't be cut that way.*

cards.subject: maths
cards.title: You can turn a sphere inside out
lines: Smale proved in 1957 that a sphere can be everted (turned inside out) if surfaces may pass through themselves, without creases.
Nobody could picture how at first.
*Bernard Morin, who was blind, helped work out an explicit way.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: The central limit theorem
lines: Add up lots of independent random things and the total tends toward a bell curve, whatever the individual distributions look like.
That's why heights, measurement errors and exam totals are roughly normal.
*Dice: one die is flat; the sum of ten dice is nearly a perfect bell.*
recall: What does the central limit theorem say?
Sums (or averages) of many independent random variables tend toward a normal distribution

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: In a normal distribution, roughly what fraction lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean?
reveal: 68% within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ.

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Fat tails: when the bell curve lies
cards.cliff: The Poisson distribution counts rare events
lines: Wealth, city sizes, earthquake energies and stock crashes follow heavy-tailed distributions.
Extreme events are far more common than a normal curve predicts.
*Under a normal model, a daily crash like October 1987 would be essentially impossible.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Horse kicks and the Poisson distribution
lines: Ladislaus Bortkiewicz (1898) counted Prussian cavalry soldiers killed by horse kicks per corps per year.
The counts fitted a Poisson distribution almost perfectly.
*Rare, independent events in a fixed window: calls to a call centre, typos per page, goals in a match.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: What a p-value actually means
cards.cliff: Run enough tests and something will be "significant"
lines: p = probability of seeing data at least this extreme *if the null hypothesis were true*.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
p < 0.05 is a convention from Fisher, not a law of nature.
recall: What does a p-value of 0.03 mean?
If there were no real effect, data this extreme would occur about 3% of the time

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Jelly beans cause acne (in 1 of 20 colours)
lines: Test 20 jelly bean colours for a link to acne at p < 0.05.
By chance alone, you'd expect about one "significant" result.
*Headline: GREEN JELLY BEANS LINKED TO ACNE.* That's the multiple comparisons problem (a famous xkcd).

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Significant doesn't mean big
lines: With a million participants, a drug that lowers blood pressure by 0.1 mmHg can be "highly significant".
That's real but medically meaningless.
*Always ask for the effect size.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Confidence intervals, carefully
lines: A 95% CI method captures the true value in 95% of repeated experiments.
For one computed interval, it's not quite "95% chance the true value is inside" (that's a Bayesian credible interval).
*Most scientists blur the two in everyday speech.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Ice cream sales predict drownings
cards.cliff: Simpson's paradox can reverse a trend
lines: Both rise in summer. Neither causes the other.
A third factor (hot weather) drives both: a confounder.
*Spurious correlations are everywhere once you look.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Simpson's paradox at Berkeley, 1973
lines: Overall, men were admitted to Berkeley's graduate school at a higher rate than women.
Department by department, women were admitted at equal or higher rates in most.
*Women had applied more to competitive departments with low admission rates for everyone.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Why randomised controlled trials work
lines: Randomly assigning treatment balances every confounder, known and unknown, on average.
That's why RCTs are the gold standard for causation.
*James Lind's 1747 scurvy trial on a ship was an early controlled comparison: citrus cured it.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Abraham Wald and the bullet holes
lines: WWII: planes returning from missions had bullet holes clustered on wings and fuselage. Engineers proposed armouring those spots.
Statistician Abraham Wald said armour the places with *no* holes: planes hit there didn't come back.
*You're only seeing the survivors.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Expected value: the long-run average
lines: EV = Σ (probability × payoff).
A fair coin paying £2 on heads and £0 on tails has EV £1.
*Casinos design every game so the EV is in their favour.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: European roulette: £1 on red pays £1 profit. Expected value per bet?
reveal: American roulette has an extra 00 slot, doubling the edge to about 5.3%.

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: UK Lotto odds
lines: Matching all 6 numbers from 59: 1 in about 45 million.
Roughly half the ticket money goes back as prizes; the rest to good causes, tax and operating costs.
*Expected return is about 50p per £1.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: The St Petersburg paradox
lines: A coin is flipped until heads. If heads first appears on flip n, you win £2ⁿ.
Expected value: ½·2 + ¼·4 + ⅛·8 + … = 1 + 1 + 1 + … = infinite.
*Yet nobody would pay much to play.* Daniel Bernoulli (1738) proposed utility grows like the log of wealth.

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Kelly betting
lines: For a repeated bet, the Kelly fraction maximises long-run growth: f = edge / odds.
Betting more than Kelly increases the risk of ruin without increasing growth.
*Edward Thorp used it in blackjack and later on Wall Street.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Bayes' theorem in words
lines: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.
Start with what you believed, weight by how well each hypothesis predicts the evidence.
*Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, because their prior is low.*
recall: Posterior is proportional to likelihood × prior

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Sally Clark and the prosecutor's fallacy
cards.cliff: Bayesian search found a lost submarine
lines: 1999: Sally Clark was convicted of murdering her two babies, partly on a claim that two cot deaths in one family had odds of 1 in 73 million.
That number wrongly assumed the deaths were independent, and the odds of innocence were confused with the odds of the evidence.
*Her conviction was overturned in 2003.* The Royal Statistical Society publicly criticised the statistics.

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Bayesian search
lines: 1968: the US submarine Scorpion vanished in the Atlantic.
Searchers built a probability map from expert scenarios and updated it as areas were searched.
*The wreck was found about 200 m from the predicted highest-probability cell.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: The poll that predicted the wrong US president, 1936
lines: The Literary Digest polled about 2.4 million people and predicted Alf Landon would beat Roosevelt.
Its mailing lists came largely from telephone directories and car registrations: wealthier voters in the Depression.
*Roosevelt won in a landslide. George Gallup, with a much smaller but more representative sample, called it right.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: A well-chosen random sample of 1,000 people gives a margin of error of roughly…
reveal: About 1/√n ≈ 1/31.6 ≈ 3%. Population size barely matters.

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Question wording changes results
lines: Asking whether to "forbid" something gets different answers from asking whether to "not allow" it, even though they mean the same.
Order matters too: earlier questions prime later ones.
*Always ask to see the exact question before trusting a poll.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Big-O: how running time grows
lines: O(1): constant. O(log n): binary search. O(n): reading a list. O(n log n): good sorting. O(n²): comparing every pair.
For a million items, n² is a trillion steps; n log n is about 20 million.
*Choosing the right algorithm beats buying a faster computer.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Which sorting algorithm is O(n log n) in the worst case?
cards.cliff: Dijkstra found shortest paths in 20 minutes
reveal: Merge sort always splits in half and merges. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) worst case.

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Dijkstra designed his algorithm at a café
cards.cliff: Some problems have no fast solution (we think)
lines: 1956: Edsger Dijkstra designed his shortest-path algorithm in about 20 minutes, without pen and paper, while shopping in Amsterdam.
It's still the core of route-finding in maps and network routing.
*He said not having a pencil forced him to keep it simple.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: The travelling salesman problem
lines: Find the shortest route visiting every city once.
Checking all routes for 20 cities: about 6 × 10¹⁶ possibilities.
*Nobody knows a fast exact algorithm, but heuristics get within a few percent.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Hash tables: instant lookup
lines: Turn a key into an array index with a hash function. Lookup is O(1) on average.
Collisions happen when two keys land in the same slot; good designs handle them.
*Python dictionaries, JavaScript objects and database indexes rely on them.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Stacks and queues
lines: Stack: last in, first out. Like a pile of plates. Your browser's back button.
Queue: first in, first out. Like a supermarket line. Your printer's jobs.
*Function calls use a stack: that's what a "stack overflow" overflows.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: A balanced binary search tree with a million items needs about how many comparisons to find one?

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Graphs: nodes and edges
lines: Social networks, road maps, the web, molecules: all graphs.
Google's original PageRank ranked pages by treating links as votes, weighted by the voter's own rank.
*It's the stationary distribution of a random web surfer.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Packets, not pipes
cards.cliff: DNS is the internet's phone book
lines: Data is chopped into packets, each routed independently, possibly by different paths.
TCP reassembles them in order and resends lost ones.
*Designed so the network keeps working when parts fail.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: DNS turns names into addresses
cards.cliff: The first message on the internet
lines: You type a domain name; DNS servers translate it into an IP address.
Results are cached at many levels so lookups are fast.
*When DNS fails, sites seem down even though they're running fine.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: The first message on ARPANET was "LO"
lines: 29 October 1969: a UCLA student tried to log in to a computer at Stanford by typing "LOGIN".
The system crashed after "LO".
*So the internet's first word was, fittingly, "lo".*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: What the padlock in your browser means
lines: HTTPS encrypts traffic between you and the site using TLS.
A certificate, signed by a trusted authority, proves the site is who it claims.
*It doesn't mean the site is trustworthy, only that the connection is private.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Public-key cryptography
cards.cliff: RSA relies on factoring being hard
lines: You publish a public key; anyone can encrypt messages to you with it.
Only your private key can decrypt them.
*It solved the ancient problem of sharing a secret key with a stranger.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: RSA in one card
cards.cliff: GCHQ invented it first, in secret
lines: Multiply two huge primes: easy. Factor the product back: extremely hard.
Public key: the product and an exponent. Private key: derived from the primes.
*A large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could break it,* which is why "post-quantum" cryptography is being rolled out.

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: British spies invented public-key crypto years before it went public
lines: James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson at GCHQ developed it between 1970 and 1974.
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman published RSA independently in 1977.
*GCHQ's work was declassified only in 1997.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: The one-time pad
lines: XOR your message with a truly random key as long as the message, used once.
Shannon proved in 1949 that this is perfectly secure.
*The catch: you need to share as much key as message, securely, in advance.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Machine learning: learning from examples
cards.cliff: Neural networks are layers of weighted sums
lines: Instead of writing rules, you show a model lots of labelled examples and let it adjust its parameters.
Training minimises a loss function by gradient descent.
*Overfitting: memorising the training data instead of learning the pattern.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: A neural network in one card
cards.cliff: Language models predict the next token
lines: Each neuron computes a weighted sum of inputs and applies a non-linear function.
Stack layers and the network can approximate almost any function (the universal approximation theorem).
*Backpropagation computes how each weight should change, using the chain rule.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: How large language models are trained
lines: Pretraining: predict the next token across a vast amount of text.
Then fine-tuning, including training on human feedback, shapes them into assistants.
*Their knowledge comes from patterns in text, which is why they can state wrong things confidently.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Turing's imitation game, 1950
lines: Turing proposed replacing "can machines think?" with: can a machine's text conversation be told apart from a human's?
He predicted that by 2000 machines would fool average interrogators 30% of the time after five minutes.
*He also anticipated many modern objections to machine intelligence.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Shannon defined information in 1948
lines: Information is surprise: a likely event tells you little, an unlikely one tells you a lot.
Entropy H = −Σ p log₂ p measures average surprise in bits.
*A fair coin flip carries exactly 1 bit.*
recall: What is the entropy of a fair coin flip?

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Why you can't compress random data
cards.cliff: Error correction lets space probes talk
lines: Shannon's source coding theorem: you can't losslessly compress below the entropy.
ZIP files shrink text because English is highly predictable.
*Compress an already-compressed file and it barely changes.*

cards.subject: cs
cards.title: Voyager still phones home with error-correcting codes
lines: Voyager's transmitter puts out about 20 watts, from over 20 billion km away.
Error-correcting codes add structured redundancy so corrupted bits can be repaired.
*Your phone, QR codes and CDs use the same idea.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Straw man
lines: Misrepresenting someone's argument as a weaker version, then attacking that.
"We should reduce car use in the city centre." "So you want to ban all cars?"
*Fix: restate their view in a form they'd agree with before replying (steelmanning).*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Ad hominem
lines: Attacking the person instead of the argument.
"Why listen to her climate views? She flies on holiday."
*Hypocrisy doesn't make an argument false.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: "You're either with us or against us." Which fallacy?
reveal: Presenting two options when more exist.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Slippery slope
lines: Claiming one step will inevitably lead to an extreme outcome, without showing the chain.
Some slopes are real. The fallacy is assuming the slide without evidence.
*Ask: what stops each step from happening?*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: "This book is true because it says it is." Which fallacy?
reveal: The conclusion is assumed in the premise.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: No true Scotsman
lines: "No Scotsman puts sugar on porridge." "My uncle's Scottish and does." "Well, no *true* Scotsman does."
Redefining terms to dodge a counterexample.
*Coined by philosopher Antony Flew.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: If something is natural, it must be good for you.
reveal: Arsenic, hemlock and botulinum toxin are natural.
Many synthetic medicines save lives. Natural vs artificial says little about safety.

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
lines: "After this, therefore because of this."
I wore my lucky socks and we won. So the socks helped.
*Sequence isn't causation.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Russell's teapot
lines: Bertrand Russell: if he claimed a tiny china teapot orbits the Sun between Earth and Mars, too small to see, no one could disprove it.
That doesn't oblige anyone to believe it.
*The burden of proof lies with the person making the claim.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Occam's razor
lines: When two explanations fit the evidence, prefer the one that assumes less.
It's a rule of thumb, not a law: sometimes the truth is complicated.
*Named after William of Ockham, a 14th-century friar.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Hanlon's razor
lines: Never attribute to malice what is adequately explained by incompetence (or error).
Most bad outcomes are mistakes, not plots.
*It's useful for keeping relationships and organisations sane.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Chesterton's fence
lines: You find a fence across a road and can't see why it's there.
Don't remove it until you know why it was put up.
*Rules and traditions often encode reasons we've forgotten.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Steelmanning
lines: Build the strongest version of the opposing argument before disagreeing.
If you can't, you probably don't understand the disagreement yet.
*Daniel Dennett's rules for criticism start with restating the other view so well they'd thank you.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Inversion: think backwards
lines: Instead of asking how to succeed, ask how you'd guarantee failure, then avoid that.
Mathematician Carl Jacobi: "Invert, always invert."
*Charlie Munger made it a favourite investing tool.*

cards.subject: philo
cards.title: Start with the base rate
lines: How likely is this kind of thing in general, before the specific details?
A detailed story about a shy, tidy person makes "librarian" feel likely, but there are many more salespeople.
*Kahneman and Tversky showed people ignore base rates constantly.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Relative risk vs absolute risk
lines: "Doubles your risk!" can mean going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000.
Always ask: double of what?
*Absolute numbers tell you whether to care.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: Truncated axes
lines: Start a bar chart's y-axis at 95 instead of 0 and a 2% difference looks enormous.
Check where the axis starts.
*Dual axes on one chart can create correlations from nothing.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: "Why most published research findings are false"
lines: John Ioannidis's 2005 paper argued that small studies, small effects, flexible designs and hot topics make false positives common.
It became one of the most-downloaded papers in its journal's history.
*Replication matters more than any single striking study.*

cards.subject: stats
cards.title: A survey reports "47.32% of people prefer tea". What should you ask first?
reveal: Two decimals look rigorous but say nothing about sampling error or bias.
options: How many people were asked, and how were they chosen?
